questions.prompt: You open your eyes in the morning. What do you do first?

options.label: Open the curtains or drink some water

insight.reveal: You look after the basics before the world gets a say. Chances are there's a water bottle on your desk and a spare snack in your bag. On a long day out, it's you who notices that everyone forgot to eat.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, notice the very first thought you have before you move. Just notice it.

options.label: Reach for my phone

insight.reveal: Other people's news reaches you before your own thoughts do. You know what happened overnight before you've brushed your teeth, and you reply fast all day. Your best ideas tend to wait for the shower or a walk, once the screen is out of reach.
insight.step: Tomorrow, wait until your feet touch the floor before you touch your phone.

options.label: Snooze, then snooze again

insight.reveal: Every snooze is a little bargain: comfort now, rush later. You probably strike the same deal elsewhere, like 'I'll reply later' to a message you actually want to answer. The upside is real: when the clock is tight, you're out the door faster than anyone.
insight.step: Next time your alarm rings, sit up before you decide anything. See if the bargain feels different sitting up.

options.label: Lie still and replay yesterday or worry about today

insight.reveal: Your mind wakes up before your body does. It tends to replay small moments, like how a comment landed or whether a message sounded cold, more than big problems. That same care makes you thoughtful with people, and the loop usually quiets once your hands are busy.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make problems harder to solve.
insight.step: Tomorrow, when the replay starts, get up and do one physical thing, like making the bed, before you keep thinking.

followUp.prompt: How did the first few minutes after waking set the tone for your day?

options.label: I started slowly and felt steady
options.reflection: A gentle start often carries further than it seems. When your first minutes belong to you, the rest of the day tends to follow that pace. Tomorrow, see if you can keep just one of those quiet minutes for yourself again.

options.label: My phone had me before I was really up
options.reflection: Days that open on a screen can feel a little borrowed, as if they began without you. That's very common, not a failing. Tomorrow, you might give yourself one small thing first, a stretch or a glass of water, before the world comes in.

options.label: Worries arrived before I'd even got up
options.reflection: When worries get in early, the whole day can feel like it's playing catch-up with your mind. That tends to ease once your body moves first. Tomorrow, you could try sitting up and putting your feet on the floor before you let a thought finish.

options.label: Honestly, it was a blur
options.reflection: Some mornings pass without leaving much of a mark, and that's okay. Your attention may simply have been needed elsewhere. Tomorrow, you could pause for one slow breath when you first sit up and notice how the day feels from there.

questions.prompt: You miss one day of a habit you were building. What happens next?

options.label: I just pick it up again the next day

insight.reveal: You judge a habit by the month, not by one day. A slip barely registers before you're back at it. It's likely the same with people: one missed call or a forgotten birthday rarely changes how you feel about a friend.
insight.research: When people repeated a new daily habit, it took 66 days on average to feel automatic, and one missed day did little harm.
insight.step: This week, give one habit a 'never miss twice' rule and see how it feels.

options.label: I do double the next day to make up for it

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet ledger with yourself, and you always pay it back. Odds are you repay small loans before anyone asks and hate owing anyone, even a coffee. That makes you deeply dependable, though you can be a tough lender to yourself.
insight.step: Next time you miss a day, do the normal amount, not double. Notice if the ledger voice complains.

options.label: I quietly let the whole habit go

insight.reveal: Once the chain breaks, the whole habit can feel finished. You may notice the same all-or-nothing switch with diets, language lessons or a tidy room. The good news: you throw yourself into fresh starts with real energy, and a gentler restart rule helps that energy last.
insight.research: New daily habits took weeks to months to feel automatic, and missing a single day did little harm to them.
insight.step: This week, pick one habit you dropped and do the tiniest version of it once. One minute counts.

options.label: I feel it proves something about me

insight.reveal: One missed day can feel like a verdict on who you are. You're a fair judge of other people's slips and a strict one of your own. That high bar is why people trust you with serious things. You deserve the same patience you'd give a friend.
insight.research: Across 27 trials, learning to treat yourself with kindness, as a good friend would, reduced self-criticism and low mood by moderate to large amounts.
insight.step: Next time you slip, ask: 'What would I say to a friend who missed one day?' Then say that to yourself.

followUp.prompt: How did a habit you're building go today?

options.label: I kept it up, even if only a small version
options.reflection: Keeping a habit going on an ordinary day, even in a smaller form, is often what makes it stick. You may be learning that showing up matters more than doing it perfectly. Tomorrow, let a small version count again if that's all there's room for.

options.label: I skipped it and I'm okay with that
options.reflection: Missing a day without turning it into a verdict on yourself is a quiet strength. Habits tend to survive gaps when there's no shame attached. Tomorrow, you could simply pick it back up as if today were just a pause.

options.label: I skipped it and I'm being hard on myself
options.reflection: It sounds like a missed day may have felt bigger than it was. One skip rarely undoes a habit, though a harsh inner voice can make it feel that way. Tomorrow, you might try the smallest possible version and let that be enough.

options.label: I'm not building a habit right now
options.reflection: Not every season is for building new habits, and there's nothing wrong with that. Sometimes keeping your days steady is the work. If something small calls to you tomorrow, you could simply notice it without needing to start.

questions.prompt: Your desk or table right now looks like…

options.label: Clear, with everything in its place

insight.reveal: Your table is part of how you think. You likely tidy right before a hard task to warm up, and nerves can make that urge stronger. At work, you're the one who can find any file in seconds while everyone else is still digging.
insight.research: In an experiment, people made nervous about giving a speech spent longer cleaning an object, with more repeated movements, than calmer people did.
insight.step: Before your next hard task, give yourself exactly two minutes to tidy, then start, even if it's not done.

options.label: Piles that only I understand

insight.reveal: Your piles have a map, and only you can read it. You remember things by where they sit, not by labels, so you can pull the right paper from a stack in one go. When someone 'helpfully' tidies up for you, you end up more lost than grateful.
insight.step: This week, notice how fast you can find one thing in your piles. Your system may be better than it looks.

options.label: Buried, and I'll fix it on some big day

insight.reveal: You're saving it all for one big sorting day. That same day is waiting elsewhere too: the inbox, the photos, the old friend you'll call properly soon. When it finally arrives, you can clear more in one afternoon than most people manage in a month.
insight.research: Putting things off is very common, and people tend to delay most when a task feels boring or unpleasant.
insight.step: Today, clear just one corner of the table, the size of a book. Stop there.

options.label: Honestly, it looks like how my head feels

insight.reveal: Your space and your mood tend to move together. You pick up a room's atmosphere quickly, and the link runs both ways. On a cloudy day, clearing one small corner may lift you more than you'd expect, long before the whole table is done.
insight.research: In a small study of 60 couples, wives who described their homes as cluttered or unfinished tended to have worse mood over the day.
insight.step: On your next heavy day, clear one small surface and check if your mood shifts, even slightly.

followUp.prompt: How did your desk or table look by the end of today?

options.label: I cleared it before I finished
options.reflection: Clearing your space at the end of the day can be a way of closing the door on work. It often makes the next morning feel lighter. Tomorrow, you might notice whether starting at a clear surface changes how quickly you settle in.

options.label: Messier, but I know where everything is
options.reflection: A busy surface can be a sign of a busy, working mind, and you may have your own quiet system in the piles. If it serves you, it serves you. Tomorrow, you might just check whether the mess is helping you or slowing you down.

options.label: It got worse and it's bothering me
options.reflection: When a cluttered space starts to bother you, it can be a sign that your head feels full too. You don't need to fix it all at once. Tomorrow, you could clear just one small corner and see if your thoughts feel a little roomier.

options.label: I wasn't at a desk or table much today
options.reflection: Some days happen away from any desk, on your feet or on the move. That can be a welcome change. Tomorrow, if you do sit down somewhere, you might notice what the space around you says about your mood.

questions.prompt: When do you usually start a new habit?

options.label: On a Monday or the first of the month

insight.reveal: Mondays feel like a clean page to you. New notebooks, fresh calendars and first-of-the-month plans give you a real lift, and you start with genuine commitment. The catch: miss that start date, and the next fresh start can feel a whole week or month away.
insight.research: Interest in fresh starts jumps on landmark dates: student gym visits rose 33% at the start of a week, and searches for 'diet' rose 82% at New Year.
insight.step: This week, start one small habit on a plain, ordinary day, like a Thursday.

options.label: Right now, the moment the idea hits

insight.reveal: When an idea grabs you, you're already halfway in. Your enthusiasm pulls friends into plans they didn't know they wanted. The habits that stick for you are usually the ones tied to something you already do, like the morning coffee or the ride to work.
insight.research: Habits tend to grow when one simple action is repeated after the same daily cue, like the morning coffee.
insight.step: Tomorrow, tie one new habit to something you already do: 'After I make tea, I will…'

options.label: After I find the best way to do it

insight.reveal: You'd rather start right than start soon. You read every review before buying, with a dozen tabs open, and then pause a long while before choosing. The upside: once you commit, you rarely have to undo it.
insight.step: This week, start one habit with the 'good enough' method, then improve it after three days.

options.label: I keep planning it but rarely begin

insight.reveal: In your head, the plan is already half done. You see the big picture better than most, and your plans are genuinely good ones. What's missing usually isn't motivation; it's a clear starting signal, a when and a where.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Tonight, finish this sentence for one habit: 'When I sit down after dinner, I will…'

followUp.prompt: Did you start, or think about starting, something new today?

options.label: I just began, right then and there
options.reflection: Starting the moment an idea lands takes a kind of trust in yourself. It often means you learn by doing rather than by planning. Tomorrow, you might give the new thing ten minutes again and see if it still feels alive.

options.label: I picked a fresh day to start
options.reflection: Choosing a clean start date can help you feel ready and give the new thing a proper welcome. The tricky part tends to be keeping that date. Tomorrow, you could write it down somewhere you'll see it, so your future self remembers.

options.label: I thought about it again but didn't begin
options.reflection: Coming back to the same idea again and again can mean it really matters to you, even if it hasn't started yet. Sometimes the first step just needs to be smaller. Tomorrow, you could try a tiny version of it, with no promise to continue.

options.label: Nothing new was on my mind today
options.reflection: Days without a new project can be restful, a chance to live with what you already have. You don't always need something to work on. Tomorrow, you might notice if any small curiosity tugs at you, and just let it be there.

questions.prompt: You're stuck waiting in a line for ten minutes. What do you do?

options.label: Watch the people around me

insight.reveal: You collect little stories from strangers without even trying. Odds are you read a room fast at parties and meetings, and friends are surprised how often you sense their mood is off before they've said a word.
insight.step: Next time you wait, guess one stranger's day from small clues. Just for fun.

options.label: Scroll on my phone

insight.reveal: Empty minutes rarely stay empty for you. You're hardly ever bored, and you usually know the news first. Yet your head can feel oddly full by bedtime, maybe because those blank moments used to give your mind room to sort itself out.
insight.research: Across 11 studies, most people did not enjoy sitting alone with only their thoughts for 6 to 15 minutes, and many gave themselves a mild shock instead.
insight.step: In your next line, leave the phone in your pocket for the first two minutes.

options.label: Make plans or lists in my head

insight.reveal: Hand you ten spare minutes and you'll plan the whole week. You're the one who remembers the birthdays and the deadlines. The flip side: switching off is hard for you, even on a beach with nothing to do.
insight.research: In about 250,000 phone check-ins, minds were wandering 47% of the time, and people were usually less happy when their minds wandered.
insight.step: Next time you wait, try to notice five sounds instead of making a plan.

options.label: Get restless and annoyed the whole time

insight.reveal: It's rarely the line that gets to you; it's the lost time. Your days are probably packed, so ten minutes of nothing feels stolen. That same drive makes you the one who gets things moving at work when everyone else is stuck.
insight.step: Next time you're stuck, decide on purpose what the ten minutes are for. See if choosing it changes the feeling.

followUp.prompt: Did you have to wait somewhere today? How did you spend the time?

options.label: I watched the people and things around me
options.reflection: Using a wait to look around suggests a mind that finds the world quietly interesting. Those small observations often stay with you. Tomorrow, you might notice one detail in a familiar place that you've never spotted before.

options.label: I went straight to my phone
options.reflection: Reaching for your phone in a wait is so common it barely feels like a choice. It can fill the time, though it rarely refreshes you. Next time you're waiting, you could try one minute of just looking around before you reach for it.

options.label: I got restless and a bit cross
options.reflection: Waiting can feel like time being taken from you, especially on a full day. Restlessness often means you had somewhere you'd rather be. Tomorrow, if you're stuck waiting, you could try a few slow breaths and see if the minutes soften.

options.label: There was no real waiting today
options.reflection: A day without queues or delays can feel smooth, or simply very full. Either way, you kept moving. Tomorrow, if a pause does come your way, you might treat it as a small gift of time rather than a delay.

questions.prompt: How do you keep track of things you need to do?

options.label: A written or phone list I really use

insight.reveal: You let a list hold what your mind would keep repeating. Your head is quieter than most on busy weeks, and you sleep a little easier for it. At work, people come to you when nobody remembers what was agreed.
insight.research: Young adults who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list fell asleep about 10 minutes faster than those who wrote about tasks already done.
insight.step: Tonight, add one thing that's been on your mind to your list and see if it stops repeating.

options.label: I keep it all in my head

insight.reveal: You trust your memory and enjoy life without a system. You adapt fast when plans change and hold on to the big things well. It's the tiny tasks that ambush you, usually at two in the morning or right as you walk past the shop you needed.
insight.step: For three days, write down only the tiny tasks. Keep the big ones in your head as usual.

options.label: I write lists, then lose them

insight.reveal: Writing the list is the part that helps you most. Putting things on paper calms your mind, so the list has often done its job before it goes missing. You're good at sorting what matters in the moment, note or no note.
insight.step: Tonight, write tomorrow's list somewhere you'll see it by accident, like your phone's lock screen.

options.label: I add things I already did, just to tick them

insight.reveal: Ticking off what you've already done feels so good, doesn't it? It's a quiet way of telling yourself you did enough today, and more people do it than admit it. Chances are you get through far more than you give yourself credit for.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily work diaries, people's best days were the ones when they made progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: Tonight, write three things you did today that were never on any list.

followUp.prompt: How did you keep track of what needed doing today?

options.label: My list helped, and I ticked things off
options.reflection: A list you actually use can take a real weight off your mind. Ticking things off often gives a small, steady sense of progress. Tomorrow, you could try adding one thing that's just for you, not only for others.

options.label: I kept it all in my head and it worked
options.reflection: Holding the day in your head can work well when things are clear and familiar. It may also mean your mind stays a little on duty. Tomorrow, you could jot down just the one thing you'd hate to forget and see if it frees up some space.

options.label: Something slipped through the cracks
options.reflection: Letting something slip is part of having a full life, not a sign you're failing. It often happens when there's simply too much to hold. Tomorrow, you might write the most important thing somewhere you'll see it early on.

options.label: It was a light day, not much to track
options.reflection: A light day can be a welcome breather, a reminder that not every day has to be busy. Your mind may have had more room to wander. Tomorrow, you could notice whether that sense of space follows you into a fuller day.

questions.prompt: A free Saturday with no plans. By noon you've usually…

options.label: Done chores and errands

insight.reveal: Fun feels more allowed once the chores are behind you. At work you probably clear the boring tasks first too, even when the exciting one matters more. Your fridge is stocked and your bills are paid, and friends quietly envy that.
insight.step: Next free day, do one fun thing before any chore. Notice whether the fun feels earned or stolen.

options.label: Gone somewhere new

insight.reveal: An empty day looks like an invitation to you. You remember your years by places more than dates, and you're the one suggesting the new spot over the usual one. A week with nothing new in it can feel strangely long.
insight.step: This week, take a different route to somewhere you go often.

options.label: Done nothing, and loved it

insight.reveal: Resting without needing a reason is a rare skill, and you have it. You tend to bounce back from busy weeks faster than friends who fill every weekend. Explaining a happy, empty Saturday to them might be the only hard part.
insight.research: Across 91 samples of 38,124 workers, people who mentally switched off from work in their free time reported less exhaustion and better sleep.
insight.step: This weekend, protect one hour with nothing in it, and tell someone it's a plan.

options.label: Done nothing, and felt guilty about it

insight.reveal: Even on a day off, part of you is keeping score. The guilt can take more energy than the rest gives back, so a lazy day may leave you oddly tired. That drive is why people rely on you, and it's also why you deserve rest you don't have to earn.
insight.research: People who mentally switched off from work in their free time tended to report less exhaustion and more life satisfaction.
insight.step: Next time you rest, give it a name in advance, like 'recharging time', and see if the guilt shrinks.

followUp.prompt: Did you get any free time today? How did you spend it?

options.label: I got chores and errands out of the way
options.reflection: Using free time to clear the decks can bring real relief and a tidy sense of control. Just watch that rest doesn't always come last. Tomorrow, you might let one free moment be for nothing useful at all.

options.label: I rested and really enjoyed it
options.reflection: Resting without needing to earn it is a lovely thing to be able to do. It often leaves you more ready for what comes next. Tomorrow, you could notice what made today's rest feel good, so you can find your way back to it.

options.label: I rested but felt I should be doing more
options.reflection: It sounds like rest came with a quiet voice saying you should be busy. Many people carry that voice, and it tends to steal the good part of resting. Tomorrow, you could try telling yourself that rest counts as something you did.

options.label: I had no free time today
options.reflection: A day with no free time can leave you running on empty by evening. That's worth noticing without blame. Tomorrow, you might look for even a few minutes that belong only to you, and protect them gently.

questions.prompt: At a café or restaurant you love, you usually order…

options.label: The same thing every time

insight.reveal: You know what you love, so why gamble on lunch? You'd rather spend your choosing on the things that matter more. You're loyal to places and brands too, and some of your closest friends have likely been around for many years.
insight.research: Choosing one snack at a time, only 9% of people picked different ones, versus 64% when choosing three at once: we plan more variety than we pick in the moment.
insight.step: Next visit, try one new item, but keep your favourite on the side as a safety net.

options.label: Something new each time

insight.reveal: A menu is a little adventure every time you sit down. You're the one ordering the dish nobody can pronounce and planning the next trip before this one ends. Friends ask you where to eat, and weeks that look the same make you restless.
insight.step: This week, bring the 'something new' rule to a different place, like the route home or a song.

options.label: Whatever the person with me gets

insight.reveal: You'll have what they're having, and you mean it kindly. You make easy, warm company and put people at ease. The risk is that what you wanted gets quietly lost, not just with lunch but with bigger choices, like where to travel or live.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, decide your order before anyone else speaks.

options.label: I change my mind at the very last second

insight.reveal: Your gut picks first, then your doubt argues back. You adapt fast and stay open to options, which friends enjoy. But the first choice is often the one you really wanted, and the switch is more about dodging regret than finding something better.
insight.step: Next time you order, keep your first choice and see if you enjoy it more.

followUp.prompt: When you picked something to eat or drink today, did you go for the usual or something new?

options.label: My usual, and it hit the spot
options.reflection: Going for the usual can be a small comfort, a way of knowing exactly what you'll get. On busy days, that's often a kindness to yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it still feels like a choice or has quietly become a habit.

options.label: Something I'd never tried before
options.reflection: Trying something new, even something small, tends to keep life feeling fresh. It suggests you're open to a bit of surprise. Tomorrow, you could see where else a small new choice might fit, like a different route home.

options.label: Whatever the people with me were having
options.reflection: Going along with others can make shared moments easy and warm. It may also mean your own preferences take a back seat more than you notice. Tomorrow, you might try saying what you'd actually like, even in a small choice.

options.label: I didn't really think about it
options.reflection: Some days, food is just fuel and choices happen on autopilot. That's perfectly normal when your mind is busy elsewhere. Tomorrow, you could slow down for one meal or drink and really notice how it tastes.

questions.prompt: How many books, shows or projects do you have half-finished?

options.label: None, I finish what I start

insight.reveal: Open loops bother you until you close them. You return borrowed books and finish the jobs others drift away from. The twist: you might still be watching a series you stopped enjoying ages ago, because quitting feels a bit like losing.
insight.research: A review of many studies found people tend to go back and finish tasks that were interrupted, though unfinished tasks are not remembered better.
insight.step: This week, pick one thing you're only finishing out of duty, and let yourself stop.

options.label: A couple, that's normal

insight.reveal: You finish what you love and let the rest go. You can drop a dull book halfway without a flicker of guilt, yet the things you care about get done. That makes you relaxed company and a good judge of where your time is best spent.
insight.step: This week, finish one small thing you're close to the end of.

options.label: Lots, I love starting things

insight.reveal: Beginnings are where you feel most alive. There's probably a lively mix of hobbies on the go, each one thrilling for a while. Friendships may look similar: lots of warm starts, and many people you'd love to see again.
insight.step: This week, pick one half-finished thing and do just one more step of it.

options.label: Lots, and they quietly weigh on me

insight.reveal: Each unfinished thing sits in your bag like a small stone. You care about your commitments, and that's a real strength. Here's the surprise: deciding out loud to stop something can lift a lot of that weight, without finishing it at all.
insight.research: Unfinished tasks are not remembered better than finished ones, but people do feel a pull to go back and complete them.
insight.step: Today, choose one unfinished thing and officially end it. Say 'done' out loud.

followUp.prompt: Did any of your half-finished books, shows or projects come up today?

options.label: I finished one off
options.reflection: Finishing something can bring a clean, satisfying kind of relief. It often frees up energy you didn't know was tied up. Tomorrow, you might take a moment to enjoy that it's done before reaching for the next thing.

options.label: I started something new instead
options.reflection: The pull of something new can be hard to resist, and it often brings real joy. Starting is a gift in its own right. Tomorrow, you could choose one older thing and decide, kindly, whether to finish it or let it go.

options.label: I thought about them and felt the weight
options.reflection: Unfinished things can sit quietly on your shoulders, even when you're not working on them. You're allowed to put some down for good. Tomorrow, you might pick one and either take a small step or give yourself permission to leave it.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Some days the unfinished pile stays in the background, and that's fine. Not everything needs your attention at once. Tomorrow, if one of them crosses your mind, you might just notice how it makes you feel.

questions.prompt: You promised yourself one small thing today. By evening…

options.label: It's done

insight.reveal: When you promise yourself something, it gets done. That quiet self-trust tends to make hard decisions feel less scary. At work you come across as steady, and when you mention a plan over dinner, friends know it'll actually happen.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make yourself one tiny promise and keep it on purpose.

options.label: It's moved to tomorrow

insight.reveal: Tomorrow is where a lot of your good intentions wait. You're realistic about today's energy and kind to yourself on hard days. The catch is that tomorrow's you ends up carrying the heaviest bag, unless the task gets a real time and place.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you move something to tomorrow, decide the exact time you'll do it.

options.label: I forgot until right now

insight.reveal: Promises to others get a reminder; the ones to yourself don't. You keep your word to friends well, because those promises live in a calendar or a chat. The ones you make to yourself live only in your head, so they're the first to slip.
insight.research: Across 47 experiments, a medium-to-large boost in people's intentions led to only a small-to-medium change in what they actually did.
insight.step: Tomorrow, write one promise to yourself in the same place you keep promises to others.

options.label: I skipped it, but I kept every promise to others

insight.reveal: You're reliable for everyone, except yourself. Chances are you're the colleague who covers the extra shift and the friend who picks up late at night, while your own needs slide to the bottom of the list without a sound.
insight.step: This week, treat one promise to yourself like a meeting with someone you respect.

followUp.prompt: Did you make yourself a small promise today? What happened to it?

options.label: I kept it
options.reflection: Keeping a promise to yourself builds a quiet kind of trust that grows over time. It may feel small, but it often matters more than it seems. Tomorrow, you could make another small one and let yourself enjoy keeping it.

options.label: I moved it to tomorrow
options.reflection: Moving a promise to tomorrow is very human, especially when today was full. The risk is that tomorrow keeps moving too. You might make tomorrow's version smaller, so it's easy to keep before lunch.

options.label: Others' needs came first and it slipped
options.reflection: It sounds like you kept your word to everyone except yourself today. That generosity is real, though your own promises deserve a place too. Tomorrow, you could treat your small promise like a date with someone you care about.

options.label: I didn't make one today
options.reflection: Not every day needs a promise to yourself, and some days are better taken as they come. You may have simply been getting on with things. Tomorrow, if something small feels worth doing, you could quietly commit to it.

questions.prompt: What usually tells you it's time to go to sleep?

options.label: The clock: it's my usual time

insight.reveal: You like your days to have a clear shape. Your meals, work and bedtime keep a steady rhythm, so groggy mornings are rare. On trips, when that shape disappears, you might feel a little lost for the first day or two.
insight.step: On your next free night, keep your usual bedtime and notice how the next morning feels.

options.label: My body: I just feel tired

insight.reveal: Your body talks, and you actually listen. You notice hunger, stress and tiredness early, before they turn into a bad mood. You're also good at knowing when to leave a party or step away from work, and you rarely regret it.
insight.step: Tonight, notice the very first sign of tiredness, like slow blinking, and go then.

options.label: The show or video finally ends

insight.reveal: Bedtime arrives when the show ends, not when you decide. You may lose the last hour of the evening without remembering what filled it. On the bright side, you know how to unwind, and friends ask you which show to watch next.
insight.research: In a survey of 423 young adults, frequent binge-watchers had worse sleep and more tiredness, linked to a busier mind at bedtime.
insight.step: Tonight, choose your stopping point before you press play.

options.label: Nothing, I stop when I can't stay awake

insight.reveal: Night feels like the only time that's truly yours. You may feel sharpest and most creative late in the evening. Going to bed can feel like handing the day back to everyone else, so you hold on until your eyes close by themselves.

followUp.prompt: Thinking of last night, what finally sent you to bed?

options.label: My usual bedtime

options.reflection: Listening to your body's tiredness is a simple kind of self-respect. It tends to work well when evenings are calm. Tonight, you could notice what your very first sleepy signal is, and try to follow it.

options.label: One more episode or video kept me up

questions.prompt: It's late, you're tired, and it's your first free moment all day. You…

options.label: Go to bed anyway

insight.reveal: Bed wins, because you look after tomorrow's you. You show the same care with meals, money and mornings. While others are running on empty by the end of the week, you still have something left in the tank.
insight.step: This week, find a small free moment earlier in the day so night isn't the only one.

options.label: Stay up a little to enjoy it

insight.reveal: You need rest, and you need something just for you. You usually manage that trade well, as long as 'a little' has a clear end. Small pleasures in a busy week matter to you, and you protect them without guilt.
insight.step: Tonight, set a gentle alarm for when 'a little' is over.

options.label: Stay up far too late scrolling

insight.reveal: The night is when you finally get your day back. Your days likely belong to other people's needs, so staying up is how you reclaim a little time. The trouble is that scrolling is rarely what you truly wanted to do with it.
insight.research: Many people go to bed later than they meant to for no outside reason, and this bedtime delay went with too little sleep and next-day tiredness.
insight.step: Tonight, ask: 'What would I really enjoy for 20 minutes?' Then do that instead of scrolling.

options.label: Stay up because sleeping makes tomorrow come faster

insight.step: Tonight, name the one part of tomorrow you're dreading, then write the first small step for it.

followUp.prompt: Have you had a free moment to yourself yet today? How are you spending it?

options.label: Winding down, ready for bed soon
options.reflection: Choosing rest when you finally get a moment shows real care for the person you'll be tomorrow. That's not always easy after a full day. Tonight, you might keep the lights low and let your mind know the day is done.

options.label: Scrolling, longer than I meant to
options.reflection: Scrolling can feel like reclaiming time after a day that wasn't yours. It often stretches further than you planned. Tonight, you could set a small stopping point, like the end of a song, and see how it feels to stop there.

options.label: Staying up because tomorrow feels heavy
options.reflection: Staying up to delay tomorrow can be a sign that tomorrow is asking a lot of you. That makes sense. Tonight, you might write down the one thing you're dreading, so it can wait on the page instead of in your head.

options.label: I haven't had a free moment yet
options.reflection: A day without a single free moment can be draining, even if it was a good day. You've been giving a lot. Tonight, you could take just a few minutes for yourself before sleep, even if it's only sitting quietly.

questions.prompt: It's mid-afternoon and your energy drops. You reach for…

insight.research: Across 24 studies, caffeine cut sleep by about 45 minutes; to avoid this, a regular coffee should be drunk at least 8.8 hours before bed.

options.label: Something sweet

followUp.prompt: When your energy dipped today, what did you reach for?

options.label: A short walk or some water
options.reflection: Reaching for a walk or water suggests you're tuned in to what your body needs. Those small choices often add up across a week. Tomorrow, you might notice what time your energy dips, so you can be ready for it.

options.label: Coffee, tea or something sweet
options.reflection: A quick lift from coffee, tea or a treat can be just what gets you through, and it's often a small comfort too. Tomorrow, you could see if a glass of water or a few minutes outside does a similar job first.

questions.prompt: On a stressful day, the way you eat…

insight.step: Tomorrow, set one reminder for a real meal break, even if the day is calm.

options.label: I snack more without noticing

insight.reveal: Your hands look for comfort while your mind is busy. If you watch closely, the snacking often starts at one exact moment, like after a certain message or meeting. Spotting that moment makes small changes much easier than any strict rule.

followUp.prompt: If today got stressful, did it change how you ate?

options.label: I ate the way I normally do

questions.prompt: When you move your body, it's mostly because…

followUp.prompt: Did you move your body today? What got you moving?

options.label: I moved because I enjoy it

options.label: A social feed

followUp.prompt: When you finally sat down to rest today, how did it feel?

options.reflection: Feeling you should be busy even while resting is very common, especially if you care about getting things right. Rest still counts. Tomorrow, you might sit down for five minutes and call it a task you've done.

followUp.prompt: How did your meals fit around your day today?

followUp.prompt: Did you wake in the night last night? Where did your mind go?

followUp.prompt: Did money come in or go out today? What did you deal with first?

options.label: I treated myself first

questions.prompt: A friend asks to borrow some money. You…

insight.step: Next time someone owes you, mention it kindly within a week instead of waiting.

options.label: Give it and don't expect it back

insight.reveal: Between friends, you'd rather give than lend. Handing it over and forgetting it beats months of wondering when it's coming back. A quiet limit in your head keeps that generosity from ever starting to sting.
insight.step: This week, notice if there's anyone you give to who never asks how you're doing.

options.label: Say no politely

insight.reveal: You protect friendships by keeping money out of them. You're generous in other ways: your time, your advice, a free weekend to help someone move. Your friendships tend to last precisely because nobody owes anybody.
insight.step: Next time you say no, offer one other kind of help instead, if you want to.

options.label: Lend it, then feel too awkward to ask for it back

insight.reveal: Asking for it back feels like it might cost you the friend. You're warm and loyal, and you'd rather lose the money than risk a moment of tension. The irony is that silence usually strains things more than one clear, friendly question would.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, get one kind sentence ready for asking it back, like 'Hey, whenever you can, no rush.'

followUp.prompt: Did lending, borrowing or owing money come up with anyone today?

options.label: I lent or gave some, no fuss
options.reflection: Helping someone out without fuss suggests generosity comes naturally to you. That's a warm trait. Tomorrow, you might check in with yourself that it feels right for you too, not just for them.

options.label: I said no, kindly
options.reflection: Saying no kindly is a skill, and it can protect both your money and the friendship. It often takes more courage than saying yes. Tomorrow, you might notice how you feel about it once a day has passed.

options.label: Someone owes me and I can't bring it up
options.reflection: Feeling unable to ask for money back is very common, and it often comes from caring about the friendship. Your needs matter too. Tomorrow, you might think about a light, friendly way to raise it, even just in your head first.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Money between friends didn't come up today, and that can be a nice break. You may have simply enjoyed people for who they are. Tomorrow, you might notice who you feel most at ease with, money or not.

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends ends. How do you split the bill?

options.label: Split it equally

insight.reveal: You care about the evening, not the exact sums. Scorekeeping between friends makes you uneasy, so you're easy to go out with. You're also quick to notice when someone else at the table is quietly counting.
insight.step: Next dinner, notice how the group decides to split. Who leads it?

options.label: Everyone pays exactly for what they had

insight.reveal: In your eyes, fair means precise. Friends trust you with group money and shared spreadsheets. And when you only had a salad, the 'let's just split it' crowd can leave you feeling quietly short-changed.
insight.research: In a restaurant experiment, diners ordered more when the bill was split evenly than when each paid for their own food.
insight.step: Next time, try splitting equally once and see if it feels as bad as expected.

options.label: I quietly put in more than my share

insight.reveal: Your generosity works best when nobody sees it. Slipping in a little extra gives you real joy, as long as nobody makes a fuss. You're quick to notice which friend is short of money this month.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Next time you treat someone, notice how long the good feeling lasts.

options.label: I offer to pay for everyone, then regret it

insight.reveal: You love being the warm, generous one at the table. You make gatherings feel special. The regret afterwards is rarely about the money; it's more about wondering whether anyone noticed, or would ever do the same for you.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to lifted the helper's well-being, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefit.
insight.step: Next time you feel the urge to pay for all, wait ten seconds before saying it.

followUp.prompt: Did you share a bill or a cost with someone today? How did it go?

options.label: We split it evenly
options.reflection: Splitting evenly often keeps things simple and friendly, and suggests you value ease over exact sums. That's a generous kind of fairness. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it feels even for everyone involved, including you.

options.label: Everyone paid for their own
options.reflection: Paying for exactly what you had can feel clear and fair, with nothing left hanging. You may like things to be tidy between people. Tomorrow, you might notice whether that clarity helps you relax around money with others.

options.label: I covered more than my share
options.reflection: Quietly covering more than your share suggests you'd rather give than make things awkward. That's kind. Tomorrow, you might ask yourself whether you did it freely, or because asking felt too hard.

options.label: Nothing to share today
options.reflection: No shared bills today, and that can be a quiet kind of freedom. You may have kept things simple. Tomorrow, you might notice the next time you share something with others, and how giving and taking feel to you.

questions.prompt: You see something you love but didn't plan to buy. You…

options.label: Walk away

insight.reveal: You can want something and still walk away calmly. Your secret probably isn't willpower: you simply don't picture owning the thing before you leave. The wanting usually fades within hours, and your money stays free for what matters.
insight.research: Across 102 studies, self-control was linked more to automatic, everyday routines than to one-off choices, suggesting self-controlled people lean on good habits.
insight.step: Next time you walk away, check in two days if you still think about it.

options.label: Wait a day and see if I still want it

insight.reveal: Sleeping on it is your quiet superpower. You probably regret fewer purchases and enjoy the ones you make more. The same patience helps when a heated message lands and you choose to answer in the morning.
insight.step: This week, start a 'wait one day' list on your phone for things you want.

options.label: Buy it right away

insight.reveal: The thrill of the find is part of what you're buying. You're decisive and spontaneous, and the best feeling often comes right at checkout. It fades faster than the item stays, so a short pause can keep the thrill and lose the regret.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: Next time you want to buy on the spot, take a photo first and decide in an hour.

options.label: Buy it and don't tell anyone

insight.reveal: Wanting something is fine; being seen wanting it is harder. What you're hiding usually isn't the item but a verdict you've already passed on yourself. Underneath it, you know exactly what delights you, and that's nothing to hide.
insight.step: Next time you buy something for you, tell one person about it plainly and see how it feels.

followUp.prompt: Did something catch your eye today that you hadn't planned to buy?

options.label: I walked away
options.reflection: Walking away from something you liked takes a calm kind of strength. It may mean you know what really matters to you right now. Tomorrow, you might notice whether you still think about it, or whether it's already faded.

options.label: I'm giving it a day to decide
options.reflection: Giving yourself a day to decide is a thoughtful way to tell a passing wish from a real want. Tomorrow, you might check in with how you feel about it, and trust whatever answer comes.

options.label: I bought it
options.reflection: Buying something you love on the spot can bring a real lift, and sometimes that's exactly what's needed. Tomorrow, you might simply notice how you feel about it, once the first excitement has settled.

options.label: Nothing tempted me today
options.reflection: A day without temptation can feel easy and light. Your attention may have been on other things. Tomorrow, you might notice what does catch your eye, and what that says about what you're longing for.

questions.prompt: You get an unexpected bit of extra money. Where does it go?

options.label: Into savings

insight.reveal: Feeling safe is its own kind of treat for you. You probably keep spare batteries, extra snacks and a plan B for most things. When the car breaks down or a surprise bill arrives, you're the calm one in the room.
insight.research: Worldwide, 79% of adults now have an account, but only 56% could reliably get hold of extra money in an emergency.
insight.step: Next time, keep a tiny part of any surprise money for something fun.

options.label: A trip, a meal out, an experience

insight.reveal: You buy memories rather than things. You'll retell those moments for years, and each retelling adds a little more value. You're the friend who still remembers the name of that tiny restaurant from a trip long ago.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This month, plan one small experience and tell someone the story afterward.

options.label: A gift or treat for someone else

insight.reveal: Giving makes you feel richer than getting. There's likely a note on your phone of things friends mentioned wanting, some from months ago. Your joy lasts longest when the gift lands as a complete surprise.
insight.research: In 120 of 136 countries, rich and poor, people who had recently spent money on others tended to feel more satisfied with life.
insight.step: This week, do one small surprise for someone, even something free.

options.label: It just disappears, I'm not sure where

insight.reveal: Surprise money never quite feels like real money to you. So it melts into small treats, coffees and lunches out. That says more about the label in your head than about carelessness, and in the moment you're relaxed and generous with it.
insight.research: People tend to split money into mental 'pots' and judge each spend by the pot it came from.
insight.step: Next time extra money arrives, give it a name, like 'shoe money', before you spend any.

followUp.prompt: Did you have a little spare money to decide on today? Where did it go?

options.label: I tucked it away
options.reflection: Tucking spare money away suggests you like the safety of something set aside. That often brings quiet confidence. Tomorrow, you might also think about one small way to enjoy what you've built.

options.label: On an outing or a meal out
options.reflection: Spending on experiences tends to leave memories that outlast things. You may value feeling alive over owning more. Tomorrow, you might think back to today's moment and enjoy it a second time.

options.label: On something for someone else
options.reflection: Using spare money on someone else suggests you get real joy from giving. That's a lovely trait. Tomorrow, you might also do one small thing just for you, so the care flows both ways.

options.label: No spare money to think about today
options.reflection: Not every day comes with spare money, and that can feel tight or simply ordinary. You're managing what you have. Tomorrow, you might notice one small free pleasure that money can't buy.

questions.prompt: How often do you look at your account balance?

options.label: About once a week

insight.reveal: Money is like the weather to you: worth a look, not a worry. You catch problems early without letting the numbers set your mood. Messages and news probably get the same treatment: checked, then left alone.
insight.step: This week, notice how you feel right before your check. Calm, or bracing?

options.label: Every day

insight.reveal: Small, regular updates beat big surprises for you. You catch odd charges early and you're the one at home who knows where everything stands. The flip side is that small dips can sting more than they deserve.
insight.step: This week, skip checking for one day and see if anything changes.

options.label: Only when I really have to

insight.reveal: Not looking is how you protect your mood. You're optimistic and focused on the present, not careless. Still, not knowing often weighs more than the real number, and a quick look on a set day often brings surprising relief.
insight.research: Tracking real logins to a money app, people looked at their accounts less often when they were in debt, and most right after pay arrived.
insight.step: This week, pick one quiet moment, with a drink you like, and check once.

options.label: Many times a day, even when nothing changed

insight.reveal: Every check buys you a moment of relief. That relief is what keeps the loop going, because money feels tied to safety for you. You're very responsible with it, the kind of person who almost never misses a payment.
insight.step: Tomorrow, check only at lunch and at night. In between, notice what you feel instead.

followUp.prompt: Did you check your bank balance today? How did it feel?

options.label: Once, quickly, and it was fine
options.reflection: A quick, calm look at your balance suggests money feels manageable for you right now. That's worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might carry that same steady attention into one other part of your life.

options.label: Several times, though nothing changed
options.reflection: Checking again and again can be a way of trying to feel safe when money feels uncertain. It's a very human habit. Tomorrow, you could pick one time to look, and gently remind yourself the number won't run away.

options.label: I avoided looking on purpose
options.reflection: Avoiding your balance often means you're bracing for news you don't want. That's understandable. Tomorrow, you might take one quick look with a warm drink in hand, and remind yourself that knowing tends to be easier than guessing.

options.label: I didn't think about it today
options.reflection: Not thinking about your balance can mean money feels steady enough to set aside. That's a nice place to be. Tomorrow, you might notice whether that ease holds when a bigger purchase comes up.

questions.prompt: Something you bought goes on sale the next day. You…

options.label: Shrug, it's fine

insight.reveal: Liking what you bought matters more to you than the price. You enjoy what you own more because of it. The same easy attitude helps you let go of small losses, like a missed train or a haircut that went wrong.
insight.step: This week, notice one thing you own that you love, regardless of what it cost.

options.label: Go and get the difference back

insight.reveal: A small unfairness bugs you until it's fixed. You keep receipts, enjoy small wins and handle forms and customer service better than most. Friends likely call you when a company gets something wrong.
insight.step: Next time you fix a small unfairness, notice how good it feels, and why.

options.label: Feel annoyed for days

insight.reveal: Feeling caught out stings far more than the money. You have high standards and a sharp eye for detail, so the same sting may follow a wrong answer said out loud in a meeting. Turning to something else, rather than replaying it, helps it fade faster.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head tends to deepen low mood and make problems harder to solve.
insight.step: Next time you feel caught out, give the feeling one sentence, then change the subject.

options.label: Feel like I always pay too much

insight.reveal: A sale sign can wake up a much bigger story. That story often sounds like 'things don't work out for me'. You're perceptive enough to catch it over a price tag, which means you can catch it in bigger moments too, where questioning it matters most.
insight.research: In six small trials, people who learned from a self-help book to catch and question gloomy thoughts had clearly better mood after four weeks.
insight.step: This week, write down one time things did work out for you, however small.

followUp.prompt: Did a purchase or a price bother you today, after you'd paid?

options.label: I shrugged it off
options.reflection: Letting a small money annoyance go suggests you don't let it take up more space than it deserves. That's a calm way to live. Tomorrow, you might notice where else that easy shrug could help you.

options.label: I sorted it out, like asking for a refund
options.reflection: Sorting it out rather than stewing on it suggests you'd rather act than worry. That often brings a clean sense of closure. Tomorrow, you might remember how good it felt to deal with it, and use that for the next small task.

options.label: It's still nagging at me
options.reflection: Some money moments stick around longer than they should, replaying in the background. That tends to happen when you care about being careful. Tonight, you might tell yourself it's done, and see if it feels lighter by morning.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: No money regrets today, and that's a gentle kind of peace. You may have been easy on yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice the next time a price surprises you, and how quickly you let it go.

questions.prompt: Someone asks how much you earn. You…

options.label: Just tell them

insight.reveal: Secrets give money too much power, so you just say it. You'll talk about pay and rent as casually as lunch plans. That openness invites trust: people bring you their own worries and ask for your honest advice.
insight.step: This week, notice whether anyone opens up to you after you're open first.

options.label: Give a vague answer

insight.reveal: You guard your privacy without making it awkward. You can make 'oh, it pays the rent' sound like a full answer, and people rarely see exactly what you think until they know you well.
insight.research: When university staff learned what colleagues earned, those paid below the middle felt less satisfied, while those paid above felt no happier.
insight.step: Next time you're vague, notice whether it's about privacy or about being compared.

options.label: Change the subject

insight.reveal: Some doors stay closed, and money talk is behind one of them. You're discreet and good at keeping other people's secrets too. Sometimes it's simple privacy, and sometimes there are feelings about money you haven't put into words yet.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself quietly: what feeling shows up when someone asks about money?

options.label: Feel judged, even if they just asked

insight.reveal: You measure yourself before anyone else gets the chance. The judging usually comes from inside, and most people who ask are just curious. You're self-aware and sensitive to others, which makes you kind when the roles are reversed.
insight.research: Life satisfaction tracked where people's income ranked among others like them, and comparisons with people above counted more than with those below.
insight.step: Next time someone asks a money question, assume curiosity first and see if it changes the feeling.

followUp.prompt: Did pay, prices or money come up in conversation today?

options.label: I talked about it openly
options.reflection: Talking openly about money suggests you're comfortable being honest, even when it's a little awkward. That can make it easier for others to do the same. Tomorrow, you might notice who else seems relieved to talk about it.

options.label: I kept it vague or changed the subject
options.reflection: Keeping money talk vague is very common and can be a way of protecting your privacy. That's your right. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it felt like a choice or a reflex, and what you'd like to share next time.

options.label: I felt judged, even if no one meant it
options.reflection: Feeling judged around money can stir up old worries about where you stand. Others may not have meant it at all. Tomorrow, you could remind yourself that your worth isn't measured by what's in your account.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Money didn't come up in conversation today, and that can feel like a small relief. You may have spent your time on other things. Tomorrow, you might notice the next time it does, and how comfortable you feel.

questions.prompt: How much money would feel like 'enough'?

options.label: About what I have now

insight.reveal: Time and people are what make you feel rich. You'd pick the slower job, the longer lunch and the evening with friends. While others chase the next upgrade, you seem quietly content, and people notice.
insight.research: People whose biggest goals were money, looks and fame tended to feel worse, while those chasing close relationships, growth and community felt better.
insight.step: This week, use some of your 'enough' feeling to give someone your time.

options.label: A bit more than now

insight.reveal: Your goal is clear and within reach. You know exactly what a bit more would change, like less stress around one bill or one extra trip a year. You're a practical planner who knows where the money goes.
insight.research: On average, happiness kept rising with income even at high salaries, but for the unhappiest group it levelled off at moderate incomes.
insight.step: This week, name the one thing 'a bit more' would change, then take one small step toward it.

options.label: I keep moving the line

insight.reveal: The finish line keeps walking away just as you reach it. The higher pay, the bigger place, the better phone: each tends to feel amazing for a few weeks, then turns normal. You aim high and work hard, and pausing to notice each arrival is what lets it count.
insight.research: In Gallup data from over 1.7 million people worldwide, extra income stopped lifting life ratings at a point, and that point was higher in richer regions.
insight.step: Tonight, write down one thing you once wanted badly and now have. Enjoy it for a moment.

options.label: I'm not sure any amount would feel safe

insight.reveal: A shield, not a tool: that's what money can feel like to you. The feeling is often older than your bank account, so a bigger number rarely calms it fully. You're careful and prepared, and naming the fear may bring more ease than growing the savings.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment when you felt safe that had nothing to do with money.

followUp.prompt: Was there a moment today when what you have felt like enough?

options.label: Yes, I felt quietly content
options.reflection: Feeling that what you have is enough is a quiet, steady kind of wealth. It often brings more peace than more money could. Tomorrow, you might notice what was around you in that moment, so you can find it again.

options.label: I caught myself wanting the next thing
options.reflection: Wanting the next thing is a very human pull, and noticing it is already a step. The line often moves as soon as you reach it. Tomorrow, you might pause before a purchase and ask what it would actually change for you.

options.label: I worried it might never feel safe
options.reflection: When no amount feels safe, the worry often runs deeper than money. That can be tiring to carry. Tomorrow, you might name one thing in your life that feels secure today, however small, and let it steady you.

options.label: Money wasn't on my mind today
options.reflection: A day without thinking about money can be a sign that other things filled you up. That's worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might look for the small things that made today feel full, and make room for them again.

questions.prompt: Choosing a gift for someone close, you usually…

options.label: Ask them what they want

insight.reveal: You want a gift to be used, not just admired. You prefer clear requests to guessing games in relationships too. You're probably the one who says exactly what you want for your birthday, and the people around you find that a relief.
insight.research: People liked gifts they had asked for more than surprise gifts, though givers expected surprises to be valued more.
insight.step: Next gift, ask what they want, then add one small surprise.

options.label: Get something practical

insight.reveal: Usefulness is how you show you care. You fix things, lend tools and remember what someone ran out of. Your gifts are likely the ones still in use years later, long after the flashy ones are forgotten.
insight.research: Gift givers tend to aim for the 'wow' moment of opening, while receivers care more about how useful a gift will be over time.
insight.step: This week, notice what someone close keeps running out of.

options.label: Find something they'd never buy themselves

insight.reveal: You hear the small wishes people say in passing. You remember them months later, which is why your gifts tend to get the biggest reaction in the room. People feel truly seen when they open something from you.
insight.step: This week, listen for one small wish someone mentions, and save it in your phone.

options.label: Spend more than I should, to show I care

insight.reveal: Part of you worries that care only counts if it shows. You'd rather stretch your budget than risk a gift looking small. Yet most people remember how a gift made them feel, not what it cost, and a few handwritten lines can carry as much love as the price.
insight.research: People given 5 or 20 dollars felt happier by evening if told to spend it on someone else, and the amount they spent did not matter.
insight.step: Next gift, add a short handwritten note and spend a little less. Watch the reaction.

followUp.prompt: Did you give, or plan, something for someone close today?

options.label: Something I knew they'd love
options.reflection: Choosing something you know they'll love suggests you pay close attention to the people you care about. That's a lovely kind of noticing. Tomorrow, you might tell them one small thing you appreciate about them, too.

options.label: Something useful they needed
options.reflection: A practical gift shows care through usefulness, which many people value deeply. You may like making life easier for others. Tomorrow, you might add a few kind words, so the care is spoken as well as given.

options.label: I spent more than I meant to
options.reflection: Spending more than you meant to can be a way of trying to show how much you care. Your care is already there. Tomorrow, you might remember that time and attention often mean more than the price.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No gifts on your mind today, and that's perfectly fine. Care shows up in many other ways. Tomorrow, you might notice a small way you already show love to someone close, without spending a thing.

questions.prompt: How do you start your working day?

options.label: With the most important task

insight.reveal: You do the hard thing first, while your head is still fresh. By mid-morning the day already feels half won, and everything after is a bonus. Chances are you're also the one who saves the best bite on the plate for last.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily diaries from 238 workers, the best days were the ones with progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: Tonight, pick tomorrow's first task, so your morning starts without a choice to make.

options.label: Clearing messages

insight.reveal: Other people's needs get your first hour, every time. You're probably the colleague who answers fast and keeps everyone unstuck. The catch: some days you reach lunch having helped five people while your own list hasn't moved.
insight.research: When students kept phone alerts on for a week, they reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness than in a week with alerts off.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do 20 minutes of your own work before opening messages.

options.label: A small, easy task to warm up

insight.reveal: Getting started is the hard part, so you make it easy. One small task gets the engine running, and at home one tidy drawer has a way of turning into a tidy room. Just keep an eye on the warm-up so it doesn't eat the whole morning.
insight.step: Tomorrow, set a limit: one warm-up task, then the real one.

options.label: Rereading what I sent yesterday

insight.reveal: You care how your words land, even a day later. You're likely a careful, kind writer, yet the rereading turns up doubt far more than mistakes. A two-line reply can stay with you long after the other person has forgotten it.
insight.step: Tomorrow, skip the rereading once. If something was wrong, someone will tell you.

followUp.prompt: How did your working day actually begin today?

options.label: I went straight at the big task
options.reflection: Starting with the big thing tends to make the rest of the day feel lighter. You may have bought yourself some calm today. Tomorrow, notice whether that early push also left you room to breathe.

options.label: Messages pulled me in first
options.reflection: Answering others first often comes from wanting to be there for people. It can also quietly hand your best hours away. Tomorrow, you might try one small piece of your own work before opening any messages.

options.label: I went back over yesterday's messages
options.reflection: Going back over yesterday often comes from wanting to be sure you got things right. It can quietly use up your freshest energy. Tomorrow, you might give yesterday one quick look, then turn to something new.

options.label: It wasn't a working day for me
options.reflection: Rest days and different days count too. How you begin a free day may say just as much as a busy one. Tomorrow, you might notice the very first thing you reach for, and whether it feels like your choice.

questions.prompt: Your boss sends: 'Can we talk later?' You…

options.label: Think nothing of it

insight.reveal: A vague message is just a vague message to you. You sleep fine before big meetings, and when office gossip starts flying, people drift toward your desk to calm down. Just remember that not everyone reads silence as kindly as you do.
insight.step: Next time you send a vague message, add one word of context. Others may not be as calm.

options.label: Ask what it's about

insight.reveal: Not knowing bothers you more than bad news ever could. So you ask, and you handle whatever comes once it's on the table. Odds are you ask for the agenda before most meetings, too, and people are secretly glad you did.
insight.research: In a lab game, people's stress rose most when the outcome was least predictable, suggesting that not knowing can be stressful in itself.
insight.step: Next time you're waiting on something, plan one small task to fill the gap.

options.label: Start preparing for every possible topic

insight.reveal: When you worry, you get busy. You'll walk in ready for questions nobody was going to ask, notes and all. The hidden cost is living through the stress twice, often for a chat that turns out to be about next month's schedule.
insight.step: Next time, prepare for only the one most likely topic and see if it's enough.

options.label: Imagine the worst until we talk

insight.reveal: Waiting starts a story in your head, and it's rarely a kind one. The same alarm probably rings when a friend replies slowly or a partner sounds flat on the phone. You pick up on moods others miss, even though most of these 'later' talks end up being about something small.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time you imagine the worst, also imagine the most boring possible reason.

followUp.prompt: Did someone at work want a word with you today? How did the waiting feel?

options.label: It came and went, no big deal
options.reflection: Letting a vague message stay vague is a quiet skill. You may trust that most talks are ordinary ones. Tomorrow, notice how that steadiness feels in your body, so you can find it again on a harder day.

options.label: I asked what it was about
options.reflection: Asking straight away often saves hours of guessing. It suggests you would rather know than wonder. Tomorrow, you could use the same simple question anywhere else a loose end is sitting on your mind.

options.label: My mind jumped to the worst
options.reflection: Filling silence with the worst story is something many caring, careful people do. It tends to cost more than the talk itself. Tomorrow, you might write down what you fear and check it against what actually happened.

options.label: Nobody asked for a talk today
options.reflection: A day without that kind of message is a small gift. You can use it to notice how you tend to feel at work when nothing is hanging over you. That calmer version of you is worth remembering tomorrow.

questions.prompt: A colleague presents your idea as theirs. You…

options.label: Mention it calmly to them later

insight.reveal: You can stand up for your work without burning a bridge. Everyone who saw what happened will remember how well you handled it. Don't be surprised if you become the person the team calls when a quarrel needs a cool head.
insight.step: This week, pick one calm line for next time, like: 'Glad that idea from our chat landed well.'

options.label: Speak up right there

insight.reveal: Fair is fair, and you'll say so right there in the room. You'll question a wrong bill at a restaurant without blushing, and friends come to you when something isn't right. Quieter colleagues may need a moment to get used to how direct you are.
insight.step: Next time you speak up, add one generous word for the other person too.

options.label: Say nothing, and feel it for weeks

insight.reveal: The perfect comeback arrives about three days too late, doesn't it? You replay the moment in the shower, polishing a reply you'll never use, and the anger stays warm instead of fading. Underneath sits a strong sense of justice and a memory for detail that makes you a sharp judge of people.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time, say one short true sentence soon, even if imperfect, instead of the perfect one never.

options.label: Say nothing, but quietly trust them less forever

insight.reveal: You don't fight back, you quietly close a door. It makes you hard to fool twice and very good at relying on yourself. The other person may never learn why things cooled, and that silent distance can outlast the original slight by years.
insight.step: This week, think of one person you quietly trust less. What small thing could they do to win it back?

followUp.prompt: Did your ideas get fair credit today, or did someone else take the bow?

options.label: People saw what I did
options.reflection: Being seen for your work can feel quietly nourishing. You may have noticed a little extra energy afterwards. Tomorrow, you could pass the feeling on by naming someone else's good idea out loud.

options.label: Someone took credit and I said so
options.reflection: Speaking up for your own work can feel bold, even uncomfortable. It suggests you value fairness, including fairness to yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice how you feel about it once the moment has cooled.

options.label: I stayed quiet, but it's still on my mind
options.reflection: Holding it in often means it keeps replaying long after the meeting ended. That may be a sign it matters more than you let on. Tomorrow, you might try one calm sentence to the person, so it has somewhere to go.

options.label: Credit didn't come up today
options.reflection: Not every day puts your work on show, and that's fine. Quiet days can be a good time to notice which of your ideas you tend to feel proud of. Tomorrow, you might jot one down so it's clearly yours.

questions.prompt: If pay didn't matter, would you keep doing your kind of work?

options.label: Yes, I'd keep doing it

insight.reveal: Your work gives you something pay never could. You tell work stories at dinner without being asked, and you enjoy the small daily parts, not just the big wins. Some of your friends probably wish they felt the same about their own jobs.
insight.research: Workers split roughly evenly into seeing their work as a job, a career or a calling, meaningful in itself, even within the same occupation.
insight.step: This week, notice which part of your work you'd do even for free.

options.label: Something close to it

insight.reveal: You love your field, just maybe not your exact chair in it. There's likely a side version of your job you've sketched in your head on long trips or in the shower. When someone mentions a role right next to yours, you light up faster than you'd admit.
insight.step: This week, spend ten minutes looking at what that nearby version looks like day to day.

options.label: Something completely different

insight.reveal: You carry a whole other life around in your head. The funny thing is, it probably shows already: in your hobbies, the books on your shelf, the videos you watch late at night. You may be closer to that life than it feels.
insight.step: Tonight, look at how you spent your last free weekend. Is that other life already in it?

options.label: I've never let myself really answer that

insight.reveal: You've been the practical one for a long time. Chances are it was for others as much as for yourself, and it's made you someone people lean on. A real answer might ask something of you, which is exactly why it's worth answering slowly, in private.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: This week, give yourself one minute to answer it honestly, with no plan to act on it.

followUp.prompt: Was there a moment today when your work felt worth doing for its own sake?

options.label: Yes, I lost track of time in it
options.reflection: Losing track of time often points to work that fits who you are. It's worth knowing exactly what you were doing in that moment. Tomorrow, you might look for a way to give that part of your work a little more room.

options.label: Today it was mainly about the pay
options.reflection: Some days work is simply a way to pay for the life you care about, and that is honest. It may help to name what the money protects. Tomorrow, you could notice one small part of the day you'd keep even if it were unpaid.

options.label: I kept daydreaming about other work
options.reflection: Daydreams about other work often carry real clues about what you're hungry for. You don't have to act on them to learn from them. Tomorrow, you might write down what the daydream had that today didn't.

options.label: I didn't work today
options.reflection: A day away from work can show what you reach for when nobody is paying you. That is often a clue about what you value. Tomorrow, you might notice which part of today you'd happily repeat.

questions.prompt: Your work gets praised in front of others. You…

options.label: Say thank you and enjoy it

insight.reveal: You let a compliment land, and that's rarer than it sounds. People enjoy praising you because you actually take it in. You're generous with kind words yourself, and one good one can keep you warm for weeks.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment underestimated how good it would make the other person feel, and overestimated how awkward it would be.
insight.step: This week, praise one specific thing a colleague did, in front of others.

options.label: Pass the credit to the team

insight.reveal: In your eyes, good work is always a group photo. Teams love you for it and trust you with credit. Big chances sometimes go to louder people, though, so naming your own part now and then is just as honest.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility, being fair, sincere and modest, predicted integrity at work better than the classic five personality traits.
insight.step: Next time, say 'thank you' first, then mention the team.

options.label: Downplay it: 'It was nothing'
