options.label: Say yes, then wish I'd said no

insight.reveal: Your yes often comes out before you've checked how you feel. A week of someone else's chores seems easier than five awkward seconds of no, so your calendar fills with other people's plans. The kindness is real. It just deserves a quick pause first.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next request you get, say "Let me check and get back to you" before answering.

followUp.prompt: Did someone ask you for a favour today? What did you say?

options.label: I said yes and was glad to
options.reflection: Saying yes felt easy today, which suggests the favour fit your life and your mood. That kind of help tends to feel good on both sides. Tomorrow, notice what made this one easy; it may help you spot the ones that won't be.

options.label: I said yes, then wished I hadn't
options.reflection: You said yes and then felt the weight of it. That pull between kindness and your own limits is very common. Tomorrow, you might try pausing for a breath before answering, just to check what you really have room for.

options.label: I found a polite way to say no
options.reflection: You found a kind way to protect your time today. A thoughtful no can be just as caring as a yes, because it keeps your later yeses honest. Tomorrow, notice whether saying it left you lighter or a little uneasy.

options.label: Nobody asked me for anything
options.reflection: No favours came your way today, so your time stayed your own. That can be a quiet gift. Tomorrow, if someone does ask, you might notice your very first feeling before you answer; it often knows what you want.

questions.prompt: Some unexpected extra money arrives. What would you enjoy most?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: You'd rather have breathing room than a new thing. You can wait for things others grab at once, and that patience quietly adds up over the years. The tricky part for you is the spending: even a treat you've fully earned can feel like it needs a good excuse.
insight.step: Next time extra money turns up, spend a tiny part on something purely fun and notice how it feels.

options.label: A treat for myself

insight.reveal: You celebrate good luck while it's still warm. You're fun to be around when things go right, and you don't wait for a perfect moment to enjoy life. One small twist: looking back, a good evening out will probably make you happier than a new thing.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money brings more joy when spent on experiences, on others, on many small treats rather than one big one, and on things to look forward to.
insight.step: Next treat, choose an experience instead of an object and compare how long the happy feeling lasts.

options.label: A day out or trip

insight.reveal: You'd trade a new gadget for a good story any day. Your phone is full of small adventures, and your cupboards hold less clutter than most. Ask you about your best day this year, and you'll describe a place, never a purchase.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, plan one small outing with someone you like: a new walk, or a meal somewhere you've never tried.

options.label: Quietly spending it on someone else

insight.reveal: Your best gifts are the ones nobody knows came from you. You remember the thing a friend mentioned wanting months ago, then turn up with it on an ordinary day. A quiet gift lifts you more than anything you'd buy yourself, which is a lovely kind of selfish.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, buy a small surprise for someone and don't tell anyone else.

followUp.prompt: Did you spend or save any money today in a way that felt good?

options.label: I put a little money aside
options.reflection: Setting something aside today suggests you like the calm of knowing there's a cushion. That steady habit often pays back in peace of mind. Tomorrow, you might also allow one small, unplanned pleasure, just to keep things balanced.

options.label: I bought myself a small treat
options.reflection: You gave yourself a little something today. Small treats can be a real way of looking after yourself, especially on long days. Tomorrow, notice whether the good feeling stayed with you or faded quickly; both tell you something.

options.label: I spent a little on someone else
options.reflection: You chose to spend on someone else today. Giving tends to bring a warmth that lasts longer than buying for yourself. Tomorrow, you might remember how they reacted, and how much of that joy came back to you.

options.label: Money didn't really come up today
options.reflection: Money stayed in the background today, which can be restful. Tomorrow, if something does come up, you might pause and ask what would bring you the most lasting joy, rather than the quickest one.

questions.prompt: Where are you with volunteering?

options.label: I do it regularly

insight.reveal: Giving is part of your week, not a mood that comes and goes. Through it you've likely made friends of every age, people you'd never have met otherwise. On a slow, rainy weekend, you have somewhere to be and someone who's glad you came.

options.label: Now and then, when someone asks

insight.reveal: A friend's ask moves you more than any poster ever could. You help through people rather than causes, so your help tends to land exactly where it's needed. When someone's plans fall apart, yours is one of the first numbers they call.

options.label: I keep meaning to start

insight.reveal: Your care is real, but 'someday' keeps winning. Full weeks push good plans to the back, and there may be a website or two you saved and never opened again. Picking an actual day, place and time is usually what turns 'soon' into a first visit.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.

That everyday kind of help is far more common than signing up to volunteer, and those close to you may only notice how much you carry once you're away for a week.
insight.research: In 2023, 28% of Americans volunteered through an organisation, but 54% informally helped neighbours, like running errands or lending tools.
insight.step: This week, keep up one quiet kindness and let it stay unseen.

followUp.prompt: Did you give some of your time to someone or something today?

options.label: I volunteered or helped out somewhere
options.reflection: You gave your time today, and time is one of the most generous things to give. People who do this often feel more connected to where they live. Tomorrow, notice whether any part of it stayed with you as a good memory.

options.label: I helped someone quietly, in my own way
options.reflection: Your help today happened quietly, without a label or an audience. That kind of everyday giving often matters deeply to the person on the other end. Tomorrow, you might let yourself count it; it really does count.

options.label: I meant to, but it didn't happen
options.reflection: The wish to help was there today, even if the moment slipped away. That gap between meaning to and doing is very human. Tomorrow, you might pick one tiny, concrete way to give, small enough to fit into an ordinary day.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Giving your time didn't come up today, and that's alright; some days are full enough already. Tomorrow, you might notice one small need around you, with no pressure to fix it, just to see what's there.

questions.prompt: You helped someone a lot and nobody noticed. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, that wasn't the point

insight.reveal: You'd help the same way with the lights off. Whether or not anyone's watching, you act the same, and people sense it. At work you get trusted with the sensitive stuff, and friends bring you the secrets they'd tell nobody else.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, do one small helpful thing that nobody will ever trace back to you.

options.label: I find a way to mention it

insight.reveal: Wanting your effort to be seen is completely fair. You're good at making invisible work visible, the kind that otherwise vanishes into 'it just got done'. A hint can get missed, though, while a plain 'I worked hard on that' usually lands and feels better too.

options.label: A little hurt, honestly

insight.reveal: That little sting shows how much care you put in. You give more thought to helping than anyone sees: the timing, the details, the extra step nobody asked for. Hoping someone notices doesn't make it less generous. It just means you're human.
insight.research: People writing thank-you letters tended to underestimate how happy and surprised the receiver would be.

options.label: I remember it for a long time

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet record of the help nobody thanked. You notice what's unfair long before others do, and you'd never short-change anyone yourself. Over the years, though, that record can grow heavier than the help ever was, and you're allowed to set some of it down.
insight.step: This week, pick one old unthanked effort and let it go out loud: "I did that because I wanted to."

followUp.prompt: Did you do something for someone today that nobody noticed?

options.label: Yes, and I didn't mind at all
options.reflection: You helped today and let it go without needing credit. That ease often comes from helping for its own sake. Tomorrow, you might still notice one thing you did well, just for yourself; quiet kindness deserves your own thanks too.

options.label: Yes, so I found a way to mention it
options.reflection: You found a way to let your effort be seen today. Wanting to be noticed is natural, not vain; it is how we feel valued. Tomorrow, you might try saying it plainly, without hinting, and see how much easier it lands.

options.label: Yes, and it stung a little
options.reflection: It hurt a little when your effort went unseen today. That sting usually means the help mattered to you. Tomorrow, you might gently tell someone what you did, or simply thank yourself before you wait for anyone else to.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Nothing like that happened today. Tomorrow, you might notice the small things others do for you that could easily go unseen, and thank one of them; it's often a quick way to feel the worth of your own efforts too.

questions.prompt: You're struggling with something. How easily do you ask for help?

options.label: Easily

insight.reveal: Asking for help feels as normal to you as offering it. That makes others feel trusted and useful, so they tend to show up fast. You sort out problems sooner than friends who struggle alone, and you rarely carry something heavy longer than you have to.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: This week, ask someone for a small piece of advice, just to let them help.

options.label: Only for practical things

insight.reveal: You'll ask for help carrying boxes, but rarely for comfort. Help with jobs feels fair and easy to repay; help with feelings feels like owing too much. Yet the friend who turns up to carry boxes is often the very one who'd happily sit and listen too.
insight.step: This week, tell one person how you're really feeling, not just what you need done.

options.label: Only when it's almost too late

insight.reveal: You hate the idea of your problems landing on anyone else. So you handle a surprising amount alone, and you're usually first to help when someone else is struggling. Meanwhile your own pile grows quietly, and things are much easier to ask about while they're still small.
insight.step: This week, ask for help with one thing while it's still small.

options.label: I'd rather help someone else

insight.reveal: Giving care feels safer to you than needing it. You're likely the steady one everyone calls in a crisis, the one who knows what to bring and what to say. Being on the receiving end can feel exposed, but the people who love you would welcome a turn at looking after you.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person being helped.
insight.step: This week, let someone do one small thing for you, and simply say thank you.

followUp.prompt: Did you need help with anything today? Did you ask for it?

options.label: I asked, and it felt easy
options.reflection: You reached out today and it came easily. Being able to lean on people tends to make hard things lighter and bonds stronger. Tomorrow, notice who you turned to; they may be someone worth thanking, or leaning on a little more.

options.label: I asked, but only for practical things
options.reflection: You asked for help with something practical today. That's a real start; the harder part for many people is asking for support with feelings. Tomorrow, you might share one small worry, not just one task, with someone you trust.

options.label: I needed help but did it alone
options.reflection: You carried something on your own today when help might have eased it. That self-reliance often grew for good reasons. Tomorrow, you might ask for one small thing, just to remind yourself that people often like being asked.

options.label: I didn't need help today
options.reflection: Today went by without needing anyone's help, which can feel nice and steady. Tomorrow, if something does feel heavy, you might notice the first person who comes to mind; that's often the one you trust most.

questions.prompt: A coworker or classmate is clearly overwhelmed. What do you do?

options.label: Offer to take something off their plate

insight.reveal: For you, help means rolling up your sleeves. Your team leans on you more than anyone says out loud. When a project gets rescued at the last minute, your name tends to come up, even if you'd rather it didn't.
insight.step: Next time you offer help, name one specific task instead of saying "let me know".

options.label: Bring them a coffee or snack

insight.reveal: A well-timed snack is your way of saying 'I see you'. You remember how each colleague takes their coffee, and who skips lunch when things get busy. Big rescues get the praise, but your small comforts often get someone through a long afternoon, and giving them probably lifts your mood too.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, surprise someone who's swamped with a small treat.

options.label: Wait until they ask

insight.reveal: You trust people to know what they need. You'd make the kind of manager who never hovers, and you give others the space you'd want yourself. Overwhelmed people rarely ask, though, which is partly how they got swamped, so one gentle question can open the door.
insight.step: Next time someone looks stressed, ask one gentle question: "How are you holding up?"

options.label: Keep my head down, I have my own pile

insight.reveal: You know your limits, and you're honest about them. You protect your energy so you can keep your own promises, and that isn't unkind. Still, a quick 'Rough week? Hang in there' takes ten seconds, and small kindnesses on busy days tend to steady your own mood too.
insight.research: In a daily diary study, on stressful days people who did more small helpful acts, like holding a door, kept their mood better than on stressful days when they helped less.
insight.step: This week, send one short kind message to a busy coworker or classmate.

followUp.prompt: Did you notice anyone around you struggling today? What happened?

options.label: I took something off their plate
options.reflection: You stepped in and shared someone's load today. That kind of practical help is often remembered long after the day itself. Tomorrow, check in with your own pile too; helping works best when you're not running on empty.

options.label: I brought a drink or a kind word
options.reflection: A small gesture from you may have changed the feel of someone's day. Little kindnesses often say I see you more clearly than big ones. Tomorrow, you might notice whether they seem a bit lighter, and how it felt to have helped.

options.label: I stayed focused on my own work
options.reflection: You kept your head down today, maybe because your own load was heavy too. Protecting your focus isn't unkind. Tomorrow, if there's a spare moment, a short check-in might be enough to let them know you noticed.

options.label: Everyone seemed fine today
options.reflection: Nobody around you seemed overwhelmed today, or it stayed out of sight. Tomorrow, you might glance around once in the afternoon, when energy tends to dip, and see if anyone could use a kind word.

questions.prompt: You find a wallet on the ground. What happens next?

options.label: Hand it in where it can be claimed

insight.reveal: Doing the right thing doesn't take you long to decide. You stay honest even when nobody would ever find out, and people pick up on it. You end up holding the spare key, the cash box or the sensitive file, without anyone quite saying why.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, notice one small rule you keep even when no one is watching, and give yourself credit for it.

options.label: Look inside and contact the owner myself

insight.reveal: Passing a job on never feels quite finished to you. Lost emails get chased and forgotten tasks get closed when you're around. Secretly, you might enjoy the detective work a little, and the owner's relief when you track them down is half the reward.
insight.step: This week, finish one small task someone else started and forgot.

options.label: Leave it where it is, they may come back

insight.reveal: You picture the owner retracing their steps. You think from the other person's side first, which makes you patient and fair. Here, though, the wallet could wait a long time on the ground, and a nearby shop or front desk is often the kinder place to leave it.
insight.research: When 17,303 'lost' wallets were handed to staff at banks, hotels and offices in 40 countries, people returned 51% of those with money in them and 40% of those without.
insight.step: Next time you see something lost, ask a nearby shop or staff member what to do.

options.label: Return it, then wonder if they'd do the same

insight.reveal: You do the right thing, then wonder if it's a two-way street. You hold yourself to high standards and quietly hope others do too. That question isn't bitterness. It shows how much you want people to be good, and you light up a little every time a stranger proves you right.
insight.research: People tend to expect lost wallets to be returned about half as often as they really are.
insight.step: This week, notice one example of a stranger being kind and remember it.

followUp.prompt: Did you have a small chance to be honest when it was easier not to be?

options.label: I returned something someone had lost
options.reflection: You made sure something found its way home today. Small acts of honesty like this often go unthanked, yet they quietly build trust between strangers. Tomorrow, you might let yourself feel a little proud of it.

options.label: I pointed out a mistake in my favour
options.reflection: You spoke up about a mistake that would have helped you. That kind of honesty tends to come from a steady sense of who you want to be. Tomorrow, notice how it felt afterwards; that feeling may be worth more than what you gave back.

options.label: I left it for someone else to sort out
options.reflection: You left it for someone else to handle today, maybe because it wasn't clear what to do, or there wasn't time. Tomorrow, if something similar comes up, you might take one small step and see how it feels to see it through.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Nothing like that crossed your path today. Tomorrow, you might notice the small honest choices you make without thinking, like waiting your turn or owning a slip; they often say a lot about you.

questions.prompt: Which small kindness did you do most recently?

options.label: Held a door or let someone go first

insight.reveal: Little courtesies come so easily you've stopped counting them. You're part of what makes shops, buses and offices feel human. Over a year you've held a hundred doors, and at least one of them was for someone having a truly terrible day.
insight.step: This week, add one word to the gesture: a smile and "after you".

options.label: Checked on someone who'd gone quiet

insight.reveal: You notice who's missing, not just who's there. You spot the friend who stopped replying in the group chat, or the colleague who's suddenly skipping lunch. Your message often arrives at exactly the right moment, and you may never find out how much it meant.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, check on one more person who has gone quiet for a while.

options.label: Gave a stranger a real compliment

insight.reveal: The nice thoughts most people keep inside, you say out loud. Waiting rooms and slow checkouts get brighter when you're in them. A sincere compliment from a stranger is the kind of thing people repeat to friends that evening, so some of yours are still being talked about.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment tend to underestimate how good it will make the other person feel.
insight.step: This week, give someone one specific compliment about a choice they made, not their looks.

options.label: I can't think of one

insight.reveal: Maybe your kindness is so automatic you've stopped seeing it. Or this season is so full there's barely room to notice anything. Either way, you likely do more for others than you give yourself credit for, and one day of paying attention would surprise you.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness gave the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being, whoever they were and whatever the kindness.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one small kind thing on purpose, and notice how it feels.

followUp.prompt: Was there a small kindness you did for someone today?

options.label: I held a door or let someone go first
options.reflection: You made room for someone today, even in a small way. These tiny courtesies often set the tone for how strangers treat each other. Tomorrow, you might notice whether anyone passes the same kindness on; it tends to travel.

options.label: I checked on someone who'd gone quiet
options.reflection: You noticed someone had gone quiet and reached out. That kind of attention can mean a lot to a person who felt overlooked. Tomorrow, you might gently follow up, even with a short message, so they know it wasn't a one-off.

options.label: I gave someone a real compliment
options.reflection: You told someone something good about them today. A sincere compliment often stays with people for longer than you'd guess. Tomorrow, notice how your own mood shifted after giving it; it can lift you both.

options.label: I can't think of one today
options.reflection: Nothing comes to mind today, and that's okay; busy or hard days can crowd out these moments. Tomorrow, you might choose one easy kindness in the morning, like a warm hello, and let it set the tone.

questions.prompt: Someone asks a favour you really don't have time for. You…

options.label: Say no, kindly

insight.reveal: You trust a good friendship to survive an honest no. People may ask you a little less often, but when you say yes, they know you mean it. That makes your word worth more than most, and your calendar stays yours.
insight.step: Next time you say no, add one thing you can do, even if it's small.

options.label: Offer a smaller version

insight.reveal: Somewhere between yes and no, you always find a path. 'I can't help all day, but I can come for the first hour' is very you. You protect your time and the friendship at once, and quietly teach people what's fair to ask.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to tended to boost the well-being of both the helper and the person helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, have one line ready: "I can't do all of that, but I can do this part."

options.label: Say yes and stretch myself

insight.reveal: Being useful is a big part of how you feel good about yourself. You're the dependable one in every group, which is lovely and also tiring. The same stretch shows up at work and at home, and the people who rely on you would cope with a 'not this time' now and then.
insight.step: Next time you want to say yes automatically, pause for one breath and ask: do I have time?

options.label: Say yes, then do it late or half-heartedly

insight.reveal: Your yes saves an awkward moment, then costs you later. You're warm and you hate letting people down, which is exactly why no feels so hard to say. A late, half-done job weighs more than a clear no ever would, and most people would honestly rather hear it early.
insight.step: Next time, say "Let me check" first, then answer within a day.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone ask for your time today when you had little to spare?

options.label: I said no, kindly
options.reflection: You said no today, and did it with care. Holding a limit gently often protects both your time and the relationship. Tomorrow, notice whether any guilt lingers; if it does, remind yourself that a kind no is still kind.

options.label: I offered a smaller version
options.reflection: You found a middle path today, giving what you could rather than all or nothing. That flexible kind of help tends to keep both of you happy. Tomorrow, you might notice how easily you can offer this again.

options.label: I said yes and stretched myself thin
options.reflection: You said yes even though your plate was full. That generosity is real, though it may have cost you some rest. Tomorrow, you might give yourself one small pocket of time that's only yours, to refill what you gave away.

options.label: Nobody asked today
options.reflection: No one asked for more than you had today. Tomorrow, if someone does, you might take a breath before answering and ask yourself what you can truly give; a smaller yes is often still a good one.

questions.prompt: Think of a really good day you had. What made it good?

options.label: Everything went to plan

insight.reveal: For you, a good day is one where nothing went wrong. With you around, tickets are booked and the charger is packed long before anyone else thinks of it. The twist is that trips can feel oddly tiring, because every surprise lands on you as one more thing to handle.
insight.step: On one free day this week, leave one hour with no plan and notice how it feels.

options.label: I finally finished something hard

insight.reveal: You like to earn your good mood before you enjoy it. You get a lot done, and finishing gives you a glow nothing else quite matches. A lazy day with nothing crossed off, though, can leave you restless, as if you skipped a step before being allowed to relax.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily diaries from 238 workers, the best days tended to be the ones where people made progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: One evening this week, note one good thing that happened that you did not have to earn.

options.label: A long talk with someone I like

insight.reveal: Your best days happen in conversation. You remember a trip less by the views and more by who said what over dinner. A good talk can keep you going for days, and you've probably missed a last bus or two because nobody wanted to stop.
insight.research: When 909 working women went back over their previous day, time relaxing with friends tended to feel the most enjoyable part of it.
insight.step: Before the week ends, invite one person for a talk with no other purpose: a walk, a call, a tea.

options.label: Hours alone where nobody needed me

insight.reveal: Bliss, for you, is a few hours when nobody needs anything. You give a lot all week, mostly without complaining, to family, work and friends. Often you only feel how much it cost when the house goes quiet and you can finally hear yourself think.
insight.step: This week, put a two-hour 'nobody needs me' block in your calendar and guard it like a meeting.

followUp.prompt: Was there a good moment in your day? What made it good?

options.label: I finished something I'd put off
options.reflection: Getting something done gave your day its lift. You may be someone who feels lightest when loose ends are tied. Tomorrow, you might pick one small, finishable task early, so that feeling arrives sooner.

options.label: I had a good talk with someone
options.reflection: A real conversation brightened your day. Connection seems to feed you, and it often does more for a mood than we expect. Tomorrow, you might reach out to that person again, or to someone you haven't talked to in a while.

options.label: I had some time to myself
options.reflection: Time on your own was the good part of today. Quiet hours may be how you recharge and hear your own thoughts. Tomorrow, you might protect a small pocket of that time on purpose, rather than waiting for it to appear.

options.label: Today was short on good moments
options.reflection: Today was short on good moments, and it's okay to say so. Hard days happen to everyone. Tomorrow, you might look for one small thing to enjoy, like a warm drink or a song you love, without expecting it to fix everything.

questions.prompt: Something small goes well for you. Who do you tell first?

options.label: Nobody, I just enjoy it quietly

insight.reveal: You hold good news like a warm drink, slowly and privately. You're steady and don't need applause. The hidden cost is that friends rarely learn what makes you happy, so they miss chances to help you get more of it.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Next time something small goes well, tell one person within the hour and watch their face.

options.label: My partner or closest friend

insight.reveal: Good news isn't finished for you until one person has heard it. You reach for your phone mid-moment, already typing their name. That reflex says a lot about the room this person holds in your life, and they'd be touched to know it.
insight.step: This week, ask your closest person about their small win before you share yours.

options.label: The group chat, with a photo

insight.reveal: Happiness gets bigger for you the more people it bounces off. You're the spark of your group chat and quick to cheer others on too. The flip side is that a silent reply can make a good moment feel smaller than it was, even when everyone's just busy.
insight.research: When people shared good news, an eager, interested reply tended to add to their joy, while a flat or dismissive reply took some of it away.
insight.step: Next time you share good news, notice if the joy peaks before the replies arrive, or after.

options.label: Someone whose approval still matters to me

insight.reveal: A win feels fully real once a certain someone has seen it. Lots of people carry one person from long ago whose nod still counts most: a parent, a teacher, an old boss. That can push you to great things, but it may also be quietly picking your goals, so it's worth asking if they're still yours.
insight.step: After your next small win, wait one minute and decide how proud you are before telling anyone.

followUp.prompt: Did something go well for you today? Did you tell anyone?

options.label: Yes, and I kept it to myself
options.reflection: You enjoyed your good moment privately today. There's something calm about savouring a win without needing an audience. Tomorrow, you might still tell one person, just to see whether sharing makes the good feeling last longer.

options.label: I told my partner or a close friend
options.reflection: You brought your good news to someone close. Sharing small wins with people who care tends to deepen both the joy and the bond. Tomorrow, you might ask about their day too, and celebrate something of theirs.

options.label: I shared it with a group or online
options.reflection: You let your good news travel today. Sharing it widely can multiply the happy feeling. Tomorrow, you might also notice which reply meant the most to you; that person may be someone worth getting closer to.

options.label: Nothing stood out as a win today
options.reflection: No clear win stood out today, which is common on ordinary days. Small wins often hide in plain sight. Tomorrow, before bed, you might name one thing that went even a little right; it can change how the day feels.

questions.prompt: An unexpected free afternoon appears. What do you do with it?

options.label: Rest on the sofa, no guilt

insight.reveal: Switching off on purpose is a real skill, and you have it. Plenty of grown-ups lose it somewhere along the way. You come back to your week genuinely refreshed, and the 'no guilt' part is rarer than the resting itself, so hold on to it.
insight.research: Across 91 samples and 38,000 people, mentally switching off from work in free time went with less exhaustion, better well-being and better sleep.
insight.step: Next free hour, rest fully, then name one thing that made it feel restful.

options.label: Go somewhere I've never been

insight.reveal: New places fill you up instead of wearing you out. One unfamiliar street can stay with you longer than a month of ordinary weeks. Chances are you know a few hidden spots in your own town that people who've lived there for years have never found.
insight.step: This week, take a different route home or eat somewhere new, and notice what you remember a day later.

options.label: Catch up on tasks I've been avoiding

insight.reveal: Free time feels like a debt you have to pay off first. You enjoy rest far more once that one nagging job is done, and that's fair. The trouble is that the list grows to fill every gap if you let it lead, and the afternoon can vanish without any rest at all.
insight.step: Next free afternoon, do exactly one task, then spend the rest on something you enjoy.

options.label: Scroll my phone and somehow lose it

insight.reveal: When choosing feels like work, your phone chooses for you. That's often tiredness, not laziness, and you may be more stretched than you let on. The free afternoons you end up remembering tend to be the ones you decided on in the first few minutes.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next free afternoon, try a when-then plan: 'When free time appears, I'll pick one thing to do before I unlock my phone.'

followUp.prompt: If a free hour opened up today, what did it turn into?

options.label: I rested, and didn't feel guilty
options.reflection: You let yourself rest today without guilt, which is harder than it sounds for many people. Real rest often makes the next day go better. Tomorrow, you might notice what made it possible, so you can find it again.

options.label: I went somewhere or tried something new
options.reflection: You used your free time to explore something new. Fresh places and ideas tend to make days feel fuller and richer in memory. Tomorrow, you might keep a little of that curiosity going, even on a short walk.

options.label: It slipped away on my phone
options.reflection: Your free time drifted into your phone today. That happens to almost everyone; screens are built to hold us. Tomorrow, you might decide one thing you'd love to do with spare time before it arrives, so it has somewhere to go.

options.label: I didn't get any free time today
options.reflection: Today was full, and there wasn't much time that felt like yours. Tomorrow, you might look for ten quiet minutes and decide in advance how you'd like to spend them, so they don't slip past.

questions.prompt: A friend shares big news online. What's your first honest feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: Other people's good news doesn't take anything from you. You measure your life against your own past, not your friends' highlights, so scrolling rarely dents your mood. No wonder friends want to tell you their news first.
insight.step: This week, send one friend a message saying exactly why their news made you happy.

options.label: Happy, then I quietly check my own life

insight.reveal: Your happiness for them comes with a quick, quiet scorecard. That's very human, and it shows you're ambitious and paying attention. Notice which part of your life you check first: work, love, money, home. It often points at what you want most right now.
insight.step: Next time you compare, notice which part of your life you checked, and name it in one word.

options.label: A small sting I'd never admit out loud

insight.reveal: You're honest enough to feel the sting and name it. That little envy is a signpost, not a flaw. It usually points at something you want but haven't let yourself go after yet, which makes it oddly useful once you stop being embarrassed by it.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone else has without wishing them harm, tended to push people to work harder, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: Next time you feel that sting, ask: what exactly do I want here? Then pick one tiny step toward it.

options.label: I scroll past fast or mute them

insight.reveal: Sometimes you protect your mood by letting less in. That can be wise, especially in a hard week. Your friend may read the silence as distance, though, even when it was only about what you were carrying, and a late reply is still a warm one.
insight.research: In a large experiment, people paid to stop using Facebook for four weeks became a little happier and spent more time with family and friends.
insight.step: If you scroll past someone's news this week, come back a day later and react when you feel ready.

followUp.prompt: Did you see someone else's good news today? How did it sit with you?

options.label: I felt truly happy for them
options.reflection: Someone else's good news lifted you today. Being able to share in others' joy tends to keep friendships warm. Tomorrow, you might tell them directly how pleased you are; it often means more to hear than to see a like.

options.label: Happy, then I compared my own life
options.reflection: You felt glad for them and also turned to look at your own life. That mix is very human, not a flaw. Tomorrow, you might remember you're seeing their highlight, and name one thing in your own life you wouldn't swap.

options.label: I scrolled past or looked away
options.reflection: You chose to look away today. Sometimes that's a wise way to protect a tender mood. Tomorrow, you might gently ask yourself what the news touched in you; it may point to something you want for yourself.

options.label: I didn't see any big news today
options.reflection: No big news from others crossed your screen today. Tomorrow, you might notice how you feel after time online, lighter or heavier, and let that guide how much of it you want.

questions.prompt: Someone does something kind for you. How do you respond?

options.label: A quick thank you, then move on

insight.reveal: You like kindness light and even, so nobody owes anyone. You're easygoing and gracious, and you never make a fuss. The same balance can make asking for help feel hard, because asking tips the scales the other way.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there really was.
insight.step: This week, thank someone with one specific detail about what their kindness changed for you.

options.label: I feel I must return it soon

insight.reveal: Somewhere in your head there's a neat list of who did what. You're a remarkably reliable friend, and borrowed dishes come back from your house clean and fast. The only downside: a gift can feel like a task until it's repaid, which drains some of the warmth out of it.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, wait a full week before giving anything back, and just enjoy receiving.

options.label: I feel awkward, like I don't deserve it

insight.reveal: Receiving is harder for you than giving. You're quick to say 'you didn't have to' and slow to just enjoy it. Part of your generosity may come from giving feeling safer, and letting a kindness simply land, with a plain thank you, gets easier every time you try.
insight.step: Next time someone is kind, try saying only 'Thank you, that means a lot', and leave out the 'you didn't have to'.

options.label: I wonder what they want from me

insight.reveal: You've learned that kindness sometimes comes with a price tag. That makes you hard to fool and sharp at reading motives. It's worth asking, gently, whether the people around you now have earned the same caution as the ones who taught it to you.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, accept one small kindness without looking for the reason, and see what actually follows.

followUp.prompt: Did someone do something kind for you today? How did you take it?

options.label: I said thanks and enjoyed it
options.reflection: You took the kindness in and let it be enough. Receiving well is its own skill, and it lets the giver feel good too. Tomorrow, you might notice one more small kindness that comes your way; they're often easy to miss.

options.label: I want to return the favour soon
options.reflection: You're already thinking about how to give back. That sense of fairness tends to make you a good friend. Tomorrow, you might also let yourself simply enjoy what you received, without rushing to balance the books.

options.label: I felt awkward, like I didn't deserve it
options.reflection: Being cared for felt a little uncomfortable today. Many people find receiving harder than giving. Tomorrow, you might try a simple thank you, that means a lot, and let the kindness land without explaining it away.

options.label: Nothing comes to mind today
options.reflection: No kindness stands out from today, and some days are like that. Tomorrow, you might watch for small ones, like someone holding a door or asking how you are; they often happen more than we notice.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected money. What would make you happiest?

options.label: Saving it

insight.reveal: Safe and steady is your kind of happy. A growing buffer quiets your mind in a way no purchase can. You check your savings the way other people check the weather, and a bigger safety net beats a bigger treat for you almost every time.
insight.step: This week, picture what 'safe enough' looks like for you, so saving has a finish line.

options.label: A trip, a concert or a great meal

insight.reveal: You spend on memories, and you get your money's worth twice. Once on the night, then again every time you tell the story. Long after the bill is forgotten, you're still describing that meal or that concert to friends, and it gets better with each retelling.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This month, plan one small outing you'll enjoy, then tell someone the story afterwards.

options.label: Treating someone I love

insight.reveal: Your happiness travels through other people's faces. You're wonderful at gifts and surprises, and you remember exactly what lights someone up. You may forget to treat yourself, though, and only notice after a generous month that your own cup has run low.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: This week, do one small kind thing for someone else, and one for yourself.

options.label: The thing I've wanted for months

insight.reveal: You've been patient with this wish, and now it gets its turn. You compare options carefully rather than buying on a whim, so you probably know the exact model and the best price already. Half the pleasure was the wanting, so enjoy the getting slowly.
insight.research: In two diary studies, things people bought gave small bursts of happiness more often over two weeks, while experiences gave stronger but rarer moments.
insight.step: Before buying, picture using it on an ordinary weekday a month from now. Still exciting? Enjoy it.

followUp.prompt: Did anything you paid for today bring you real joy?

options.label: A meal, an outing or an experience
options.reflection: You spent on an experience today. Moments like a meal or an outing often keep giving through memory, long after the money's gone. Tomorrow, you might retell the best part to someone, and enjoy it a second time.

options.label: Treating someone I love
options.reflection: You chose to treat someone you love. Spending on others tends to bring a warm glow that outlasts most purchases. Tomorrow, you might notice whether that warmth is still there, and what it tells you about what matters to you.

options.label: Something I'd wanted for ages
options.reflection: You finally got the thing you'd been wanting. That rush is real and worth enjoying. Tomorrow, you might notice how it feels once the newness settles; it can show you which wants run deep and which are passing.

options.label: I didn't spend on anything fun today
options.reflection: Nothing fun went on spending today, and that can be a relief. Tomorrow, you might think about which small purchase would truly bring you joy, perhaps a shared moment rather than a new thing.

questions.prompt: How do your mornings usually start?

options.label: Slowly, with something warm to drink

insight.reveal: Your first cup is a small ritual that sets the tone for your day. You're calmer than most in the first meeting or class of the day. When the ritual gets skipped, everything can feel slightly off for hours, and you might not connect the two until the afternoon.
insight.research: A review of ritual research found that set rituals, religious or everyday, tend to help people manage worry, feel more in control and feel bonded to the people they share them with.
insight.step: On a rushed morning this week, keep just two minutes of your ritual and see if the day feels different.

options.label: Phone first, before my feet touch the floor

insight.reveal: Other people's news gets to you before your own thoughts do. You're quick to reply and know what happened overnight before you've brushed your teeth. Moving the phone just out of reach tends to make mornings feel longer, and your best ideas may be waiting in that quiet gap.
insight.step: For three mornings, keep the phone out of reach until you've had water or daylight.

options.label: Rushing, already a bit behind

insight.reveal: Your mornings start in a hurry, owing time you never had. You probably guard your late evenings fiercely, because night is the only time that feels truly yours. You may be at your sharpest after dark, which is great for ideas and rough on alarms.
insight.research: Many people go to bed later than they meant to for no outside reason, and this 'bedtime procrastination' was linked to too little sleep and next-day tiredness.
insight.step: For the next three mornings, try one when-then plan: 'When my alarm rings, I'll stand up and drink water.'

options.label: With a heavy feeling about the day ahead

insight.reveal: You feel the weight of the day before it has even started. That's tiring, and it says you take what's ahead seriously. The heaviness is often tied to one specific thing, and naming it can lighten the rest. The day doesn't have to be carried all at once.
insight.step: Tomorrow morning, name the one thing behind the heavy feeling, then do the smallest part of it first.

followUp.prompt: Looking back, how did your morning actually start today?

options.label: Slowly, with something warm
options.reflection: Your day started gently today. A calm first hour often sets a softer tone for everything after it. Tomorrow, you might notice what helped make that possible, and protect it on busier mornings too.

options.label: Phone first, before I got up
options.reflection: Your phone was the first thing you met today. That's very common, and it can pull your mind into other people's needs before your own. Tomorrow, you might try a few slow breaths or a glass of water before you look at the screen.

options.label: Rushed and already behind
options.reflection: You started today on the back foot. Rushed mornings often leave a buzz of hurry that lingers into the afternoon. Tomorrow, you might set out one thing tonight, like clothes or keys, so the morning starts a little kinder.

options.label: Honestly, it's a blur now
options.reflection: Your morning has faded into a blur, which often happens on full days. Tomorrow, you might pause for a moment after waking, notice one thing, like the light or a sound, and give the day a gentle start you'll remember.

questions.prompt: Which of these has given you the most joy lately?

options.label: A really good meal

insight.reveal: Joy finds you through your senses, one bite at a time. You notice the weather, the smell of fresh bread and the sound of rain that other people walk straight past. Friends ask you where to eat, and you're rarely wrong.
insight.research: Training people to slow down and enjoy good moments, called savouring, moderately boosted good feelings and eased low ones across 20 trials with 4,805 people.
insight.step: At one meal this week, eat the first three bites with no phone and full attention.

options.label: Helping someone with a problem

insight.reveal: Nothing lifts you quite like fixing someone's problem. You're first in line when a friend is stuck, whether it's a broken phone or a broken heart. On a long break with nobody needing anything, you might feel oddly lost, so it helps to keep a little usefulness in your rest too.
insight.research: Across 27 studies with over 4,000 people, doing acts of kindness tended to give the kind person a small-to-medium boost in well-being.
insight.step: This week, offer help with something small that nobody asked for, and notice your mood after.

options.label: Getting better at something

insight.reveal: You enjoy the climb more than the view from the top. You pick up new skills fast and love the moment something finally clicks. Once you've mastered one, restlessness creeps in, and you're probably already eyeing the next hard thing to learn.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily work diaries, people's best days tended to be the ones where they made progress on work that mattered to them; setbacks hit harder.
insight.step: This week, pick one skill and spend ten minutes on it on three different days. Missing one is fine.

options.label: Honestly, it's hard to say right now

insight.reveal: It sounds like you've been carrying a lot lately. When duty fills every corner, joy tends to go quiet rather than disappear. Small, specific pleasures, like a song you love or a few minutes in the sun, often bring it back sooner than big plans do.
insight.research: Across 26 trials, a method built on planning small enjoyable or meaningful activities, and noticing how they feel, lifted persistent low mood a lot.
insight.step: Each evening this week, notice one moment that was even a little bit good, however small.

followUp.prompt: What gave you a little joy today?

options.label: Something I ate or drank
options.reflection: Food brought you joy today, and that's a real, simple pleasure. Small sensory moments often anchor a good day. Tomorrow, you might slow down for one meal or drink and really taste it; it can turn an ordinary moment into a lift.

options.label: Helping someone with a problem
options.reflection: Being useful to someone gave you joy today. You may be someone who feels most alive when you're making a difference. Tomorrow, you might let someone help you too; that can bring a quieter kind of joy.

options.label: Getting better at something
options.reflection: Progress made you happy today. Feeling yourself improve tends to be one of the most lasting kinds of joy. Tomorrow, you might jot down one thing you can do now that you couldn't before; it helps on slower days.

options.label: Honestly, it's hard to say today
options.reflection: Joy was hard to find today, and that's okay to admit. Some days are flatter than others. Tomorrow, you might lower the bar and look for something small, like sunlight or a kind voice, without needing it to be big.

questions.prompt: You reach a goal you worked hard for. How do you celebrate?

options.label: Properly, with people around me

insight.reveal: You celebrate out loud, and you bring everyone along. You're just as good at cheering for others, the one who sorts out the cake and the speech. All that celebrating quietly builds the circle of people who'll show up for you when things go wrong.
insight.research: When someone shares good news, an interested, enthusiastic reply is linked to more trust and closeness, while a flat or distracted reply is linked to less.
insight.step: This week, celebrate someone else's small win as loudly as you would your own.

options.label: A small private treat

insight.reveal: Success sits calmly with you, no fireworks needed. Because you never pour all your joy into one big moment, you rarely get the slump that follows. Your treats tend to be small and oddly specific, like one particular pastry from one particular shop.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money tends to bring more joy when spent on many small treats rather than one big one.
insight.step: This week, choose your next small treat before you reach the goal, and tie it to a clear finish line.

options.label: I'm already thinking about the next goal

insight.reveal: Your finish line moves the moment you touch it. You get a lot done and remember surprisingly little of it, because you rarely stop long enough for the good feeling to sink in. Ask yourself what you achieved last year and the list may surprise you.
insight.research: Across 20 trials with 4,805 people, savouring exercises, which train people to notice and enjoy good moments, moderately boosted good feelings and eased low ones.
insight.step: Next time you finish something, wait one full day before starting a new goal.

options.label: It feels oddly flat when I get there

insight.reveal: You found out the chase meant more than the prize. That flat feeling can be confusing, but it isn't failure. You're thoughtful and searching, and it often means the next goal needs a deeper reason behind it, not a bigger target.
insight.research: People whose biggest life goals were money, looks and fame tended to have less energy and more aches and pains, while those chasing close relationships, growth and community felt better.
insight.step: Before your next goal, say in one sentence why it matters to you, not only what it is.

followUp.prompt: Did you finish or reach something today? What did you do next?

options.label: I celebrated it with someone
options.reflection: You marked your achievement with someone today. Sharing a win tends to make it feel real and complete. Tomorrow, you might notice who was glad for you; those are people worth keeping close.

options.label: I went straight on to the next thing
options.reflection: You reached something and moved right on. That drive may serve you well, though it can rush past the good part. Tomorrow, you might take one quiet minute to look back at what you did and let it count.

options.label: It felt flatter than I expected
options.reflection: The finish line felt flatter than you hoped. That often happens when the real reward was the effort along the way. Tomorrow, you might remember a moment from the process you enjoyed; that may be where the joy was hiding.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: No finish line came up today, and most days are like that, full of steps rather than endings. Tomorrow, you might notice one small step forward and give it a little credit, even if the goal is still far off.

questions.prompt: It's the last day of a holiday. What's on your mind?

options.label: Grateful it happened

insight.reveal: You close good chapters cleanly, with thanks. Because your happy memories aren't mixed with the sadness of endings, they tend to stay bright for years. You're good at goodbyes too, the guest who leaves on time without lingering at the door.
insight.research: Simple gratitude exercises, like writing down things you are thankful for, led to small improvements in mood and worry on average, though the evidence is uncertain.
insight.step: On the last day of your next break, tell someone your three best moments out loud.

options.label: Already planning the next one

insight.reveal: Something on the calendar keeps you going. The weeks of waiting can hold as much joy for you as the trip itself, so the size of the plan matters less than having one. Even a dinner booked three weeks out can carry you through a dull month.
insight.research: Holidaymakers tended to be happier than others before their trip, mostly from looking forward to it, but once home most were no happier than people who stayed.
insight.step: This week, put one small thing to look forward to in your calendar, even just coffee with a friend.

options.label: Dreading normal life and messages

insight.reveal: Coming back to normal life feels heavy for you right now. Often it isn't the whole week that drains you, just one part of it: a certain meeting, a certain inbox, a certain person. Pinpointing that one piece can help more than any trip you could book.
insight.step: This week, notice which single part of your normal week you dread most. Just name it to yourself.

options.label: Sad that I never really relaxed

insight.reveal: You brought your to-do list along on the trip. Your body rested while your mind kept checking things. You spend the first days of any break learning how to switch off, and often unwind fully just as it's time to go home, which is worth planning around.
insight.research: Across 91 samples of 38,124 workers, people who mentally switched off from work in their free time reported less exhaustion and better sleep and life satisfaction.
insight.step: On your next day off, put your work apps out of sight for the whole day.

followUp.prompt: Did you get a real break today, and how does it feel now it's over?

options.label: I had one and I'm grateful for it
options.reflection: You found a real pause today and you're holding onto it with thanks. Gratitude tends to make good moments last longer in memory. Tomorrow, you might look for another small break, even a short walk, and enjoy it fully.

options.label: I'm already planning my next break
options.reflection: Your mind has already jumped to the next break. Looking forward to something often brings as much pleasure as the thing itself. Tomorrow, you might also notice one good moment in the ordinary day, so not all your joy lives in the future.

options.label: I'm dreading going back to normal
options.reflection: The end of your break brought a heavy feeling about what's next. That dread is common and often worse than the reality. Tomorrow, you might start with the easiest task first, so the return feels gentler than you fear.

options.label: I didn't get a break today
options.reflection: There was no real pause in your day. Long stretches without rest tend to wear people down quietly. Tomorrow, you might plan one small break in advance, even five minutes outside, and treat it as something that matters.

questions.prompt: After a bad day, what helps you first?

options.label: Food and a show

insight.reveal: You comfort the body first and save the thinking for later. You let a bad day be over before you try to understand it. Usually you're ready to talk it through the next morning, not that night, and you wake up seeing it more clearly.
insight.step: After your next bad day, take the comfort first, and give yourself until morning before thinking it over.

options.label: Telling someone the whole story

insight.reveal: You make sense of your day by saying it out loud. You think best in conversation, and you often find the answer halfway through the story, before the listener has said a word. For you, a good friend is mostly a good pair of ears.
insight.step: Next bad day, ask someone to just listen for five minutes, no advice needed.

options.label: Walking or moving until it fades

insight.reveal: Your feet sort out your feelings before your words do. You think more clearly in motion, and some of your best decisions arrive mid-walk or halfway through scrubbing the kitchen. A bad day often looks smaller to you by the end of the street.
insight.research: Across more than 1,000 trials, regular physical activity, from walking to yoga or weights, tended to give medium-sized relief from low mood and worry.
insight.step: On your next stressful day, take a ten-minute walk before replying to anything important.

options.label: Nothing really, I replay it in bed

insight.reveal: Your mind keeps trying to fix the day after it's over. You're careful and thorough, and you want to get things right. After the first replay, though, the loop rarely finds anything new. You've done enough thinking for today, and it can wait until morning.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make problems harder to solve.
insight.step: Tonight, if the replay starts, write down the one thing you'd do differently, then close the notebook.

followUp.prompt: If something went wrong today, what helped you shake it off?

options.label: Food and something to watch
options.reflection: You turned to comfort and distraction to soften the day. That's a very human way to reset, and often it works. Tomorrow, you might notice whether the bad feeling has faded, or whether it needs more care than a show can give.

options.label: I told someone the whole story
options.reflection: You let someone hear the whole story. Talking things through tends to shrink a bad day down to its real size. Tomorrow, you might thank the person who listened; being heard is a gift worth naming.

options.label: Nothing yet, I'm still replaying it
options.reflection: The day is still playing on a loop in your head. That's common when something matters to you. Tonight, you might write down the worst bit and one thing you'd do differently, then let the page hold it until tomorrow.

options.label: Nothing went wrong today
options.reflection: Nothing went badly today, which is worth noticing on its own. Easy days often slip by unremarked. Tomorrow, you might take a moment to enjoy a calm stretch while it's happening, rather than only in hindsight.

questions.prompt: When stress builds up, how do you usually notice it first?

options.label: My shoulders or jaw get tight

insight.reveal: Your body hears stress before your mind admits it. You have a built-in early warning, sometimes days ahead of the worried thoughts. Chances are you've caught your shoulders up near your ears in the middle of something perfectly ordinary.
insight.step: Three times this week, check your jaw and shoulders and let them drop for one slow breath.

options.label: I snap at people over small things

insight.reveal: When you're stressed, it leaks out sideways onto whoever's near. It takes honesty to notice that about yourself. The snapping rarely has anything to do with the person in front of you, and a quick 'sorry I snapped, that was my stress' repairs more than you'd expect.
insight.research: Of six parts of an apology, admitting it was your fault mattered most to people, then offering to fix it; asking for forgiveness mattered least.
insight.step: Next time you snap, say 'Sorry I snapped. That was my stress, not you' within the hour.

options.label: Someone else tells me I seem stressed

insight.reveal: Others often see your strain before you do. You're the calm one in a crisis, the one who keeps going while everything shakes. That's a gift, but it can make you the last to notice your own tank running low, so the people who mention it are worth hearing.
insight.step: This week, ask one person you trust: 'What's the first sign you notice when I'm stressed?'

options.label: My sleep goes first

insight.reveal: Your worries wait until the house is quiet to speak up. In daylight you're busy and capable, so the thoughts only get their turn at night. They look huge at two in the morning and much smaller over breakfast, and nothing needs solving in the dark.
insight.step: Tonight, keep paper by your bed. If a worry wakes you, write it down so your mind can set it aside until morning.

followUp.prompt: Did stress show up in you today? Where did you notice it first?

options.label: My shoulders or jaw felt tight
options.reflection: Your body carried today's stress before your mind named it. Tight shoulders or a clenched jaw are often early signals. Tonight, you might drop your shoulders and unclench your teeth, and tomorrow notice when the tightness starts.

options.label: I snapped at someone over something small
options.reflection: Stress spilled out in a sharp moment today. That usually means the pressure had been building for a while, not that you're unkind. Tomorrow, you might watch for the moment just before, and give yourself a breath or a step away.

options.label: Someone told me I seemed stressed
options.reflection: Someone else saw your stress before you did. That can mean you push through without checking in with yourself. Tomorrow, you might pause once around midday, ask yourself how you're really doing, and listen to the answer.

options.label: I felt fairly calm today
options.reflection: Stress kept its distance today, which is good to notice. Tomorrow, you might think about what helped, whether sleep, pace or people, so you can lean on it again when things get busier.

questions.prompt: You don't get something you really hoped for. What happens next?

options.label: I shrug and move on quickly

insight.reveal: Setbacks slide off you faster than off most people. You're resilient and easy to work with when things go sideways. Sometimes, though, you move on before learning what the hope was really about, then find yourself chasing something very similar a year later.
insight.step: Next disappointment, give it five minutes and ask: what did I actually want from this?

options.label: I look for what I did wrong

insight.reveal: You'd rather take a lesson than a loss. You improve quickly and turn disappointment into something useful. The risk is taking the blame for things that were mostly timing or luck, and being harder on yourself than you'd ever be on a friend.
insight.research: Across 27 trials, learning to treat yourself with kindness, as a good friend would, reduced self-criticism, dwelling on problems, stress and low mood by moderate to large amounts.
insight.step: Next time, name one part that was in your control and one part that was simply luck.

options.label: I tell myself not to hope so much next time

insight.reveal: Disappointment teaches you to want a little less. It's a way of protecting yourself, and it keeps you steady under pressure. Over time, though, you may notice you've quietly stopped going after things you truly wanted, and some of those hopes still deserve a chance.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, rather than failing a duty, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: This week, say out loud one thing you still hope for, even if it might not happen.

options.label: I feel low for days and keep it to myself

insight.reveal: You feel things deeply, and you carry them quietly. From the outside you look fine, which makes it easy for others to miss and hard for you to bring up. Sharing even one small piece with someone you trust tends to make low days lighter, and if a low stretch lasts for weeks, tell a doctor too.
insight.research: People who usually hide their feelings tended to feel worse inside, share less with others and feel less close to friends than people who rethink what upset them.
insight.step: Next time you feel low for more than a day, tell one person one sentence about it.

followUp.prompt: Did anything not go your way today? How did you handle it?

options.label: I shrugged and moved on
options.reflection: You let a letdown roll off you today. That ability to bounce back is a real strength. Tomorrow, you might check whether it truly passed, or just got tucked away; both are fine, but it helps to know which.

options.label: I went over what I did wrong
options.reflection: You went looking for what you did wrong. Learning from setbacks can help, though it can tip into being hard on yourself. Tomorrow, you might also name one thing outside your control, so you're not carrying all of it.

options.label: I felt low and kept it to myself
options.reflection: You felt the disappointment and held it quietly. Keeping it in can feel safer, yet it often makes the low last longer. Tomorrow, you might share a small piece of it with someone you trust; it may lighten more than you expect.

options.label: Nothing really let me down today
options.reflection: No real disappointments today, which is something to be glad of. Tomorrow, if something doesn't go your way, you might give yourself the same kindness you'd offer a friend in that spot.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most alone?

options.label: The last evening of the weekend

insight.reveal: The quiet end of a weekend can feel strangely empty to you. It's often less about missing people and more about the gap between free time and the week ahead. A small plan for that evening, like a call, a walk or a meal you love, tends to fill it nicely.
insight.research: Across 26 trials, planning small enjoyable or meaningful activities and noticing how they feel tended to lift persistent low mood.
insight.step: Next weekend, plan one small thing for its last evening: a call, a walk or a meal with someone.

options.label: In a crowd or at a party

insight.reveal: A room full of small talk can feel lonelier than an empty one. You need depth, not just people. You might slip out of parties early, then talk for an hour with one friend on the way home, and that one real conversation is the part you remember.
insight.research: In 12 experiments with over 1,800 people, conversations with strangers felt less awkward and more enjoyable than expected, especially deeper ones.
insight.step: At your next gathering, aim for one real conversation instead of many short ones.

options.label: When good news comes and there's no one to tell

insight.reveal: Loneliness finds you most in your happy moments. For you, sharing is what makes good news feel complete. The pang usually points straight at someone you wish you could call, and that person might be really glad to hear from you.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message, call or small gift out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: Next time you have good news, send it to one person you've drifted away from.

options.label: Sometimes even with my partner or family

insight.reveal: Even close to the people you love, you sometimes feel unseen. That's a painful feeling, and it doesn't mean the bond is weak. More often a part of you hasn't been shared yet. You deserve to be known, and it can start with one small sentence.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: This week, tell someone close one thing you care about that they may not know.

followUp.prompt: Did you feel alone at any point today? When was it?

options.label: In a group, oddly enough
options.reflection: You felt alone even with people around today. That happens when the company doesn't quite reach the real you. Tomorrow, you might look for one person to talk with on their own; small, honest chats often feel less lonely than crowds.

options.label: When I had news and no one to tell
options.reflection: You had something to share and nowhere for it to land. That particular loneliness can sting. Tomorrow, you might send it to someone anyway, even late; people are often gladder to hear from you than you'd expect.

options.label: Even around people close to me
options.reflection: You felt alone even near people who matter to you. That can be painful and confusing. Tomorrow, you might gently share one small, true feeling with one of them; closeness often grows from moments like that.

options.label: I felt fairly connected today
options.reflection: You felt in touch with people today, which is worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might think about who helped you feel that way, and send them a quick message to say you're glad they're around.

questions.prompt: Your to-do list is far too long. What do you actually do?

options.label: Do the easy things first

insight.reveal: Small wins warm you up for the big stuff. Ticking off a few quick ones gets you going, and that can genuinely help. The risk is a day full of crossed-off lines while the one thing that really mattered sits waiting at the bottom.
insight.step: Tomorrow, do one easy task, then the hardest one before lunch.

options.label: Rewrite the list in a better order

insight.reveal: You calm the chaos by putting it in order. Making a fresh list feels like progress, and sometimes it is. You may own more than one notebook full of half-finished lists, and you do best when the new one starts with something doable in the next ten minutes.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time you rewrite a list, add one when-then plan: 'When I finish lunch, I will start task one.'

options.label: Freeze and scroll instead

insight.reveal: When everything feels urgent, nothing can start. That freeze is overload, not laziness, and it tends to hit hardest when a task feels unpleasant or you doubt you'll manage it. Shrinking the list to one single thing often gets you moving again faster than you'd expect.
insight.research: People tend to put tasks off most when a task feels unpleasant and they doubt they will manage it; perfectionism did not predict delay.
insight.step: Next time you freeze, cover the list and do only the top line for ten minutes.

options.label: Work late until it's all done

insight.reveal: You trust effort more than limits. When something has to get over the line, people know to bring it to you. Past a point, though, extra hours tend to get less done, so late nights rarely keep the list short for long, and you deserve evenings that belong to you.
insight.research: Among British munition workers a century ago, output rose with hours up to a point, then more and more slowly as hours got longer.
insight.step: This week, pick a stop time for one evening and keep to it, even with tasks left.

followUp.prompt: How did you get on with your to-do list today?

options.label: I did the easy things first
options.reflection: You started with the easy wins today. That can build momentum and make the day feel like it's moving. Tomorrow, you might slot in one harder task straight after a couple of easy ones, while you still have that early lift.

options.label: I rewrote or reordered the list
options.reflection: You took time to bring order to the list. Making a plan often calms the mind as much as doing the tasks. Tomorrow, you might circle just one thing that truly matters, and do that before re-planning again.

options.label: I froze and scrolled instead
options.reflection: The list felt so big that you froze and reached for your phone. That's a very common way to cope with overwhelm. Tomorrow, you might pick the tiniest first step, small enough to feel almost silly, and start there.

options.label: My list was manageable today
options.reflection: Your list stayed manageable today, which can be a nice breathing space. Tomorrow, you might notice what kept it that way, whether saying no, planning ahead or a quieter day, so you can come back to it.

questions.prompt: Something sad happens. What do you do with the feeling?

options.label: Keep busy so I don't think about it

insight.reveal: Busy hands get you through hard weeks. You keep life running when others stall, and that's a real strength. The feeling usually waits patiently, though, and may surface in a quiet moment, on a trip or late at night, asking for a few minutes of your attention.
insight.research: Grieving people tend to move back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with daily life, and taking breaks from grief is a normal part of coping.
insight.step: This week, give a sad feeling ten minutes on purpose, then go back to your day.

options.label: Music or a film that matches the mood

insight.reveal: You let sad feelings run their whole course. There's probably a playlist for every mood on your phone and a film you save for a good cry. Letting the feeling finish instead of fighting it often helps you feel better sooner than pushing it away would.
insight.research: Many people enjoy sad music because it feels safe, beautiful and comforting, and listeners often feel nostalgia or mixed feelings rather than real sadness.
insight.step: This week, while you feel fine, make a short playlist for low days.

options.label: Let myself cry if it comes

insight.reveal: Tears are a release for you, not a weakness. You tend to recover quietly and fully once the feeling has passed through. You're also the person others feel safe enough to cry in front of, because you never make it awkward.
insight.research: Crying often helps people feel better, though usually not straight away; comfort from one close person helps, while embarrassment or a big audience can cancel the relief.
insight.step: Next time someone near you is sad, sit with them for a minute before saying anything.

options.label: Hide it so nobody worries

insight.reveal: You keep your sadness tucked away to spare the people you love. That's a kind instinct, and it makes you strong when others fall apart. It also means they rarely get to care for you back, and many would welcome that chance. You don't have to hold it all by yourself.
insight.research: People who habitually hide their feelings tended to share less, feel less close to friends and be less satisfied with life than people who rethink what upset them.
