insight.step: This week, tell one trusted person 'I'm a bit sad today' and let them respond.

followUp.prompt: Did something sad touch your day? What did you do with it?

options.label: I kept busy so I didn't dwell on it
options.reflection: You kept moving to stay ahead of the sadness today. Keeping busy can help you get through, though feelings tend to wait for a quiet moment. Tomorrow, you might give it a few gentle minutes on your own terms, so it doesn't catch you off guard.

options.label: I let myself feel it, maybe cried
options.reflection: You let the feeling come today instead of pushing it away. That openness often helps sadness pass through rather than settle. Tomorrow, be gentle with yourself; you might feel a bit tired, and that's part of it.

options.label: I hid it so nobody would worry
options.reflection: You kept your sadness out of sight to protect others. That's caring, yet it can leave you holding it alone. Tomorrow, you might let one trusted person in, even a little; most people would want to be there for you.

options.label: Nothing sad happened today
options.reflection: Nothing sad touched your day, and that's something to be glad of. Tomorrow, if a heavy moment does come, you might remember that letting yourself feel it is often kinder than pushing it away.

questions.prompt: It's the night before a hard day. How do you spend it?

options.label: Go to bed early

insight.reveal: Sleep is your preparation of choice, and it serves you well. You trust that a rested mind will handle what a worried one couldn't plan. You arrive at big days looking calmer than you feel, and people may assume you weren't nervous at all.
insight.research: Among 88 students wearing sleep trackers, sleep in the month before exams went with better grades, while sleep the night before did not.
insight.step: In the week before your next hard day, set an alarm for bedtime, not just for waking up.

options.label: Prepare everything, then prepare again

insight.reveal: You turn worry into checklists, spare pens and backup files. You're impressively ready for almost anything. After the first round, though, the extra checking is mostly for comfort rather than catching anything you missed, and that time could go to rest.
insight.step: Next time, prepare once, then put everything in your bag and agree with yourself not to reopen it.

options.label: Distract myself with something fun

insight.reveal: You know worrying tonight won't change tomorrow. So you'd rather laugh, play or go out, and you show up fresh because of it. Some of your best days have probably followed nights other people would have spent pacing.
insight.step: This week, pick a fun thing to save for the night before your next hard day.

options.label: Lie awake running through what could go wrong

insight.reveal: Your mind tries to live tomorrow tonight, every version of it. It's trying to protect you, and you do end up ready for surprises. The real day is rarely like the ones you rehearse, and usually kinder. Let your shoulders drop and breathe out slowly.
insight.research: Young adults who spent five minutes writing tomorrow's to-do list before bed fell asleep in about 15 minutes, compared with about 25 for those who wrote about tasks already done.
insight.step: Tonight, write the worst case and one thing you'd do if it happened. Then put the paper away.

followUp.prompt: Is something hard coming up tomorrow? How are you spending tonight?

options.label: I'm planning an early night
options.reflection: You're giving yourself rest before a big day. That simple care often does more than any last-minute preparation. Tonight, you might put your phone across the room, and trust that you've done enough for now.

options.label: I've prepared, then prepared again
options.reflection: You've prepared carefully, and maybe then some. That thoroughness shows how much you care about doing well. Tonight, you might tell yourself out loud that it's ready, and let the extra checking go until morning.

options.label: Running through what could go wrong
options.reflection: Your mind is busy rehearsing what could go wrong. That's a common way of trying to stay safe. Tonight, you might write the worries down, add one thing you'd do if each happened, and let the paper keep them till morning.

options.label: Tomorrow looks like an ordinary day
options.reflection: Nothing hard is waiting for you tomorrow, which is a quiet relief. Tonight, you might enjoy that lightness on purpose, perhaps with something you love, since easy evenings are worth noticing too.

questions.prompt: A friend asks 'How are you?' during a hard week. What do you say?

options.label: "Fine, thanks!"

insight.reveal: You save the real answer for the right time and person. You come across as steady and composed, and you don't like to make a scene. The small cost is that friends may not know when to show up for you, because 'fine' looks the same on good weeks and bad ones.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others feel low or upset, partly because others hide it, and those who underestimated it most felt lonelier.
insight.step: This week, answer 'How are you?' with one true detail, just once.

options.label: "A bit tired, but OK"

insight.reveal: You leave the door half open to see who notices. A little hint, then you wait. You feel closest to the friends who gently ask a second time, and you're good at catching hints in others too, which is why people open up to you so easily.
insight.step: Next time you hint, add one more sentence even if they don't ask.

options.label: I make a joke about how bad it is

insight.reveal: A joke lets you share the hard stuff without making it heavy. It invites people in while keeping them at a safe distance, and you can lift a room even in a rough week. The right friend laughs first, then asks what's really going on, and you deserve that friend.
insight.step: After your next joke about a hard week, add one serious sentence.

options.label: The real answer, even if it's messy

insight.reveal: You'd rather be honest than tidy. You likely have fewer but deeper friendships, and your openness gives others permission to be real too. It's why people confide in you first, sometimes before they've told anyone else.
insight.research: Strangers who spent 45 minutes taking turns answering slowly deeper personal questions felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: This week, ask someone 'How are you, really?' and wait through the pause.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone ask how you were today? What did you tell them?

options.label: I said fine, even if it wasn't quite true
options.reflection: You gave the easy answer today. That's often what we say to keep things simple or to spare others. Tomorrow, you might go one step more honest with someone you trust, like a bit tired actually, and see how they respond.

options.label: I made a joke of it
options.reflection: You met the question with humour today. Jokes can be a lovely way to share something hard without making it heavy. Tomorrow, you might follow the joke with one honest sentence, so the person can really be there for you.

options.label: I told them how I really was
options.reflection: You gave a real answer today, even if it was messy. That kind of honesty tends to invite real closeness back. Tomorrow, you might notice how that person treats you; it may show you who you can lean on.

options.label: Nobody really asked today
options.reflection: No one checked in on you today. That can feel a little lonely, even on a fine day. Tomorrow, you might ask someone how they really are; it often opens the door for them to ask you back.

questions.prompt: Nobody has messaged you all day. What goes through your mind?

options.label: Nice, a quiet day

insight.reveal: Silence on your phone sounds like peace, not a message. You feel secure without constant proof of connection. In relationships you tend to stay calm too, and a slow reply rarely sends your mind racing.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, message someone you've been meaning to, just because.

options.label: I message someone first

insight.reveal: You start the conversation instead of waiting for it. Thanks to you, friendships that would have faded are still alive. You've probably wondered why you're always the one who writes first, and part of the answer is that others are glad you do.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much others appreciate a quick message or call out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: This week, notice who messages you first, and thank one of them for it.

options.label: I keep checking my phone

insight.reveal: A silent phone makes you wonder where you stand. You're tuned in to people and you care how they feel about you. The gaps you read meaning into are usually just busy days on the other side of the screen: people cooking, working or asleep.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: On your next quiet day, leave your phone in another room for one hour and notice what you feel.

options.label: I wonder if people have forgotten me

insight.reveal: You think of others often, and wonder if they think of you. Quiet days can feel like proof you've slipped from people's minds, but the gap is usually in messages, not in care. Plenty of people think of you and forget to say so. You matter to more people than your phone shows.
insight.research: After chatting with someone new, people tend to think the other person liked them less than they really did, and this 'liking gap' lasted for months between new roommates.
insight.step: This week, ask one friend: 'Do you ever think of messaging someone and then forget?'

followUp.prompt: Was your phone quiet today? How did that feel?

options.label: It was quiet, and I enjoyed it
options.reflection: A quiet phone felt like a gift to you today. Being comfortable with stillness often comes from feeling secure in your connections. Tomorrow, you might keep a small phone-free stretch on purpose and enjoy it again.

options.label: I messaged someone first
options.reflection: You reached out instead of waiting. That small step often keeps friendships alive, and people are usually glad to be thought of. Tomorrow, you might notice who replied warmly; they're likely glad you made the first move.

options.label: I kept checking it
options.reflection: You found yourself checking your phone often today. Silence can stir worry that people have drifted, even when they're just busy. Tomorrow, you might set the phone aside for a while, or send one message yourself, and see how it feels.

options.label: Plenty of people got in touch
options.reflection: People were in touch with you today, so silence wasn't the issue. Tomorrow, you might notice which messages lifted you and which drained you; that can help you choose where your attention goes.

questions.prompt: On a tired, low evening, what are you most likely to reach for?

options.label: Something warm and a blanket

insight.reveal: You comfort yourself the way you'd comfort a child. Warmth, softness and quiet tell your body it's safe before your mind has caught up. You look after yourself without fuss, and there's probably one mug and one blanket that are officially yours.
insight.step: This week, set up one corner of your home as your low-day spot, ready before you need it.

options.label: An old favourite show I've seen many times

insight.reveal: On low nights, knowing the ending is the whole point. You rest best when nothing can surprise you. In hard weeks you lean on familiar food, places and faces too, and that steady sameness is how you recharge.
insight.research: Nostalgia often comes on when people feel low or lonely, and thinking back to fond memories tended to lift mood and make people feel closer to others.
insight.step: Next low evening, notice which old favourite you pick. It may point to a time you felt safe.

options.label: A call with someone who knows me well

insight.reveal: A familiar voice that needs no backstory brings you back. No advice, just someone who already knows the whole picture. You probably have one or two people like that, and they may have no idea how much those calls mean to you.
insight.research: People expected a phone call with an old friend to feel more awkward than a text or email, but calls built a stronger bond and weren't more awkward.
insight.step: This week, tell the person you'd call that they are your low-day person.

options.label: Online shopping I don't really need

insight.reveal: On a low night, a delivery on its way feels like a small promise. You're great at spotting a bargain, and half the fun is waiting for the knock at the door, more than the thing itself. Something else to look forward to, like a plan with a friend, can meet the same need.
insight.research: Waiting for an experience, like a trip, a concert or a party, tends to feel more pleasant and exciting than waiting for a new thing to arrive.
insight.step: Next low evening, put items in the basket but wait until morning to decide.

followUp.prompt: If this evening feels tired or low, what are you reaching for?

options.label: Something warm and a blanket
options.reflection: You're giving yourself simple comfort tonight. Warmth and softness can be a real way to settle a tired mind. Tomorrow, you might notice what made today draining, and see if one small part of it could be lighter.

options.label: A call or chat with someone close
options.reflection: You reached for a person tonight, not just a thing. Being heard by someone who knows you often soothes in ways nothing else can. Tomorrow, you might send them a short thank you; they may have needed the chat too.

options.label: Browsing or buying things online
options.reflection: Browsing or buying online is your comfort tonight. That little lift is very common on low evenings, though it tends to fade fast. Tomorrow, you might leave items in the basket overnight and see if you still want them in the morning.

options.label: I'm not feeling low tonight
options.reflection: This evening isn't a low one, and that's good to notice. Tomorrow, you might remember what helped you feel steady today, so you have it ready on an evening that's harder.

questions.prompt: Someone cuts in front of you in a queue. What do you do?

options.label: Let it go, not worth it

insight.reveal: Not worth it, you decide, and you actually mean it. In traffic, at family dinners or at a busy counter, you're often the one who shrugs and moves on. Now and then a small slight sneaks back later, but it usually comes out as a funny story, not a grudge.
insight.step: Next time you let something go, check an hour later: is it still on your mind?

options.label: Politely point out where the line starts

insight.reveal: You say what's fair out loud, and you keep it friendly. You're probably the one who sends back a wrong order or questions an odd charge, and nobody even feels told off. In meetings, colleagues quietly hope you'll speak up, and you usually do.
insight.step: This week, practise one calm, short sentence for small unfair moments, like 'Sorry, the line starts here.'

options.label: Say nothing, but fume inside

insight.reveal: On the outside you look calm; inside, you're writing a speech. Staying quiet spares you a scene, and the speech gets sharper every time you replay it on the way home. That inner voice makes you a keen judge of how people treat each other; it just shouldn't cost you the whole evening.
insight.research: Across 154 studies with over 10,000 people, calming activities like slow breathing, meditation or relaxing the muscles tended to reduce anger, while revving-up ones mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you fume silently, breathe out slowly three times, then decide: say it or drop it.

options.label: Tell them clearly, even if it gets loud

insight.reveal: You can't stand by and watch something unfair happen. You're likely first to challenge a rude waiter or a boss who crosses a line, and friends know you'll fight for them just as hard. The volume can make people defend themselves instead of listening, even when you're completely right.
insight.step: Next time you confront someone, lower your voice on purpose and notice whether they listen more.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone cut ahead of you or skip their turn today? What did you do?

options.label: Someone did, and I let it go
options.reflection: Letting it slide often means you chose your peace over a small win, which can be a quiet strength. If it nags at you later, the moment may have mattered more than you let on. Tomorrow, you might notice which small things you truly don't mind.

options.label: I spoke up about it
options.reflection: Speaking up tends to take a steady kind of courage: you named what was fair instead of swallowing it. That's a skill you can lean on elsewhere too. Tomorrow, you might notice how your body felt right after you spoke, and remember it.

options.label: I stayed quiet, but it bugged me
options.reflection: When you stay quiet but the feeling stays loud, it often means fairness matters to you and you haven't found an easy way to say so yet. Tomorrow, you might try putting one small irritation into words, even just to yourself, and see if it passes faster.

options.label: Nobody cut ahead of me today
options.reflection: A day without those small frictions can be a gift, even if you barely noticed it. When fairness isn't tested, you may get a little more room to breathe. Tomorrow, you might notice the people who do wait their turn, and how that feels.

questions.prompt: On the road, another driver nearly hits you. What's your reaction?

options.label: A deep breath, then I forget it

insight.reveal: You assume people mess up by accident, not on purpose. That's partly why a rough day rarely follows you to bed. When everyone in the car is shouting, you're the calm voice, and you bounce back from setbacks faster than people expect.
insight.research: People who tend to rethink what upset them, instead of hiding their feelings, felt better inside and closer to friends than habitual hiders did.
insight.step: Next time someone cuts you off, imagine one innocent reason they might be rushing.

options.label: The horn, and maybe a gesture

insight.reveal: Your temper flares fast and is gone just as fast. Your passenger may still be talking about it two streets later, while you've already forgotten it happened. People rarely have to guess how you feel, which is honest, though not everyone cools down as quickly as you.
insight.step: On your next journey, notice how long the feeling lasts after you use the horn.

options.label: Shout at them where no one can hear

insight.reveal: The car might be the only place your frustration gets loud. At work and at home you're patient and polite, so the car is where it spills over. A rough drive often says more about your week than about the other driver.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: Next time you want to shout, try one long out-breath instead and compare how you feel a minute later.

options.label: Still angry about it hours later

insight.reveal: A scare like that stays in your body long after the road is clear. You probably feel it all over again each time you tell the story, and some of the tension can land on whoever's home first. That vivid memory is also what makes you such a careful driver.
insight.step: When you get home after a bad drive, tell the story once, then change the topic on purpose.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone on the road or street give you a scare today? How was it after?

options.label: Yes, and I shook it off quickly
options.reflection: Shaking off a scare quickly often shows a body that knows how to settle itself, and that's worth trusting. Tomorrow, you might notice what helped it pass, a breath, music, a thought, so you can reach for it again on a harder day.

options.label: I let them know how I felt
options.reflection: A flash of anger after a fright is common: your body was protecting you and the energy had to go somewhere. It may help to notice whether it eased the feeling or kept it going. Tomorrow, you might try one long breath out in the moment and see what shifts.

options.label: It stayed with me for hours
options.reflection: When a scare keeps replaying, your mind is often still trying to keep you safe long after the danger has passed. That isn't weakness. Tomorrow, if it returns, you might gently tell yourself 'that's over, I'm okay' and notice whether it loosens its grip.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: A calm trip can slip by unnoticed, yet it may have given your mind a little rest you needed. Not every day tests your patience. Tomorrow, you might notice one moment on the move that felt easy, and let yourself enjoy it.

questions.prompt: In an argument with someone close, what do you tend to do?

options.label: Talk it through calmly

insight.reveal: You believe most problems shrink once they're said out loud. At home you're often the steady one, finding words for the mess. A very calm reply can make an upset partner feel their feelings are too big, though, so letting a little of yours show really helps.
insight.step: Next disagreement, say what you feel in one word before you explain your logic.

options.label: I need space before I can talk

insight.reveal: You need a walk before you can find the right words. A drive, a tidy kitchen, a quiet hour: that's where your head clears. It works best if you say how long you'll be, so the other person doesn't feel shut out while you're gone.
insight.research: Across 74 studies of over 14,000 people, couples stuck in a pattern where one pushes to talk and the other goes quiet tended to be less satisfied and feel less close.
insight.step: Next time you need space, say 'Give me twenty minutes, then let's talk' and come back on time.

options.label: I need to fix it right now

insight.reveal: An argument left hanging won't let you rest. You might follow someone from room to room or send one more message, just to settle it. That urge to repair is a real gift in love, though it can push someone who needs space a little further away.
insight.research: Couples caught in a pattern where one partner pushes to talk and the other withdraws tended to feel less close, whichever partner played which role.
insight.step: Next argument, wait ten minutes before trying to fix it, and notice what the waiting feels like.

options.label: I get sarcastic or roll my eyes

insight.reveal: When you feel unheard, your wit gets sharp. On a good day that quick tongue makes friends laugh, and in a fight it saves you from saying the hurt plainly. An eye-roll tends to land as 'I look down on you', though, and that's rarely what you mean.
insight.research: In long-running studies of couples, contempt, such as mockery, sarcasm and eye-rolling, was the strongest single predictor of divorce.
insight.step: Next time sarcasm rises, say the real complaint underneath it in plain words instead.

followUp.prompt: Did you have a disagreement with someone close to you today? How did it go?

options.label: We talked it through
options.reflection: Talking it through with someone close tends to build trust, even when the topic is uncomfortable. It suggests you both felt safe enough to stay. Tomorrow, you might notice one thing they said that you understand a little better now.

options.label: I stepped away to cool down
options.reflection: Needing space can be a wise way to protect a relationship, as long as you come back to it. You may simply sort things out better alone first. Tomorrow, you might let them know when you'll be ready to talk, so the space feels like a pause, not a wall.

options.label: I tried hard to fix it fast
options.reflection: Rushing to repair often comes from caring a lot and disliking the feeling of distance. That warmth is real. Tomorrow, you might try letting a small silence sit for a moment, and trust that the bond can hold while things settle.

options.label: No disagreements today
options.reflection: A day without friction with the people close to you can be a quiet comfort. It may be a good moment to notice what's working between you. Tomorrow, you might tell one of them something you appreciate, while things feel easy.

questions.prompt: Someone wronged you years ago. How do you feel about them now?

options.label: I barely think about it

insight.reveal: They stopped being important to you, so you moved on. You tend to leave breakups, lost jobs and old rivalries behind cleanly. At a reunion you might be perfectly friendly while someone else is still bracing for drama.
insight.step: This week, notice one small annoyance you're still carrying and choose to drop just that one.

options.label: Forgiven, but I remember everything

insight.reveal: You can forgive someone and still keep the lesson. You'll be warm to them again, but they won't get the same key twice. That makes you smart about who to lend money to and who gets to hear your secrets.
insight.step: This week, think of one person you've forgiven and one small piece of trust you could safely give back.

options.label: It still stings when I think of it

insight.reveal: It still stings, maybe because you never got a real answer. Often what stings most isn't what they did, but that they never seemed to understand what it cost you. The same deep memory makes you a loyal friend who remembers what matters to people.
insight.research: People who looked back on an angry or upsetting moment as if watching from a distance, like a fly on the wall, tended to get less worked up.
insight.step: Tonight, write what happened as if you were a kind stranger watching, including what it cost you. Then put it away.

options.label: I'd still like them to admit it

insight.reveal: You still want them to own what they did, and that's fair. You notice unfairness others miss, and you won't pretend it didn't happen. The hard part is that your peace ends up waiting on someone who may never act, and you deserve that peace sooner.
insight.research: Across 175 studies of 26,006 people, forgiving tended to be most likely when people felt empathy for the wrongdoer, felt the hurt wasn't meant and got an apology.
insight.step: This week, ask yourself: what would I feel if they never admit it? Let the answer sit for a day.

followUp.prompt: Did an old hurt, or the person behind it, cross your mind today?

options.label: It came up, then passed quickly
options.reflection: When an old hurt shows up and then drifts off, it often means you've done some quiet healing, even without planning to. Tomorrow, you might notice what you were doing just before it passed, since that may be part of what helps you.

options.label: It came up and still stung
options.reflection: Old hurts can sting again without warning, and that usually means something mattered deeply to you. There's no rush to be over it. Tomorrow, you might be extra kind to yourself for a moment and remember you're not the same person you were back then.

options.label: I wished they'd admit what they did
options.reflection: Wanting them to admit it tends to come from a wish to have your side truly seen. That wish makes sense. Tomorrow, you might write down what happened and how it felt, so your own voice does some of the work their apology hasn't.

options.label: It didn't cross my mind today
options.reflection: A day when the old hurt stayed quiet can be a small sign of how much room you've made for other things. You don't have to force that. Tomorrow, you might simply notice what filled your mind instead, and enjoy it.

questions.prompt: A colleague takes credit for your idea in a meeting. What do you do?

options.label: Nothing. It's not worth it

insight.reveal: A calm team matters more to you than your name on the idea. You're easy to work with, and often the reason projects run smoothly. Just keep an eye on one thing: a few colleagues may slowly learn that your ideas are free to take.
insight.step: Next time you share an idea, send a short written summary afterwards.

options.label: Add a detail only the real author would know

insight.reveal: You set the record straight without raising your voice. One clever detail and the whole room quietly works out whose idea it was. That same skill probably helps you negotiate, write sharp emails and win debates while others are still getting heated.
insight.step: Before your next meeting, prepare one follow-up point about your own idea.

options.label: Talk to them privately afterwards

insight.reveal: You give people a quiet chance to put things right. It protects the work and the relationship at once, and it earns you a name for fairness. You'll also remember, very clearly, who took that chance and who didn't.
insight.research: People were most likely to forgive when they got an apology, felt the hurt wasn't intended and felt empathy for the wrongdoer, across 175 studies.
insight.step: Next time it happens, start the private talk with 'I noticed…' and describe only what happened.

options.label: Stay angry for days and avoid them

insight.reveal: It hurts this much because your work matters so much to you. Staying quiet in the meeting kept the peace, but you might carry it for a week while they don't even know. That means you end up paying the whole cost of something they did.
insight.research: In polls of 800 workers, among those treated rudely at work, 80% lost time worrying about it and 48% cut back their effort.
insight.step: This week, choose one sentence you could say to them, then decide whether to say it or let it go.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone take credit for your work or ideas today? How did you handle it?

options.label: Someone did, and I spoke up
options.reflection: Claiming your own work can feel awkward, yet it often protects your energy and how others see you. It suggests you value fairness, including for yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice how you felt afterwards; next time it may come a bit easier.

options.label: Someone did, and I let it go
options.reflection: Letting it go may have kept the peace, and sometimes that's the right call. Still, your ideas deserve a home. Tomorrow, you might find one small way to put your name on your next idea early, like a quick note or message, so it's clearly yours.

options.label: It happened and I'm still stewing
options.reflection: Feeling stung when your work goes unseen is natural, and the feeling often lingers when it wasn't spoken. Tomorrow, you might write down what you'd want to say, even if you never send it, and see if it eases the weight a little.

options.label: Nothing like that came up today
options.reflection: A day where your work simply stood as yours can be easy to overlook. It may be worth noticing the people around you who play fair. Tomorrow, you might thank someone who backed your idea or gave you room to share it.

questions.prompt: At home, which small thing irritates you most?

options.label: Dishes left in the sink

insight.reveal: Those dishes in the sink aren't really about dishes, are they? You spot what needs doing before anyone else and keep the house running. What usually stings is the message underneath: 'nobody sees what I do'.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we tend to notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: This week, thank someone at home for one small thing they do, and see whether the dish issue softens.

options.label: Noise when I want quiet

insight.reveal: Quiet is how you recharge, like a phone on its charger. Early mornings, good headphones and the empty house after everyone leaves are probably your favourite things. When it stays loud too long, people may call you grumpy when you're simply running on empty.
insight.step: This week, agree on one quiet hour at home with everyone, and enjoy every minute of it.

options.label: Being interrupted when I'm focused

insight.reveal: Your focus takes ages to build and seconds to break. The irritation is really about the cost of starting over. You do your best work in long, protected stretches, and it shows: your jigsaws, reports and big projects actually get finished.
insight.research: In a study of 48 people, those interrupted while answering emails felt more stress, frustration and time pressure, even though they made no more mistakes.
insight.step: Next time you need focus, tell people at home: 'Give me 30 minutes, then I'm all yours.'

options.label: Feeling like I'm the only one who helps

insight.reveal: You carry the jobs nobody else even sees. Birthdays, the shopping list, noticing the soap has run out: you're the glue at home, whether anyone says so or not. That load gets heavier the longer it stays unspoken, and it's fair to ask for help carrying it.
insight.research: Interviews with 35 couples found that the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often goes unseen and causes friction.
insight.step: This week, name one invisible task you do and ask someone to take it over for a week.

followUp.prompt: How did home feel today? Did any small thing get under your skin?

options.label: Mess or chores left undone
options.reflection: Mess left for you to deal with often bothers people who like things in order, and that care keeps a home running. Tomorrow, you might ask for one specific bit of help instead of quietly doing it all, and see how that feels.

options.label: Noise or interruptions
options.reflection: If noise or interruptions wore you down, it may be a sign you needed more quiet than you got. That's a real need, not fussiness. Tomorrow, you might claim a small window of calm, even ten minutes, and protect it gently.

options.label: Feeling like I did it all
options.reflection: Feeling like the only one who helps can be tiring and lonely, and it tends to build up quietly. Your effort counts, even when no one says so. Tomorrow, you might name one thing you need help with, plainly and kindly, to someone at home.

options.label: Home felt calm today
options.reflection: A calm day at home is worth noticing, since those days can slip by without credit. It may help to spot what made it easy. Tomorrow, you might keep one of those things going, like a tidy corner or a quiet hour.

questions.prompt: You read an online comment that makes you angry. What do you do?

options.label: Close it and move on

insight.reveal: Your attention is precious, and you guard it well. You skip pointless fights with strangers and relatives alike, and you probably sleep better for it. All that saved energy goes to the people and plans that actually matter to you.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment your mood dropped because of something on a screen.

options.label: Read all the replies

insight.reveal: Down you scroll, hoping someone out there agrees with you. Wanting to know how others think is a real strength. The trouble is that the replies are usually packed with other angry people, so your anger tends to grow instead of settling.
insight.research: In over 560,000 tweets on hot political topics, each extra word mixing morals and emotion raised sharing by about 20%, mostly among people who already agreed.
insight.step: Next time, read only the first three replies, then close the app.

options.label: Write a reply, then delete it

insight.reveal: Your anger needs words, but it doesn't need an audience. Chances are you've written the furious email, slept on it and sent something kinder. The wait lets you cool down without the cost of a public fight, and people see you as level-headed because of it.
insight.research: Across 154 studies, calming down, such as slow breathing or taking a time-out, tended to reduce anger, while revving-up activities mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time, write the reply, wait an hour, then decide whether it's still worth sending.

options.label: Reply, then keep checking who answered

insight.reveal: If something online is wrong, you feel you have to fix it. You know your facts and care about getting things right. It's the checking back that keeps the anger alive, sometimes for a whole evening after the comment has scrolled away.
insight.research: People who vented anger while dwelling on the person who annoyed them became angrier and more aggressive than people who did nothing.
insight.step: This week, if you reply to a post, turn off its notifications straight after.

followUp.prompt: Did something you read online stir you up today? What did you do with it?

options.label: I closed it and moved on
options.reflection: Closing it and moving on often shows you know where your energy is best spent. That's a skill many people are still learning. Tomorrow, you might notice what you did with that saved attention, and let it be a quiet win.

options.label: I got pulled into the replies
options.reflection: Getting pulled into the replies is very common: angry posts tend to grab and hold attention. It doesn't mean you did anything wrong. Tomorrow, you might pause before opening the comments and ask yourself if they'll leave you feeling better.

options.label: I typed a reply, then deleted it
options.reflection: Writing a reply and then deleting it can be a healthy release: you got the words out without adding to the fire. It suggests you weigh how things land. Tomorrow, you might notice if writing things down helps with other irritations too.

options.label: Nothing online bothered me today
options.reflection: A day online without getting stirred up can leave more room for the people and things right in front of you. Tomorrow, you might notice which corners of the internet tend to leave you calmer, and spend a little more time there.

questions.prompt: Someone is 30 minutes late to meet you, with no message. How do you feel?

options.label: Fine, I find something to do

insight.reveal: Waiting hardly bothers you, because you come prepared. A book, a podcast, a short walk: you turn dead time into free time. You're likely the relaxed one at airports, and the friend people feel safe being a little late for.
insight.step: This week, keep one small time-filler with you and notice how waiting feels.

options.label: Annoyed. It's rude

insight.reveal: Turning up on time is your way of showing respect. You're probably early yourself, keep a tidy calendar and get trusted with deadlines. You may also have quietly worked out who's always late, and you plan around them without saying a word.
insight.research: People told to share honest feedback with someone close found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: Next time someone is late, tell them kindly how it felt instead of staying quiet.

options.label: Worried something happened to them

insight.reveal: Your mind goes to danger long before it goes to rudeness. You're the friend who texts 'home safe?' after a night out. When the late one finally walks in, relief and anger often arrive together, and the anger can come out louder than you meant.
insight.step: Next time you wait, send one message asking if they're OK, then set a time to stop worrying.

options.label: Wondering if I matter to them

insight.reveal: A late friend can make you wonder where you stand. You notice every small signal, and friends feel truly seen by you. Most of the time the delay is about their messy day, not about you, even when the feeling insists otherwise.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety (worry about rejection) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with closeness), and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time, think of two other reasons they might be late before deciding what it means.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone keep you waiting today? How did you feel while you waited?

options.label: I found something to do
options.reflection: Filling the wait with something of your own often means you feel steady in your own company, and that's a calm kind of strength. Tomorrow, you might keep a small thing on hand, a book, a song, a thought, for any gaps in your day.

options.label: I got annoyed
options.reflection: Feeling annoyed when someone is late often comes from valuing time and respect, yours and theirs. That's fair. Tomorrow, if it happens again, you might tell them simply how it felt, without blame, and see how they respond.

options.label: I wondered if I mattered to them
options.reflection: When waiting turns into wondering if you matter, it can hurt more than the lateness itself. That feeling often says more about how much you care than about what they meant. Tomorrow, you might ask yourself what you know for sure, not what you fear.

options.label: No one kept me waiting
options.reflection: A day where no one kept you waiting can quietly ease the pressure on your patience. It may be worth noticing who in your life tends to show up when they say. Tomorrow, you might thank one of them, even in a small way.

questions.prompt: You're blamed for something you didn't do. What's your first move?

options.label: Explain the facts calmly

insight.reveal: Calm, clear facts are how you clear your name. You're often the steady voice in a crisis, the one a manager leans on when things get messy. Calm works, but now and then people also need to hear that it hurt, not just that you were right.
insight.step: Next time, add one sentence about how it felt, not just what happened.

options.label: Gather proof before I say anything

insight.reveal: Words alone don't feel like enough to protect you. You probably keep old emails, receipts and screenshots, and your team turns to you when someone asks who agreed to what. A habit like that can come from a time when your word wasn't enough.
insight.step: This week, try clearing up one small misunderstanding quickly, with words alone and no proof.

options.label: Take the blame to keep the peace

insight.reveal: You'd give up being right to keep the peace. You smooth over family tension, and you're easy to live and work with. Over time, though, people may start to see you through mistakes you never made, and your side of the story deserves airtime too.
insight.step: Next time, try: 'That wasn't me, but I can help fix it.' Both parts are true.

options.label: Get angry and defend myself hard

insight.reveal: Being wrongly blamed feels like an attack on who you are. Your sense of fairness wakes up fast, and you'd defend a friend just as fiercely. The heat can drown out the facts you're right about, so one pause before you answer often wins it for you.
insight.research: Calming activities like slow breathing or a short time-out tended to reduce anger across 154 studies, while revving-up activities like jogging mostly did not.
insight.step: Next time you feel blamed, take one breath and say one calm fact before anything else.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone blame you today for something that wasn't really yours?

options.label: I explained the facts calmly
options.reflection: Explaining calmly when you feel wronged tends to take real self-control, and it often helps others hear you. Tomorrow, you might remind yourself that you can stand your ground without raising your voice, because today you did.

options.label: I took it to keep the peace
options.reflection: Taking the blame to keep the peace can come from a kind heart, but it may leave you carrying something that isn't yours. Tomorrow, you might try one small, gentle sentence that sets the record straight, and notice that the peace can usually hold.

options.label: I got heated defending myself
options.reflection: Getting heated when you're blamed unfairly is a very human reaction: it often means honesty matters to you. Tomorrow, you might try naming the facts first and see whether people listen more closely when the heat comes a little later.

options.label: Nobody blamed me for anything
options.reflection: A day with no blame flying around can feel lighter, even if you didn't notice at the time. Tomorrow, you might be the one who quietly gives someone the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: After you lose your temper, what usually happens next?

options.label: I apologise quickly

insight.reveal: Until things are right between you again, you can't relax. You're usually first to send the 'sorry' message after a family fight. A quick apology mends a lot, though it can skip the part where the other person gets to say how it felt.
insight.research: Across 175 studies, people tended to forgive most readily when they got an apology, felt the hurt wasn't intended and felt empathy for the wrongdoer.
insight.step: Next time you apologise, add 'How did that feel for you?' and really listen.

options.label: I act normal and hope it's forgotten

insight.reveal: You say sorry with a cup of tea, not a speech. A small favour, a joke, their favourite snack: you show love by doing. Some people read that perfectly, while others are still quietly waiting to hear the words.
insight.step: Next time, pair your kind action with one short spoken sentence: 'Sorry about earlier.'

options.label: I feel bad about it for a long time

insight.reveal: Nobody judges you as harshly as you judge yourself. You may replay the moment at night long after the other person has forgotten it. That conscience is what makes you so careful with people's feelings, and you deserve a little of that care too.
insight.research: Across 65 samples with nearly 18,000 people, those better able to forgive themselves after doing wrong tended to have better well-being.
insight.step: Next time, ask the person directly: 'Are we OK?' Then believe the answer.

options.label: I explain why I was right to be angry

insight.reveal: You need your reasons heard before you can soften. Your anger usually had a fair point inside it, and you can argue it well. The trick is getting the point across without the heat, because people rarely hear reasons while they still feel stung.
insight.research: In apology studies, admitting it was your fault mattered most to people, then offering to fix it; asking for forgiveness mattered least.
insight.step: Next time, start with what you regret, and explain your reasons after that.

followUp.prompt: Did you lose your temper at all today? What happened afterwards?

options.label: I lost it, then said sorry
options.reflection: Saying sorry soon after losing your temper tends to repair things quickly, and it shows you care about the people around you. Tomorrow, you might be just as gentle with yourself as you were with them, since everyone slips sometimes.

options.label: I moved on and acted normal
options.reflection: Moving on and acting normal can feel easier than going back over it, and sometimes it works. Yet small things left unsaid may linger for the other person. Tomorrow, you might check in lightly, even a simple 'about yesterday', and see how it feels.

options.label: I've been feeling bad about it
options.reflection: Still feeling bad about it often shows how much you care about doing right by others. But guilt that hangs on too long can wear you down. Tomorrow, you might make one small repair, then give yourself permission to put it down.

options.label: I kept my temper today
options.reflection: Keeping your temper through a day is worth noticing, whether it was easy or took effort. Tomorrow, you might remember what helped you stay steady, so you can reach for it on a day that pushes you harder.

questions.prompt: A friend gives you a gift you don't like. What do you say?

options.label: "I love it!"

insight.reveal: A small white lie can be your gift back to them. You protect warm moments, and friends trust you with their feelings because of it. Somewhere in your home there's probably a drawer of kindly received presents only you know about.
insight.research: In 8 experiments, people trusted partners who told a kind lie for their benefit more than honest partners, but relied less on their word for facts.
insight.step: Next time, find one thing about the gift you can honestly praise, and say that.

options.label: Thank them for the thought, not the gift

insight.reveal: You find the words that are both kind and true. It's a quiet talent that shows up at work too, in feedback, references and tricky emails. You'd rather be gently honest than smoothly fake, and that makes your kind words worth trusting.
insight.step: This week, give one compliment that is completely true and very specific.

options.label: Hint later at what I'd really like

insight.reveal: Why correct this gift when you can steer the next one? You deliver honesty in small, careful doses. You're likely just as skilled at steering plans, menus and trips, without anyone noticing they were steered.
insight.research: People liked gifts they had asked for, and even money, more than surprise gifts, though givers expected surprise gifts to be valued more.
insight.step: This week, tell one close person about something you'd truly love to receive.

options.label: Tell them gently it's not really me

insight.reveal: Close friends get the truth from you, even about small things. It might sting for a second, but it makes your praise worth more. You're the one people ask 'does this really suit me?' before a big day.
insight.research: People asked to be fully honest for three days found it more pleasant and connecting than they expected, and listeners reacted better than feared.
insight.step: Before your next honest talk, choose the kind first sentence you'll open with.

followUp.prompt: Did you have to choose between kind words and honest ones today?

options.label: I told a kind white lie
options.reflection: A small kind lie often comes from wanting someone to feel good, and that care is real. Tomorrow, you might notice whether there was a true thing you could have said that was just as warm, and keep it ready for next time.

options.label: I told the truth, gently
options.reflection: Telling the truth gently tends to build trust that lasts, because people learn your words mean something. It can feel risky in the moment. Tomorrow, you might notice how the other person responded, and let that guide you.

options.label: I found words that were both
options.reflection: Finding words that are both honest and kind is a real skill, and you may be better at it than you think. Tomorrow, you might notice the phrases that worked for you today, and use them again when it matters more.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Not every day asks you to weigh kindness against honesty, and a simple day like this can be a rest. Tomorrow, you might notice the small moments where you say exactly what you mean, and how easy that feels.

questions.prompt: You promised to help a friend, but now you'd rather stay home. What do you do?

options.label: I go anyway

insight.reveal: Once you've said yes, your word is as good as signed. You're the friend who turns up with a van on moving day. You're probably careful about promising in the first place, which can make you seem slow to commit.
insight.step: This week, before agreeing to something, say 'Let me check and confirm tomorrow.'

options.label: Go, but feel quietly grumpy

insight.reveal: Duty beats mood for you, nearly every time. Friends can count on you even on bad days, and they value that more than they say. They may still pick up on the grumpiness, though, and a simple 'I'm tired, but I'm here' often clears the air.
insight.research: Across four studies, helping because you chose to lifted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: Next time you go anyway, pick one thing to enjoy on the way there.

options.label: Tell them honestly I'm too tired

insight.reveal: Showing up empty isn't kind, and you'd rather be honest. With you, 'no' is safe, which makes your 'yes' mean more. You likely guard your energy at work the same way, and people learn that when you're in, you're really in.
insight.research: In 8 experiments, people trusted kind liars' good intentions more than honest partners', but relied less on the liars' word for facts.
insight.step: Next time you cancel, offer one specific other time, so it feels like a change of plan, not a no.

options.label: Make up a reason I can't come

insight.reveal: You worry that 'I don't feel like it' won't sound good enough. The excuse comes from kindness: you want to spare their feelings, and yours. Over time, though, it can teach you that your real needs require a cover story, and they don't.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than people predicted.
insight.step: Next time, try a short true reason: 'I'm out of energy today. Can we move it?'

followUp.prompt: Was there a plan or promise today that you'd rather have skipped? What did you do?

options.label: I kept it, though I'd rather not
options.reflection: Keeping a promise when you'd rather rest often says a lot about how much you value your word. It's okay if part of you was tired. Tomorrow, you might give yourself a bit of the care you gave them, and plan one easy thing just for you.

options.label: I told them honestly I couldn't
options.reflection: Telling someone honestly that you can't make it can feel hard, yet it often builds more trust than a forced yes. It suggests you're learning to respect your own limits. Tomorrow, you might notice how they took it, probably better than you feared.

options.label: I made an excuse to get out of it
options.reflection: Reaching for an excuse often happens when 'I'm tired' feels like not enough of a reason. That's very common, and the feeling is worth gently questioning. Tomorrow, you might try one small honest no, and see that your reasons can be enough.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: A day without a promise pulling at you can feel spacious. It may be a good time to notice which plans you look forward to and which you dread. Tomorrow, you might say yes a little more carefully to the ones that drain you.

questions.prompt: You make a mistake at work that no one has noticed yet. What do you do?

options.label: Fix it and tell my team

insight.reveal: You treat a mistake as news to share, not a secret to bury. Teams with you in them raise problems sooner, because you've made it feel safe. Managers likely hand you the projects where an early warning matters most.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: This week, mention one small mistake you made and what you learned, in a casual moment.

options.label: Fix it quietly, no need to say

insight.reveal: You'd rather fix it than make an announcement. You're efficient, low-drama and quietly good at your job. The catch is that nobody sees how well you handle problems, so when a bigger one comes, a little visibility now will help you.
insight.step: Next small fix, mention it in one line: 'Found and fixed an error in this.'

options.label: Wait and see if anyone notices

insight.reveal: Looking bad can feel scarier to you than the mistake itself. You care how you come across, which keeps your standards high. It also means you might spend a whole weekend worrying about something a ten-minute fix would have settled.
insight.research: In a study of 281 scientists, colleagues who admitted a finding of theirs was wrong were judged at least as well as those who refused to, and on some measures better.
insight.step: Next time, set yourself a short deadline: if it isn't fixed by then, tell someone.

options.label: Hope it looks like a system problem

insight.reveal: At some point, you learned that mistakes at work get punished. That instinct protects you, and you've become a sharp reader of office politics. It often comes from the room more than the person, so it's fair to ask whether your room is really that unsafe.
insight.research: In interviews with 40 employees, most had stayed silent about a concern at work, and the top reason was fear of being seen or labelled negatively.
insight.step: This week, watch how your manager reacts to someone else's mistake. It shows how safe honesty is there.

followUp.prompt: Did you make a slip today that nobody else noticed? What did you do?

options.label: I fixed it and told someone
options.reflection: Fixing it and saying so out loud tends to build quiet trust with the people around you. It suggests you care more about getting things right than looking perfect. Tomorrow, you might notice that owning a slip rarely costs as much as it feels like it will.

options.label: I fixed it quietly
options.reflection: Fixing it quietly shows you take care of your work, even when no one is watching. That's a real strength. Tomorrow, you might ask yourself whether sharing small fixes could help others learn too, or whether quiet is simply right here.

options.label: I've left it for now
options.reflection: Leaving a mistake for later can come from feeling stretched or unsure what to say, and that's understandable. It may sit in your mind tonight. Tomorrow, you might take one small step, even a short note, so it stops taking up room in your head.

options.label: No slips that I know of
options.reflection: A day with no slips you know of can feel good, and it's also a reminder that mistakes are normal when they come. Tomorrow, you might think about how you'd like to respond to your next one, so you're ready to be kind to yourself.

questions.prompt: A shop gives you too much change by mistake. What do you do?

options.label: Give it back right away

insight.reveal: Keeping what isn't yours just feels wrong to you. You're probably quick to mention the item the cashier forgot to scan. The same instinct shows up with time and credit: you hate taking more than your share.
insight.research: Pooling 72 experiments where people could lie in private for money, people lied far less than they could have; wanting to be honest, and to look honest, explained it best.
insight.step: This week, notice one moment you got a little more than was fair, and decide what to do about it.

options.label: Small shop, I return it. Big company, maybe not

insight.reveal: Your honesty is about people, not about rules. You protect whoever would actually lose out, which makes you loyal to small local shops and cafés. When no single person seems to get hurt, rules may feel easier to bend than you'd admit.
insight.research: When 17,303 'lost' wallets were handed in across 40 countries, people returned 51% with money in them but 40% without, the opposite of what experts predicted.
insight.step: Next time you think 'it's a big company', picture the cashier who has to balance the till.

options.label: I'd notice later and not go back

insight.reveal: Honesty comes easy to you; going back is the hard part. Lots of people work this way. You'll probably follow through best with a simple plan, like popping in the next time you're passing that shop anyway.
insight.step: Next time you spot a mistake after you've left, fix it on your very next visit.

options.label: Keep it. Their mistake, not mine

insight.reveal: Life, to you, is a series of fair trades where luck cuts both ways. You're practical, hard to guilt-trip and unsentimental about money. We all tend to assume others would choose what we'd choose, so it helps to picture the cashier who comes up short at closing time.
insight.research: People tend to overestimate how many others share their own choices and opinions (the false consensus effect).
insight.step: Next time luck goes your way, ask: would I want this back if I were the cashier?

followUp.prompt: Did you get more than you should have today, like extra change or a missed charge?

options.label: Yes, and I gave it back
options.reflection: Giving it back, even when no one would know, often reflects a steady inner compass. It may have felt small, but small choices like this shape who you are. Tomorrow, you might notice how good it feels to walk away with a clear mind.

options.label: Yes, and I kept it
options.reflection: Keeping something extra can feel harmless in the moment, especially with a big company or a busy day. It may be worth noticing how it sits with you tonight. Tomorrow, you might think about which choice you'd feel proudest of if it came up again.

options.label: I noticed too late to fix it
options.reflection: Noticing too late is very common, and it doesn't say much about your honesty. What matters more is how you feel about it now. Tomorrow, you might decide what you'd do if it happened again, and keep that ready for next time.

options.label: Nothing like that today
options.reflection: A day with no mix-ups at the checkout means no tricky choices to make. It might be a nice moment to think about what you'd do if it happened. Tomorrow, you might notice the small honest acts of the people who serve you.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you a secret. Who might you tell?

options.label: Nobody, ever

insight.reveal: Secrets go into you and never come out. When a friend is in trouble, you're probably their first call. The quiet cost is that you may rarely share your own, because you know exactly how heavy a secret can be.
insight.research: Studying over 13,000 secrets, people's minds drifted to their secrets far more often than they had to hide them, and that drifting went with lower well-being.
insight.step: This week, share one small personal thing with someone you know keeps secrets well.

options.label: Only my partner

insight.reveal: Your partner feels like part of you, not a third person. You probably share almost everything at home and have built a close, private world together. Your friends might see it differently, though, and it's worth asking them once.
insight.step: Next time someone shares a secret, ask: 'Is it OK if my partner knows?'

options.label: Maybe one person, if it's not too serious

insight.reveal: You sort secrets into heavy ones and light ones. You're a lively storyteller who keeps conversations moving. Your friend may have sorted it differently, though, and people rarely say which kind it was.
insight.step: Next time you hear a secret, simply ask: 'Is this just for me?'

options.label: It sometimes slips out without meaning to

insight.reveal: Closeness, for you, means swapping stories. You're warm, open and easy to talk to, so a secret can end up feeling like a gift for the next person. Noticing the moment one reaches the tip of your tongue is often enough to slow it down, and to make your warmth feel safe too.
insight.step: When a secret is on the tip of your tongue this week, switch to a story about yourself instead.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone share something private with you today, or ask you to keep a secret?

options.label: Yes, and I've kept it to myself
options.reflection: Keeping something private safe tends to be one of the quiet ways people learn they can trust you. It may have taken a little effort. Tomorrow, you might notice how it feels to be someone others come to with what matters.

options.label: I mentioned it to one person
options.reflection: Sharing with one trusted person is common, especially when something feels heavy to hold alone. It may be worth asking whether your friend would be okay with that. Tomorrow, you might check what you'd want if it were your own secret.

options.label: It nearly slipped out
options.reflection: Things nearly slipping out often happens when you're relaxed or excited, not because you don't care. Noticing it is already a good step. Tomorrow, you might picture your friend's face before you share a story that isn't fully yours.

options.label: Nothing private came up today
options.reflection: A day without secrets to hold can feel light and simple. It may be a nice moment to notice who you'd trust with your own private things. Tomorrow, you might let one of those people know they matter to you.

questions.prompt: Splitting a group bill when you ordered much less. What do you do?

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: An easy evening is worth more to you than an exact split. Small losses are a fair price for smooth friendships, and you likely get invited back a lot. You may also quietly notice who orders the priciest dish every single time.
insight.step: Next group meal, notice how you feel when the bill arrives. That feeling is useful information.

options.label: Pay for exactly what I had

insight.reveal: For you, fair means exact. You're often trusted with group money and shared trip budgets, and sometimes called tight when you're really just precise. You probably know your bank balance better than most of your friends know theirs.
insight.step: Next time, suggest your way kindly before the bill comes, not after.

options.label: Split evenly, but feel annoyed

insight.reveal: You pay twice: once with money, once with irritation. Putting the group's comfort first is why you're such a generous host and easy company. The money is often the smaller cost; the replay on the way home is what really adds up.
insight.research: Most diners in a restaurant experiment said they preferred paying for their own food, yet even splits led people to order more.
insight.step: Next time, try one light sentence: 'I'll just pay for mine tonight, if that's OK.'

options.label: Order more so it feels fair

insight.reveal: If the bill won't balance, you'll find a way to balance it. You've got a sharp eye and a creative streak with money, like finding the best deal on a trip. It shows how strongly fairness pulls on you, even when the fix ends up costing you more.
insight.research: In a restaurant experiment, diners ordered more when the bill was split evenly than when each paid for their own food, even though most preferred paying individually.
insight.step: Next group meal, try paying only for your share and see if anyone even notices.

followUp.prompt: Did you share a bill, a cost or a chore with others today? How did it feel?

options.label: We split it and it felt fine
options.reflection: Letting it be easy often shows you value the time together more than the exact sums. That's a generous way to be. Tomorrow, you might notice whether that ease feels true for you, or whether there's a limit you'd like to say out loud next time.

options.label: I paid exactly my share
options.reflection: Paying exactly your share tends to come from a sense of fairness that keeps things clear between people. It's not stingy, it's tidy. Tomorrow, you might notice whether others welcome that clarity too; it often makes things easier for everyone.

options.label: I went along, but it felt unfair
options.reflection: Going along while feeling it wasn't fair can leave a small weight behind, and your sense of fairness is valid. Tomorrow, you might have one easy line ready, like 'shall we each pay for what we had?', so it's there when you need it.

options.label: Nothing to split today
options.reflection: No bills or chores to split today means no small tests of fairness to weigh up. Tomorrow, you might notice the times when someone else quietly covers a bit extra for you, and find a way to thank them.

questions.prompt: When is it hardest for you to tell the truth?

options.label: In small talk, like 'How was your day?'

insight.reveal: Your real answers are saved for moments that matter. To you, 'fine, thanks' is just how small talk goes, not a lie. You likely open up fully with a chosen few and keep it light with everyone else.
insight.research: In a survey of 2,980 people in the UK, most said they are honest most of the time, and white lies were more common than big ones.
insight.step: Once this week, answer 'How was your day?' with one real detail.

options.label: When it would hurt someone I love

insight.reveal: With people you love, you'd pick kind over exactly right. You're the friend people go to after a bad haircut or a failed exam, because you listen well and go gently. You probably hear far more truth than you ever say.
insight.research: In week-long diaries, US students told about 2 lies a day and other adults about 1; most were minor, and about a quarter were told to protect or please someone else.
insight.step: Next hard truth, start with 'I'm telling you because I care' and see how it lands.

options.label: When it makes me look bad

insight.reveal: You know exactly where your honesty bends, and that's rare. Most of us spot this in others long before we see it in ourselves. You tend to own up in the end, and that self-awareness keeps you fair with other people too.
insight.research: People tend to see bias in others much more than in themselves, and even after learning about a bias, they insisted their own judgement was objective.
insight.step: This week, admit one small thing that makes you look a little less perfect, and watch the reaction.

options.label: When I'm being honest with myself

insight.reveal: The hardest truths for you are the private ones. You probably question your own motives more than most, late at night or in a notebook. Seeing this is already a start, and honesty with yourself tends to grow quietly, one small admission at a time.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves, while we know our own anxiety better than they do.
insight.step: This week, ask one trusted friend: 'What's one thing about me you think I don't see?'

followUp.prompt: Was there a moment today when telling the truth felt hard?

options.label: Saying 'I'm fine' when I wasn't
options.reflection: Saying 'I'm fine' when you're not is one of the most common small untruths, often a way to keep the day moving. Tomorrow, you might give one trusted person a slightly truer answer, and see what it opens up between you.

options.label: To spare someone's feelings
options.reflection: Holding back to spare someone's feelings tends to come from real care. The tricky part is that honest words, said gently, can also be a gift. Tomorrow, you might look for one small true thing you can say kindly.

options.label: Being honest with myself
options.reflection: Being honest with yourself can be the hardest kind, because there's no one else to blame or comfort. Noticing it at all takes courage. Tomorrow, you might write down one thing you know is true, even if you're not ready to act on it.

options.label: The truth came easily today
options.reflection: A day where the truth came easily can be a sign you're among people you feel safe with. That's worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might spot who makes honesty feel easy for you, and spend a little more time with them.

questions.prompt: You realise you were wrong in an argument you 'won'. What do you do?

options.label: Go back and say I was wrong

insight.reveal: You'd rather get it right than win, and you know the difference. Being willing to lose is rare, and it makes the people around you more open to changing their minds too. Your opinions carry extra weight precisely because you'll take them back.
insight.research: Scientists who admitted a finding of theirs was wrong were judged at least as well, and on some measures better, than colleagues who refused to admit it.
insight.step: This week, say 'I was wrong about that' about one small thing, out loud.

options.label: Mention it casually much later

insight.reveal: You get there in the end, once the heat has gone. Weeks later you'll slip a 'you were right about that' into a chat. The other person may have stopped waiting by then, yet it usually lands more warmly than you expect.
insight.step: Next time you realise you were wrong, say so within one day.

options.label: Let it stand. The moment has passed

insight.reveal: Once an argument's over, you close the file and move on. It keeps life light, and you hold few grudges. The other person may still be carrying the old version, though, and it can quietly shape what they believe about you.
insight.step: This week, think of one argument you won but shouldn't have, and find a light way to mention it.

options.label: Look for a new reason I was still right

insight.reveal: Being wrong feels like losing a little piece of you. Most minds work this way, and a quick one like yours wins a lot of debates. Catching yourself hunting for new reasons is already the hard part, and you just did it.
insight.research: Even after learning about a bias, people tended to insist their own judgement was objective, while easily seeing bias in others.
insight.step: Next time you hunt for new reasons, ask: 'If they had said this, would I accept it?'

followUp.prompt: Did you notice today that you'd got something wrong? Did you own it?

options.label: I said so openly
options.reflection: Saying you were wrong out loud takes a kind of strength people tend to respect, even if it felt awkward. It shows you care more about the truth than about winning. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it made the other person more open with you too.

options.label: I let it pass without a word
options.reflection: Letting it pass quietly can be fine for small things, and you may still have learned from it. If it mattered to someone else, it might be worth a word. Tomorrow, you might check whether anyone would appreciate hearing 'you were right'.

options.label: I looked for reasons I was right
options.reflection: Hunting for reasons you were still right is a very human reflex, because being wrong can sting. Noticing that pull is the first step. Tomorrow, you might try the words 'I see it differently now' and notice how much lighter they feel.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day without being caught out can feel easy. Still, being wrong now and then is part of learning. Tomorrow, you might stay curious about one view that's different from yours, and see what it teaches you.

questions.prompt: When you post about your life online, how true is the picture?

options.label: I rarely post at all

insight.reveal: Your real life and your online life barely meet. You'd rather share news face to face, and you value your privacy. The flip side is that friends may miss the good things happening to you, from a new job to a new hobby.
insight.step: This week, share one small good moment directly with one friend, not online.

options.label: True, but only the best bits

insight.reveal: You edit your life for others, the way nearly everyone does. Funny thing: we compare our behind-the-scenes with everyone else's highlights and forget we're editing too. You likely have a good eye for what makes a moment worth sharing.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others feel low and overestimate how often they feel good, partly because others hide it; those who did this most felt lonelier.
insight.step: Next time you compare yourself to a post, remember one thing you chose not to post.

options.label: I share the hard parts too

insight.reveal: You'd rather be known than admired. Chances are you get quiet 'me too' messages after a post, and you've become a safe place for others without planning to. Your friendships are more honest because of it.
insight.step: This week, reply kindly to someone who shared something hard online.

options.label: A bit better than real life, honestly

insight.reveal: Even a small audience pulls on you, and you admit it. You've got real flair for style and storytelling. The gap between the post and the life can feel a bit lonely, though people tend to see more of the real you than you'd think.
insight.research: When strangers rated people's social media profiles, their impressions tended to match the person's real personality rather than the idealised self they wished to be.
insight.step: For one week, post nothing, or post one thing exactly as it is.

followUp.prompt: Did you post or share anything about your life today? What did it show?

options.label: The good parts of my day
options.reflection: Sharing the good parts is natural; most people like to keep the hard bits close. It may help to remember that everyone else's feed is edited too. Tomorrow, you might notice one ordinary moment you enjoyed without needing to share it at all.

options.label: The real mix, ups and downs
options.reflection: Sharing the ups and the downs tends to invite real connection, because it lets others feel less alone. It can also feel exposed. Tomorrow, you might notice who responded warmly, and let that remind you it was worth it.

options.label: A slightly polished version
options.reflection: A little polish is very common online, and it doesn't make you false. Still, it may be worth asking who the picture is for. Tomorrow, you might notice how you feel about your day before you share it, not after the likes come in.

options.label: I didn't share anything today
options.reflection: A day without posting can leave more room to simply live it. You might notice whether that felt freeing or a little quiet. Tomorrow, you could tell one person directly about something that happened, instead of sharing it widely.

questions.prompt: A work rule seems pointless and no one would notice if you skipped it. What do you do?

options.label: Follow it anyway

insight.reveal: You trust that a rule has a reason, even when you can't see it. You're the colleague trusted with tasks where details really matter. You also read the instructions before building the furniture, and quietly enjoy it when there are no screws left over.
insight.step: This week, ask the reason behind one rule you follow without knowing why.

options.label: Follow it, but ask to change it

insight.reveal: You respect a system enough to try to make it better. You improve workplaces slowly and without drama. You've probably rewritten at least one confusing form just so nobody else has to struggle with it.
insight.step: This week, pick one pointless rule and suggest one clear fix to the person who can change it.

options.label: Depends on my mood that day

insight.reveal: Your rule-keeping is strongest on your good days. Tiredness can lower the bar for anyone, and you're honest enough to say so. You're flexible, easy company, and knowing what your tired self tends to do late in the week is half the battle.
insight.step: This week, notice one choice you made differently because you were tired.

options.label: Skip it quietly

insight.reveal: A rule has to earn your respect by making sense. That makes you quick and practical, happy to cut through red tape that slows everyone else down. It also means your own sense of 'pointless' becomes the rule, so check it now and then.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Before skipping a rule this week, ask one colleague why it exists.

followUp.prompt: Did you run into a rule today that felt pointless? What did you do?

options.label: I followed it anyway
options.reflection: Following a rule even when it seems pointless often reflects steady reliability, and that's something others can count on. Tomorrow, you might notice whether the rule had a reason you couldn't see, or whether it's worth gently raising.

options.label: I followed it and asked why
