options.reflection: Following a rule while asking why tends to be a healthy balance of respect and curiosity. Questions like yours can make things better for everyone. Tomorrow, you might notice if anyone else was quietly wondering the same thing.

options.label: I quietly skipped it
options.reflection: Skipping a rule that feels empty is a common choice, and it may have saved you time. It might still be worth asking whether it'll matter later. Tomorrow, you could mention the rule to someone, in case it can be changed for everyone.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day without silly rules in your way can feel smooth. It may be a good moment to notice which systems in your life work well for you. Tomorrow, you might appreciate one of them, a routine or a habit, that makes things easier.

questions.prompt: It's 3 a.m. and something has gone badly wrong. How many people could you call?

options.label: Lots. I have a wide circle

insight.reveal: You've got someone for every kind of problem. You're the connector at parties, and no single friendship has to carry too much. The hidden cost: you may know a lot about others while few people know the whole story of you.
insight.research: Across 148 studies of over 300,000 people, those with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival.
insight.step: This week, tell one friend something real about your life that you usually keep light.

options.label: Two or three, and that feels like plenty

insight.reveal: A few deep friendships are plenty for you. You likely keep friends for decades. The same habit often shows up in how you shop and work: fewer things, chosen with care, kept for a long time.
insight.step: Today, send one of those two or three people a message with no question or request in it.

options.label: One, and I'd still hesitate to wake them

insight.reveal: You'd get up in the night for anyone, but you hate to ask. Asking, to you, feels too close to being a burden. Your friend would probably be glad you called, exactly the way you would be.
insight.research: In studies with over 14,000 strangers, people asking for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%.
insight.step: This week, ask that one person for a small favour and notice how they actually respond.

options.label: Honestly, I'd handle it alone

insight.reveal: You learned to rely on yourself, and it mostly works. In a crisis you're resourceful: you read the manual and fix the leak yourself. That skill is real, but it can make closeness feel like a risk instead of a rest.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time something small goes wrong, tell one person about it the same day instead of after it's fixed.

followUp.prompt: When something went wrong today, big or small, did you reach out to anyone?

options.label: Yes, I reached out to someone
options.reflection: Reaching out when things go wrong tends to strengthen the very bonds you rely on. It suggests you trust that you're allowed to need people. Tomorrow, you might thank the person who answered, even with a short message.

options.label: I wanted to, but held back
options.reflection: Holding back often comes from not wanting to be a burden, which shows how much you consider others. Yet the people who care about you often want to help. Tomorrow, you might send one small message to someone you trust, just to stay close.

options.label: I handled it on my own
options.reflection: Handling it alone shows real self-reliance, and sometimes that's the right call. It may also be worth noticing if going it alone is a habit more than a choice. Tomorrow, you might share one small part of your day with someone, just to let them in a little.

options.label: Nothing went wrong today
options.reflection: A day where nothing went wrong is worth a quiet moment of thanks. It may also be a good time to remember who's in your corner. Tomorrow, you might reach out to one of them simply to say hello, so the line stays warm.

questions.prompt: You open your wardrobe. What do you mostly see?

options.label: A few pieces I love and wear all the time

insight.reveal: You know what works for you, and you stick with it. Long menus probably tire you, and you may secretly enjoy ordering the same favourite dish again and again. Your mornings are quicker than most, because half the choices are already made.
insight.step: Tonight, pick tomorrow's outfit and notice whether your morning feels lighter.

options.label: Lots of choice, some never worn

insight.reveal: You buy clothes for the person you might become. The bold shirt, the fancy coat for a life you're still picturing: those unworn pieces are less about clothes and more about lives you're trying on. You're more open to reinvention than people think.
insight.step: This week, wear one never-worn item just once, and see who you feel like in it.

options.label: Things I'm keeping for 'one day'

insight.reveal: You save the best things for a future version of you. You probably keep 'one day' plans too: the trip, the class, the call you keep meaning to make. It's real hope, though sometimes the future you gets all the good stuff while today's you waits.
insight.research: Owning something tends to make it feel worth more: in classic experiments, people given a mug asked far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: This week, choose one 'one day' item, then wear it or give it away before the week ends.

options.label: Things I bought to feel better on a bad day

insight.reveal: Your wardrobe is partly a diary of hard days. When a week gets heavy, a little treat helps, and you know it. Being this honest with yourself is rare, and it's exactly where the pattern starts to loosen.
insight.step: Next time a bad day pulls you toward a shop, wait one night first and see if the wish is still there.

followUp.prompt: When you got dressed today, what did you reach for?

options.label: Something I love and wear a lot
options.reflection: Reaching for something you love and wear often suggests you know what makes you feel like yourself. That's a quiet kind of self-knowledge. Tomorrow, you might notice how that piece makes you stand or move, and enjoy it a little more.

options.label: Something I'd saved for 'one day'
options.reflection: Wearing something you'd been saving can turn an ordinary day into a small occasion. It may be a sign you're ready to enjoy things now, not later. Tomorrow, you might look for one more 'one day' thing you could simply use.

options.label: Something I bought to cheer myself up
options.reflection: Wearing something bought on a low day can be a reminder of how you looked after yourself then. It may also be worth noticing what you really needed in that moment. Tomorrow, you might find one free way to give yourself that same lift.

options.label: I didn't really think about it
options.reflection: Not thinking about what you wore can mean your mind was busy elsewhere, or that you're comfortable as you are. Tomorrow, you might pick one piece on purpose, just for how it makes you feel, and see if it changes your day.

questions.prompt: You get one free week to travel. Which trip do you choose?

options.label: One place, slowly, like I live there

insight.reveal: A bakery and a bus ride tell you more than any famous sight. You judge a place by its ordinary moments, and you likely come home knowing a café owner by name. You bring the same instinct to friendships, where small routines often beat big events.
insight.step: This week, visit one place near home twice instead of trying somewhere new.

options.label: Five places. See as much as I can

insight.reveal: Missing the one great thing scares you more than being tired. You pack your days tight and come home with a camera roll full of stories. You collect moments the way some people collect things, and remember the rush more than the details.
insight.research: People's minds wandered almost half the time they were awake, and they tended to feel less happy then than when focused on what they were doing.
insight.step: On your next outing, pick one moment and stay with it for five full minutes before moving on.

options.label: The trip that will look best when I share it

insight.reveal: A trip feels even better to you once it's been shared. You have a good eye for beauty and a knack for telling a story. Admitting it takes honesty, because most of us pretend other people's opinions don't shape our choices.
insight.research: In four studies, people free to take photos remembered more of what they saw but less of what they heard, even if they never looked at the photos again.
insight.step: This week, take one outing with no photos at all, then notice what you remember.

options.label: Stay home and finally do nothing

insight.reveal: You may be running on less fuel than you let anyone see. You carry a lot quietly, at work and at home. Wishing for a blank week often means your ordinary weeks hold more than the people around you know.
insight.step: This week, block one evening with nothing planned, and protect it like a meeting.

followUp.prompt: When you had a little time for yourself today, did you fill it up or slow down?

options.label: On one thing, slowly
options.reflection: Giving your free time to one thing, slowly, often lets you sink into it and come back more rested. That's a lovely way to recharge. Tomorrow, you might notice what made it feel good, and protect a little time for it again.

options.label: I squeezed in as much as I could
options.reflection: Squeezing in a lot can feel exciting, and it often means you're hungry for life. It may also leave you tired by evening. Tomorrow, you might try choosing just one thing to enjoy fully, and see how it compares.

options.label: Resting and doing nothing
options.reflection: Resting and doing nothing is not wasted time: it's often exactly what a tired mind needs. Notice whether you felt guilty or simply calm. Tomorrow, you might give yourself permission to rest again without needing to earn it.

options.label: I didn't get free time today
options.reflection: A day with no free time at all can be draining, even when everything you did mattered. You may be running low. Tomorrow, you might find a small pocket, even a few minutes with a hot drink, that belongs only to you.

questions.prompt: You arrive at a big buffet. What's your plan?

options.label: A little bit of everything

insight.reveal: Closing doors isn't your thing, even at dinner. The same pull shows up in work and hobbies, where you'd rather keep options open than bet it all on one. You'll probably order several small dishes for the table to share.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the first dish that catches your eye without reading the rest.

options.label: Find the best dish and go back for it

insight.reveal: You're a scout first, then a loyal regular. You do the same with music, places and friends: a short search, then years of steady loyalty. There's probably a restaurant somewhere that already knows your order.
insight.research: A review of 268 tests found people tend to like things more the more often they see them, though liking can dip again after too many repeats.
insight.step: This week, go back on purpose to one favourite thing: a song, a café or a person.

options.label: Eat enough to make it worth the price

insight.reveal: You keep a quiet scoreboard to make sure things are fair. It makes you savvy and hard to cheat, the one who knows which deal is actually a deal. The same scoreboard, though, can turn a lovely evening into a test you feel you have to win.
insight.step: Next time you pay for something, judge it by how you felt after, not by how much you got.

options.label: Take more than I want, then feel bad

insight.reveal: Your fear of missing out is louder than your stomach. You're enthusiastic and up for anything, which people love about you. You might spot the same pattern in your calendar: saying yes to everything, then wishing you hadn't.
insight.step: At your next meal, serve half of what you think you want and go back only if you're still hungry.

followUp.prompt: Did you get to enjoy what you ate today, or was it more of a rush?

options.label: I really enjoyed a meal
options.reflection: Really enjoying a meal often means you were present for it, and that's a small gift to yourself. Tomorrow, you might eat one thing a little slower, noticing its taste and warmth, and see if the feeling returns.

options.label: I ate more than I wanted
options.reflection: Eating more than you wanted happens to most people, often when food is tasty, you're tired or the plate is big. No need for guilt. Tomorrow, you might pause halfway through a meal and simply ask yourself how hungry you still are.

options.label: I ate on the run
options.reflection: Eating on the run often means your day was full and your own needs came last. That's understandable on busy days. Tomorrow, you might set aside a few minutes to sit down with one meal, even a simple one, just for you.

options.label: Food didn't stand out today
options.reflection: Not every meal needs to be memorable, and a plain day of food can be just fine. Tomorrow, you might pick one snack or meal to really taste, and notice whether a little attention makes it more satisfying.

questions.prompt: You're offered one more project at work. What do you do?

options.label: Say yes. More is more

insight.reveal: You run on momentum, not rest. You probably do your best work slightly overloaded, juggling side projects with ease. Quiet weeks and long breaks can leave you feeling strangely flat.
insight.step: Before your next yes, take ten seconds to name what you will do less of to make room.

options.label: Say no to protect the work I already have

insight.reveal: Finished work is how you measure a good day, not busy hours. Colleagues tend to admire the quality you turn out, and the ones who can't say no may secretly envy you for it. Your 'no' protects the very work that earned you that respect.
insight.research: In about 12,000 daily diaries from 238 workers, the best days were the ones where people made progress on work that mattered to them.
insight.step: This week, name the one task that deserves your best hours, and do it first thing one morning.

options.label: Say yes, even though I'm already stretched

insight.reveal: You feel you've earned your place when people can count on you. You protect everyone's deadlines except the ones for your own life, like the exercise plan or the trip you keep putting off. Being reliable is lovely; being reliable to yourself counts too.
insight.step: This week, move one small request to 'next week' and see if anything actually breaks.

options.label: Say yes because saying no scares me

insight.reveal: Saying no feels like a risk to you, not just a choice. You're generous, hard-working and quick to read other people's moods. That fear often runs even deeper at home than at work, and admitting it here takes a quiet kind of courage.
insight.research: Helping because you chose to lifted the well-being of both helper and helped, while helping under pressure did not bring the same benefits.
insight.step: This week, try one small, kind no, like turning down a meeting you don't need.

followUp.prompt: Were you asked to take on anything extra today? What did you say?

options.label: I said yes, and I was glad to
options.reflection: Saying yes gladly often means you had room for it, or that it lit something up in you. That energy is worth following. Tomorrow, you might notice what drew you to it, so you can look for more work that feels this way.

options.label: I said no to protect my time
options.reflection: Saying no to protect your time can feel uncomfortable, yet it often keeps your best work possible. It suggests you know your limits. Tomorrow, you might notice what you were able to give more care to because of that no.

options.label: I said yes, though I'm stretched
options.reflection: Saying yes when you're already stretched tends to come from wanting to help, and that kindness is real. But your energy has limits too. Tomorrow, you might look at your list and choose one thing you can let go of or hand over.

options.label: Nothing extra came my way
options.reflection: A day without extra asks can give you a little breathing room. It may be a good moment to notice how full your plate really is. Tomorrow, you might decide in advance what you'd say if something new came along.

questions.prompt: How do you usually read books, or watch series?

options.label: One at a time, start to finish

insight.reveal: You like a story to end before the next one starts. An unanswered message or a half-made plan probably bugs you more than it bugs anyone else. It's also why you're the one confirming the time and place the day before.
insight.research: Unfinished tasks are not remembered better than finished ones, but people do tend to feel a pull to go back and finish what was interrupted.
insight.step: Tonight, leave one small thing unfinished on purpose and notice how long it nags at you.

options.label: Several at once, depending on my mood

insight.reveal: You pick your story to match your mood. Your tastes run wide, and you may keep different friends for different moods too, rarely mixing the groups. Knowing what you need on a given day is a quiet skill.
insight.step: This week, notice which story you reach for on a hard day. It may tell you what you need.

options.label: I go back to the same favourites again

insight.reveal: A story you already know is a safe place for you to rest. When the rest of life is full of unknowns, a known ending can't surprise you. You likely stay loyal to favourite songs, cafés and people for years, and they're lucky to have you.
insight.research: Nostalgia often came on with low mood or loneliness, and recalling fond memories helped people feel more connected and better about themselves.
insight.step: This week, try one new show or book that someone who knows you well recommended.

options.label: I start many and finish almost none

insight.reveal: You love beginnings, when anything still feels possible. Ideas come easily to you, and starting is your gift. You might notice the same pattern with plans and projects, where the exciting start fades long before the slow middle.
insight.step: This weekend, pick one thing you started and finish just the next chapter or episode.

followUp.prompt: Did you read or watch anything today? How did you go about it?

options.label: I stuck with one thing
options.reflection: Sticking with one thing tends to let you sink in and really follow a story through. That focus is a quiet pleasure. Tomorrow, you might notice what kept you hooked, and whether that's something you'd like more of in your day.

options.label: I jumped between a few things
options.reflection: Jumping between things often reflects a curious mind that follows its mood, and that can be fun and refreshing. Tomorrow, you might notice which one you kept coming back to, since that's often the one that matters most to you.

options.label: I went back to something I love
options.reflection: Going back to something you love can feel like visiting an old friend, and it's often a sign you wanted comfort. That's okay. Tomorrow, you might ask yourself what you were needing, and whether there's another way to give it to yourself too.

options.label: I didn't get to it today
options.reflection: A day without reading or watching anything may mean your time went to other things, or you simply needed a break. Tomorrow, you might set aside a short window for a story you enjoy, if that sounds good to you.

questions.prompt: How many photos are on your phone right now?

options.label: Not many. I delete as I go

insight.reveal: You trust your memory more than your phone. You probably keep a tidy inbox and a clear desk. You may also let go of old arguments, old things and old versions of yourself faster than most.
insight.step: Tonight, pick one photo you kept and send it to the person in it, no message needed.

options.label: Thousands. I'll sort them one day

insight.reveal: You keep everything, just in case it matters later. You're a curious collector of moments, and the 'one day' pile likely grows in other places too: inboxes, browser tabs, half-planned trips.
insight.step: Tonight, spend five minutes deleting photos from one single day, and stop when the timer ends.

options.label: Thousands, and I never look back at them

insight.reveal: You take the photo for the moment, not to look at it again. You live forward, and the past rarely holds you for long. Old mistakes don't tend to haunt you, because whatever comes next is simply more interesting.
insight.research: People free to take photos remembered more of what they saw, even if they never looked at the photos again, though they remembered less of what they heard.
insight.step: Tonight, open a photo from exactly one year ago and notice what you had forgotten.

options.label: I photograph moments instead of being in them

insight.reveal: You worry good moments will vanish if you don't catch them. That's because you treasure them deeply, which is a real strength. The camera is your way of holding on, even while it puts a screen between you and the moment you wanted to keep.
insight.research: Across 20 trials with 4,805 people, savouring exercises, which train people to notice and enjoy good moments, moderately boosted good feelings.
insight.step: At the next good moment, leave the phone in your pocket and describe it to someone later instead.

followUp.prompt: Did you take any photos today, or spend time with the ones you have?

options.label: I took a few, then put my phone away
options.reflection: Taking a few photos and then putting the phone away often lets you keep the memory and still live the moment. That's a nice balance. Tomorrow, you might look back at one of today's pictures and notice what you remember beyond the frame.

options.label: I watched a lot through my screen
options.reflection: Seeing a lot through your screen is very common, since most of us want to hold on to good moments. It may help to notice what you missed while framing them. Tomorrow, you might take one photo, then let yourself just look for a while.

options.label: I sorted or deleted some photos
options.reflection: Sorting or deleting photos can feel like clearing a little space in your mind as well as your phone. It suggests you like to keep what matters. Tomorrow, you might pick one picture you kept and share it with someone who's in it.

options.label: I didn't take any today
options.reflection: A day with no photos can mean you were busy, or simply living without stopping to record it. Both are fine. Tomorrow, you might notice one small scene worth remembering, and decide whether to capture it or just enjoy it.

questions.prompt: Which sounds most like your hobbies?

options.label: One thing I've gone really deep on

insight.reveal: When you love something, you go all the way in. You lose track of time in your hobby and can get grumpy when someone interrupts. That same depth often shows up in love: you probably care for a few people, but very fully.
insight.step: This week, teach someone one small thing about your hobby and see how it feels to share it.

options.label: Lots of things tried, none mastered

insight.reveal: The first weeks of learning something are your favourite part. Progress is fast then, and you love that feeling. You're great company at dinner, and you often link ideas from different worlds in ways specialists miss.
insight.step: Over the next few days, spend twenty minutes on one past hobby, just to see what you still know.

options.label: I don't really have hobbies anymore

insight.reveal: Your hobbies slipped away one busy month at a time. You're responsible, and probably stretched thin. Here's the interesting part: you already know what you'd pick back up first if you had a free afternoon, and that answer is still in you.
insight.research: Across 93,263 people aged 65 and over in 16 countries, having a hobby went along with more happiness and life satisfaction.
insight.step: This weekend, spend thirty minutes on something you used to love, with no goal at all.

options.label: I quit once I'm not quickly good at it

insight.reveal: Being bad at something feels personal to you. You're capable and curious, just not used to feeling like a beginner. The first clumsy weeks feel harder than they really are, and almost everyone you admire went through them too.
insight.research: People who believed passions are 'found' rather than built tended to lose interest faster when a new interest got hard.
insight.step: This week, try something new where the only goal is to be bad at it for ten minutes.

followUp.prompt: Did you spend any time on a hobby or something just for fun today?

options.label: I spent time on my main hobby
options.reflection: Giving time to something you love tends to refill you in a way that work and chores rarely do. It suggests you're protecting a part of yourself. Tomorrow, you might notice how you felt afterwards, and remember it on busy days.

options.label: I tried something new
options.reflection: Trying something new often shows a curious, open side of you, and first steps are rarely graceful. That's part of the fun. Tomorrow, you might give it a second go, just to see what it feels like when it's a little less new.

options.label: I tried, but got frustrated
options.reflection: Feeling frustrated when something isn't easy yet is very common, especially when you care about doing things well. It may help to treat the clumsy stage as part of the hobby. Tomorrow, you might try it for just a few minutes, with no goal at all.

options.label: No time for fun today
options.reflection: A day with no time for fun can happen, especially when life is full. You may be running on duty more than joy right now. Tomorrow, you might find a small pocket, even a short walk or a song, that's just for the pleasure of it.

questions.prompt: Think about your group chats. Which is true?

options.label: One or two that really matter

insight.reveal: You treat messages as real conversations, not noise. You remember small things people told you weeks ago and ask how the job interview went. You also notice, a little sadly, when others don't do the same for you.
insight.research: Time spent side by side didn't, on its own, make people closer friends; catching up on each other's lives and joking did.
insight.step: Tomorrow, reply to one message with a question that shows you remembered something.

options.label: Many, and I keep up with all of them

insight.reveal: You're the quiet glue in a lot of friend groups. Chances are you know what everyone's up to, and you're the one who plans the next meet-up. Sometimes you'll notice that few people check in on you the same way.
insight.step: This week, notice who in your chats asks how you are, and spend a little more time with them.

options.label: Many, and the unread ones make me guilty

insight.reveal: You hold yourself to a standard nobody actually asked for. You're a thoughtful friend who replies properly, never with a lazy thumbs-up. That same rule, though, can make rest feel like something you have to earn first.
insight.research: When students kept phone alerts on for a week, they reported more trouble focusing and more restlessness than in a week with alerts off.
insight.step: Today, mute one busy chat for three days and notice whether anyone actually needed you.

options.label: Many, but no one I really talk to

insight.reveal: Your phone is busy, but you're missing someone to really talk to. You're good at keeping things light and friendly. You're likely closer to one real friendship than you think, and it usually starts with a single honest message.
insight.research: Across 148 studies, people with stronger social ties had about 50% better odds of survival, and rich, many-sided connection mattered more than just living with others.
insight.step: In the next few days, message one person outside the group and ask how they really are.

followUp.prompt: Did any message or group chat today feel like real connection?

options.label: I had a real chat with someone
options.reflection: A real conversation, even in one small chat, tends to matter more than many quick replies. It suggests you value depth. Tomorrow, you might reach out to that person again, or to someone else you'd like to feel closer to.

options.label: I kept up with all of them
options.reflection: Keeping up with all your chats often shows how much you enjoy being connected and in the loop. That's a warm thing. Tomorrow, you might notice which chats leave you lifted and which just keep you busy, and give the first kind a bit more time.

options.label: Unread ones piled up and nagged me
options.reflection: Unread messages piling up can nag at you, especially if you hate letting people down. It's okay to fall behind. Tomorrow, you might mute one busy chat, or reply to just one person who matters, and let that be enough.

options.label: I barely looked at them today
options.reflection: Barely checking your chats can give your mind real rest, and nobody needs you to be available all the time. Tomorrow, you might send one message to someone you miss, so the quiet feels like a choice and not a drift.

questions.prompt: Your ideal birthday dinner looks like…

options.label: A big party. Everyone's invited

insight.reveal: Half your friends probably met through you. You feel most like yourself with your whole world in one room. You're a generous host, and you might enjoy introducing people to each other more than talking to any one of them.
insight.step: This month, introduce two people you know who've never met but would get along.

options.label: A few close people around a long table

insight.reveal: Your best evenings are the ones where something real gets said. You care more about the talk than the noise. You're likely the last one still at the table long after dessert, asking one more question.
insight.research: In every world region, people who share more meals with others tend to report higher well-being.
insight.step: This month, invite two people for a simple meal, even if it isn't a special day.

options.label: Just one person who really knows me

insight.reveal: One person who truly sees you beats a room full of cheers. Big celebrations of you can feel a little uncomfortable, and on ordinary days you'd pick one deep talk over an evening of small talk. Someone came to mind when you answered, didn't they?
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there really was.
insight.step: Before the week is out, tell the person you thought of what they mean to you. No birthday needed.

options.label: Alone, with something great to eat

insight.reveal: Attention on your big day can feel more like pressure than a gift. You enjoy your own company and know how to treat yourself well. You often give generously on other people's birthdays while quietly hoping your own passes softly.
insight.step: This week, treat yourself to one great meal alone, and let it be enough.

followUp.prompt: Who did you share a meal or a good moment with today?

options.label: A big group, lively and busy
options.reflection: Being among a lively group often fills you with energy and a sense of belonging. If you're smiling tonight, that may be why. Tomorrow, you might reach out to one person from that group for a quieter moment, just the two of you.

options.label: A few people I'm close to
options.reflection: Time with a few close people tends to feel warm and easy, the kind where you can just be yourself. That's worth treasuring. Tomorrow, you might tell one of them what you enjoyed about today.

options.label: Just one person
options.reflection: Sharing a moment with just one person often allows a depth that bigger groups can't. It suggests you value being truly known. Tomorrow, you might think about what made it feel good, and whether that person knows how much it meant.

options.label: Nobody today, I was on my own
options.reflection: A day on your own can feel peaceful or a little lonely, and both are okay to feel. You may have needed the quiet. Tomorrow, if you'd like some company, you might reach out to one person, even with a short message.

questions.prompt: You win a huge amount of money tomorrow. What do you do first?

options.label: Call my family and share the news

insight.reveal: Good news isn't real for you until someone you love hears it. You probably tell your people before you've even put your bag down, and you cheer loudest when they have news too. A win you couldn't share would feel strangely flat, like cake eaten alone.
insight.research: Telling someone about a good thing that happened tends to lift your mood beyond the good news itself, especially when they respond with real interest.
insight.step: Today, share one small piece of good news with someone, even if it feels too small to mention.

options.label: Stay calm, make a plan, change little

insight.reveal: Even a fortune wouldn't rush you, and that's rarer than it sounds. You read the small print, keep the routines that already work, and friends tend to phone you first when things go wrong. The flip side: exciting news can take a while to actually feel exciting.
insight.research: Swedish lottery winners, on average, cut their work earnings only modestly after winning, and that small drop lasted for years.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three things in your life you'd keep exactly the same, whatever happened.

options.label: Quit my job that same week

insight.reveal: The real prize for you would be getting your time back. Chances are you already know which part of your week you'd cut first, down to the day. Once a door opens you move fast, and you bring real energy to fresh starts that others would plan to death.
insight.step: This week, name the part of your work week you'd drop first, and find one small way to shrink it.

options.label: Tell no one, afraid of how people would change

insight.reveal: You want to be loved for who you are, not for what you've got. You notice who stays close when life shifts, and big news stays inside a very small circle. It can make you seem guarded, but once someone earns your trust, you're about as loyal as a friend gets.
insight.step: This week, notice who you'd trust with big news. That short list is worth knowing.

followUp.prompt: Did money or a lucky break cross your mind today? Where did your thoughts go?

options.label: I pictured sharing good news with my people
options.reflection: When your mind drifts to good fortune, it seems to head straight for the people you love. That instinct to share often says more about you than any windfall could. Tomorrow, you might pass on one small piece of good news, just because.

options.label: I made a careful, sensible money choice
options.reflection: You may tend to meet money with a steady hand rather than a daydream, and that calm can be a real strength. Tomorrow, see whether it also leaves a little room for something that simply brings you joy.

options.label: I daydreamed about walking away from work
options.reflection: A daydream about walking away from work often carries a message about what you are hungry for: rest, freedom or something new. It may be worth listening to. Tomorrow, try naming one small piece of that wish you could have now.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Money and big wins stayed in the background today, and that can be restful. Your attention may have been on things that mattered more. Tomorrow, you might notice where your mind goes when it has a free moment.

questions.prompt: Do brand names on clothes and bags matter to you?

options.label: Not at all. I want comfort

insight.reveal: You dress for how it feels, not for what it says. Your most-loved clothes probably stay in rotation long after they've earned retirement. How someone treats a waiter tells you far more than their bag ever could.
insight.step: This week, notice one sign of status you do care about that has nothing to do with things.

options.label: Quality yes, logos no

insight.reveal: You like nice things that whisper, not things that shout. You compare before you buy, check the stitching and read the reviews, then keep it for years. Being underestimated by people who only notice loud labels quietly amuses you.
insight.research: Wealthy buyers with little need for status tended to prefer luxury goods with quiet logos, while status-seekers chose loud ones.
insight.step: Tomorrow, use one 'good' thing you've been saving, on a completely ordinary day.

options.label: A little. I notice what others wear

insight.reveal: You catch the details most people walk right past. You'd spot a friend's new haircut first and might remember what someone wore to a party months ago. On a wobbly day, that same sharp eye can slide into quiet comparing, and it's rarely kind to you when it does.
insight.step: Next time you notice what someone wears, also notice one thing about them that cost nothing.

options.label: Yes. I feel more respected in them

insight.reveal: The right clothes let you walk into a room already accepted. Somewhere along the way you learned that respect gets decided on sight, so you take real care with how you show up. Friends likely call you before a big interview, though you deserve that respect in your plainest shirt too.
insight.research: People overestimate how much others notice them: students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about 46% of the room noticed, but only about 23% did.
insight.step: This week, wear your plainest outfit somewhere ordinary and notice how people actually treat you.

followUp.prompt: Did you notice what you or others were wearing today? What caught your eye?

options.label: I just wore what felt comfortable
options.reflection: Reaching for comfort without a second thought often means you feel fairly settled in yourself. That ease is worth protecting. Tomorrow, you might notice one other place where you could choose what feels good over what looks good.

options.label: I noticed how well something was made
options.reflection: You seem to look past the label to how something is made, which tends to reflect a patient, careful eye. Tomorrow, you could give that same attention to something you already own, and enjoy that it has lasted.

options.label: I noticed a logo or label and felt a pull
options.reflection: Feeling a pull toward labels is very human, and it often says more about what you are measuring yourself against than about the item. Tomorrow, when one catches your eye, gently ask what you hoped it would say about you.

options.label: It didn't cross my mind today
options.reflection: Clothes and labels didn't take up much room in your day, and that can feel light. Your attention may have been somewhere it was needed more. Tomorrow, you might notice what you reach for first when you get dressed, and why.

questions.prompt: A close friend suddenly becomes rich. Your honest first feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: With the people you love, you never keep score. You're first to raise a glass at a friend's promotion, with no edge in your voice at all. Friends call you early with good news because they know your joy will be real, and that's a kind of wealth too.
insight.research: When someone shares good news, an interested, enthusiastic reply is linked to more trust and closeness, while a flat reply is linked to less.
insight.step: Next time a friend shares good news, ask which part of it they're proudest of.

options.label: Curious how they did it

insight.reveal: A friend's sudden luck is a puzzle you want to solve. You learn more from friends than from books, and you ask the questions others feel too polite to ask. Odds are you leave dinners like that with a new idea for your own life, typed into your phone on the way home.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you admire one specific question about how they got where they are.

options.label: A small sting of envy

insight.reveal: Admitting that sting takes honesty, and you've got plenty. You're probably the friend who tells the truth about a bad haircut. And envy works like a compass for you: it points straight at something you want for yourself, which is useful, not shameful.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy, wanting what someone has without wishing them harm, pushed people to work harder, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: Next time you feel envy, finish the sentence 'I wish I had…' in your head. That's the real goal.

options.label: Worry they'll leave me behind

insight.reveal: When a friend's life changes fast, you quietly wonder where you fit. You stay loyal for years and likely keep quiet track of who reached out last. The worry says more about how much you care than about them, and many people whose lives change still want their old friends close.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Over the next few days, reach out to a friend whose life has changed lately, and talk about anything but the change.

followUp.prompt: Did you hear about someone else's good fortune today? How did it sit with you?

options.label: I felt glad for them, simple as that
options.reflection: Feeling simply glad for someone else's luck tends to come from a generous, secure place in you. That kind of warmth is easy for others to feel. Tomorrow, you might tell them out loud that you're happy for them.

options.label: I felt a small pinch of envy
options.reflection: A pinch of envy is a normal human feeling, and noticing it honestly takes some courage. It often points to something you want for yourself. Tomorrow, you might ask what that want is, without being hard on yourself for feeling it.

options.label: I worried where it leaves me
options.reflection: Worrying that someone's good news might pull them away from you often comes from how much they matter to you. That care is real. Tomorrow, you might reach out to them in a small way, and see how the connection actually feels.

options.label: No one's news came my way today
options.reflection: No one's good fortune crossed your path today, so your attention could stay on your own life. That can be a calm place to be. Tomorrow, you might notice how you feel when someone else shares a win with you.

questions.prompt: Which life pulls at you more?

options.label: A small home, lots of free time

insight.reveal: You count your wealth in hours, not things. A slow morning with nothing booked feels richer to you than any shopping trip. A promotion that eats your evenings might not tempt you at all, and you're often happier on a tight budget than people expect.
insight.step: This weekend, give yourself one slow morning with nothing scheduled before ten.

options.label: Comfort, plus a few real luxuries

insight.reveal: Some luxuries are worth it to you, and you know exactly which. A great bed, really good coffee or one proper trip a year gets your money, and little else does. Choosing your splurges this carefully makes everything stretch further, and you enjoy the chosen few more for it.
insight.research: In over 76,000 bank transactions, people whose spending matched their personality were more satisfied with life, a stronger link than total income or spending.
insight.step: This week, enjoy your one 'worth it' luxury slowly, with no rushing and no guilt.

options.label: Big success, whatever it takes

insight.reveal: It's proof you're after, more than possessions. Proof you were right, proof you could, and that hunger probably started long before money was the reason. Give you a bold target and a scoreboard everyone can see, and you'll rally a whole team around it.
insight.step: Tonight, write down who you'd most want to see your success. Then ask yourself: why them?

options.label: I want simple, but I keep chasing more

insight.reveal: Part of you wants enough, and part of you can't stop running. You might look at little houses by the sea on your lunch break, then go back to pushing harder at work. Seeing both pulls this honestly is the first real step to choosing between them.
insight.research: In Gallup data from over 1.7 million people worldwide, extra income stopped lifting life ratings beyond a certain point, which was higher in richer regions.
insight.step: This month, picture an ordinary week in your 'enough' life, and claim one small piece of it now.

followUp.prompt: Did today feel more like time for living, or time for getting ahead?

options.label: I had real free time and enjoyed it
options.reflection: You found some real free time today and let yourself enjoy it, which suggests you value time more than things. That is a gift many people forget to give themselves. Tomorrow, you might protect one small pocket of time the same way.

options.label: I pushed hard to get ahead
options.reflection: You put your energy into getting ahead today, and that drive can carry you far. It may also be worth checking that the effort is taking you somewhere you truly want. Tomorrow, you might name one thing you're working toward and why.

options.label: I wanted to slow down but kept going
options.reflection: Wanting to slow down but keeping going anyway is a very common pull, and noticing it is a good first step. You may be carrying more than you need to. Tomorrow, you might pick one small thing to let go of, just for the day.

options.label: Just an ordinary day, nothing either way
options.reflection: Your day sounds ordinary, neither rushing nor resting, and ordinary days often hold more than they seem to. Tomorrow, you might notice one moment where you felt most like yourself, and what made it so.

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends who earn more than you. The bill comes. You…

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: You'd rather keep the evening warm than keep the numbers exact. You remember who was fun, not who ordered the pricey bottle, and group plans run smoother with you in them. Just check now and then that easygoing hasn't turned into always paying more than your share.
insight.research: In a restaurant experiment, diners ordered more when the bill was split evenly than when each paid for their own food.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, suggest one place that you choose, and see how it feels to lead.

options.label: Quietly do the math in my head

insight.reveal: There's a quiet calculator running behind your smile. You're scrupulously fair, and you probably know your monthly spending almost to the coin. When a split comes out uneven, you feel a pinch nobody else notices, then say nothing to keep the peace.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, honesty felt better and more connecting than predicted.
insight.step: Next time it feels uneven, say so lightly once and watch how little drama it causes.

options.label: Order less so I don't overspend

insight.reveal: You protect your friendships by quietly making yourself smaller. You're modest with money and generous with attention. The same habit may show up elsewhere too: the worse seat, the smaller room, the last turn, taken without a word and rarely noticed.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the thing you actually want, just once.

options.label: Act fine, then stress about it later

insight.reveal: You'd rather pay with worry than risk one awkward moment. You're often the most generous person at the table, and the one replaying the evening on the way home. Hardly anyone sees what it cost you, which is kind of you, and also a bit lonely.
insight.step: Next time you make plans, suggest a cheaper one to a friend, like a walk or cooking together.

followUp.prompt: Did you pay for something alongside others today? Did it feel even?

options.label: We split it easily, no fuss
options.reflection: Sharing a cost without fuss suggests money doesn't come between you and the people around you, which tends to keep things warm. Tomorrow, you might notice whether that ease feels true for you, or just easy to show.

options.label: I quietly worked out my share
options.reflection: Quietly working out your share suggests you like to stay on top of things, and that care can protect you. Tomorrow, you might notice whether it also lets you relax and enjoy the moment once the sums are done.

options.label: I paid more than felt right, then fretted
options.reflection: Paying more than felt right and then turning it over afterward is a very human loop. It often comes from not wanting to make things awkward. Tomorrow, you might practise one gentle sentence you could use next time, so it feels easier to say.

options.label: No shared costs today
options.reflection: There were no shared costs to manage today, so that small tension stayed away. Tomorrow, if a bill or a shared cost comes up, you might notice the very first feeling it brings, before you decide what to do.

questions.prompt: You walk into a very fancy hotel lobby. How do you feel?

options.label: At ease. I enjoy places like this

insight.reveal: Fancy rooms don't shrink you one bit. You chat with the front desk like old friends and help a nervous companion relax without making a show of it. Most rooms feel like yours, which is exactly why the rare one that doesn't is worth noticing.
insight.step: This week, go somewhere you're a beginner, and notice how you carry yourself there.

options.label: Excited, like it's a special treat

insight.reveal: Nice things still give you a little thrill, and that's precious. Odds are you've taken photos of a hotel breakfast before. One rare treat gives you more joy than daily luxury gives most people, and ordinary outings feel like an occasion when you come along.
insight.research: A review of happiness research suggested money brings more joy when spent on many small treats rather than one big one, and on things to look forward to.
insight.step: Today, plan one small treat for later this week, and enjoy the waiting as much as the treat.

options.label: A bit bored. It's all for show

insight.reveal: You can spot a performance from across the room. You'd pick the small family-run place over the grand chain, and marketing tricks rarely get past you. The catch: that same radar can make a sincere compliment hard to enjoy without checking whether it's real.
insight.step: Next time someone compliments you, just say 'thank you', with no checking and no brushing it off.

options.label: Like someone will notice I don't belong

insight.reveal: A small voice asks whether you're allowed to be here. You likely hear it in meetings and new groups too, even when you're clearly welcome. The upside is real: it can make you one of the kindest guests in any room, the first to spot who else feels out of place.
insight.research: Using luxury goods can make people feel like impostors, as if the luxury were an unearned privilege, which can leave them acting less confidently.
insight.step: This week, ask a friend what kind of room they think you shine in. Their answer may surprise you.

followUp.prompt: Were you somewhere today that felt a bit fancier than usual? How did you feel there?

options.label: Comfortable. I enjoyed it
options.reflection: You felt at home somewhere a little fancy, which often means you don't let surroundings tell you who you are. Tomorrow, you might notice whether you carry that same ease into places that feel less familiar.

options.label: It felt like a small treat
options.reflection: Enjoying a fancier place as a small treat suggests you can still find delight in the unusual, which is a lovely trait to keep. Tomorrow, you might look for one small, ordinary thing that could feel special too.

options.label: I felt a little out of place
options.reflection: Feeling out of place somewhere polished is common, and it often comes from old stories about where you belong. Those stories may not be true. Tomorrow, if that feeling shows up, you might remind yourself that you are allowed to be there.

options.label: I stayed in my usual places today
options.reflection: You stayed in your usual places today, and familiar spaces can be a real comfort. Tomorrow, you might notice which of your everyday places makes you feel most at ease, and what it is about them.

questions.prompt: You meet someone wearing a very expensive watch. First thought?

options.label: Nice watch. That's it

insight.reveal: You let people start with a clean slate. You judge someone by what they do next, not by what's on their wrist, and you're slower than most to decide who a person is. It's likely why your friends are such a wonderfully mixed bunch.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, guess one thing about them, then check it later.

options.label: I wonder what they do for work

insight.reveal: Where others see a watch, you see a life story. You're the one asking strangers how they ended up in their job, and other people's paths pull you right in. You probably hold those paths up against your own a little more than you let on.
insight.step: This week, ask one person how they ended up in their job, and listen for the turning point.

options.label: They're trying to impress someone

insight.reveal: Showing off makes you itch, and you spot it fast. People at work trust you because you play it straight and play down your own wins. The cost is that even your own nice things can come with a flicker of guilt, as if enjoying them were bragging.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Today, tell someone one thing you're proud of, plainly, without a joke to soften it.

options.label: I quietly compare myself and come up short

insight.reveal: Someone's expensive watch can turn into a scoreboard you're losing. You're ambitious and you notice details, so the comparing likely runs on many fronts, not just money. What you rarely do is count the things you have that someone else would quietly wish for.
insight.research: Life satisfaction tracked where people's income ranked among others like them more than the amount itself, and comparing upward counted more than downward.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three things someone might envy about your life, and reread them each day this week.

followUp.prompt: Did someone's car, phone or nice things catch your eye today? Where did your mind go?

options.label: I noticed, then moved on
options.reflection: You noticed and then moved on, which suggests other people's things don't easily pull at your sense of worth. That steadiness is worth keeping. Tomorrow, you might notice what does tend to catch your eye instead.

options.label: I got curious about their life
options.reflection: Getting curious about someone's life rather than their price tag tends to show an open, interested mind. Tomorrow, you might let that curiosity lead to a real question with someone you meet.

options.label: I compared myself and came up short
options.reflection: Comparing yourself and coming up short can sting, and it's something most people do more than they admit. It often leaves out everything you have that can't be seen. Tomorrow, you might name one thing in your life you wouldn't trade.

options.label: Nothing like that caught my eye
options.reflection: Nothing flashy caught your attention today, so your mind was free for other things. That can be quietly restful. Tomorrow, you might notice what you tend to look at first when you meet someone new.

questions.prompt: Growing up, how did money feel in your home?

options.label: Rarely talked about. It was just there

insight.reveal: Money sat quietly in the background of your childhood. Bills don't rattle you much, and money surprises tend to roll off. Funny thing is, you probably know more about your friends' love lives than their money lives, because money talk still feels a bit awkward.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you trust one simple money question, like what they most enjoy spending on.

options.label: Tight, but we managed

insight.reveal: You learned early how to make a little go a long way. You check prices out of habit even when you don't need to, and nobody stretches a budget like you. Spending generously on yourself probably still feels a little like breaking a rule.
insight.step: Sometime this week, buy yourself one small thing without checking the price first.

options.label: Money caused arguments

insight.reveal: Money talk can still make your shoulders tighten. You might steer around money talk with the people closest to you, just to keep the peace. Yet you may also be the one keeping money calm and open in your home now, which is no small thing given where you started.
insight.research: In a 2022 US survey, 66% named money as a major stress, and of those, 55% said it caused fights or tension in the family.
insight.step: This week, at a relaxed moment, start one calm, short money chat with someone close.

options.label: Something I still feel uneasy about today

insight.reveal: Some of your money worries are older than your bank account. Your unease probably doesn't rise and fall with your balance, a clue that it's about feeling safe more than about numbers. Seeing that clearly is a big deal, and it's often where feeling settled begins.
insight.step: Next time money worry rises, ask: 'Is this about today, or about back then?' and just notice the answer.

followUp.prompt: Did anything today remind you of how money felt when you were growing up?

options.label: I caught myself repeating a family money habit
options.reflection: Catching yourself repeating a family money habit can be surprising, whether the habit helps you or not. Habits from home often run quietly in the background. Tomorrow, you might ask whether this one still fits the life you want now.

options.label: An old money worry crept back in
options.reflection: An old money worry creeping back in is very understandable, especially if money felt tense when you were young. That feeling may be older than today's situation. Tomorrow, you might gently check what is true right now, not back then.

options.label: I felt calmer about money than I used to
options.reflection: Feeling calmer about money than you used to suggests you may have built some steadiness of your own. That is worth noticing. Tomorrow, you might give yourself a little credit for how far you have come.

options.label: No echoes of that today
options.reflection: No old money memories came up today, and that can be a relief. Not every day has to carry the past. Tomorrow, you might notice if anything small, like a price or a bill, stirs up a feeling from home.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected extra money this month. Where does it go?

options.label: Put aside for later

insight.reveal: Feeling safe beats a quick thrill for you, every time. You build a cushion before friends have even made a plan, and money scares don't knock you over. The catch is that small joys can wait for years, long after you could easily afford them.
insight.step: This weekend, do one small thing you've been 'saving up' to enjoy, even a tiny one.

options.label: A meal or trip with people I love

insight.reveal: You turn money into memories with people in them. You're likely the one who gets the group trip off the ground, and you can describe a shared meal from years ago in detail. Those stories get retold every time you meet, so the spending keeps paying you back.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: This week, suggest a simple shared plan to someone, like a picnic or a cheap dinner.

options.label: Something just for me

insight.reveal: A treat for yourself is your way of saying your wants count too. Chances are you put others first most of the year, so this is a rare moment where you come first. Enjoy it while it's fresh, and skip the guilt.
insight.step: Today, notice one want of your own and say it out loud to someone.

options.label: It's gone before I even notice

insight.reveal: Money slips through your fingers into a hundred small joys. You're spontaneous and generous, the one who gets the coffees and says yes to last-minute plans. 'Later' just feels very far from 'now' for you, which makes saving seem a bit unreal.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: For three days, write down one small thing you spent on each evening, just to see the pattern.

followUp.prompt: Did you have a choice today between spending and saving? Which way did you go?

options.label: I put a little aside
options.reflection: Choosing to put a little aside suggests you are thinking kindly about your future self. That patience tends to pay off over time. Tomorrow, you might also allow yourself one small, guilt-free pleasure, so saving never feels like going without.

options.label: I treated myself to something
options.reflection: Treating yourself can be a healthy way of saying you matter, and you may have needed it today. Tomorrow, you might notice whether the treat still feels good, and whether there's a small way to look after future you too.

options.label: Money went out and I barely noticed
options.reflection: Money slipping away without you noticing is very common, especially on busy or tiring days. It often reflects how much else you are carrying. Tomorrow, you might simply notice one purchase as it happens, with curiosity rather than blame.

options.label: No money choices came up today
options.reflection: No spending or saving choices came up today, so money could stay in the background. Tomorrow, if one does, you might notice whether your first pull is toward now or toward later.

questions.prompt: Your income doubles overnight. Would you be happier?

options.label: Yes, clearly

insight.reveal: More money would erase a few daily stresses, and you can name them. You're practical about trade-offs and keep a mental list of upgrades ready to go. Better still, you can usually tell which problems are really about money and which only look like it.
insight.research: On average, happiness kept rising with income even at high salaries, though for the unhappiest group it levelled off at moderate incomes.
insight.step: This week, name the one daily stress more money would fix, and find one free way to soften it.

options.label: A bit, then I'd get used to it

insight.reveal: You already know how fast a new comfort turns normal. Things rarely impress you for long, but surprises delight you every single time. You'd likely spend on new experiences over new stuff, because that's what keeps life feeling fresh.
insight.research: Swedish lottery players who won large prizes were more satisfied with their lives for over a decade, but day-to-day happiness changed much less.
insight.step: Tomorrow, surprise someone with a small unexpected gesture, and notice your own mood after.

options.label: No. My real problems aren't about money

insight.reveal: There's one problem in your life no amount of money could touch. It might be a relationship, a choice or a feeling, and you know exactly which one keeps you up at night. You think deeply about what matters, so quick fixes rarely fool you.
insight.research: Extra money did not lift people who were well-off but unhappy, even though on average happiness kept rising with income.
insight.step: This week, spend ten quiet minutes on the problem money can't fix, just thinking it through.

options.label: I'd mostly worry about losing it

insight.reveal: For you, having more mostly means having more to lose. You plan carefully, check your accounts often and insure what you own. The middle feels safest to you, where nothing can fall too far, and good news may need a day before you trust it.
insight.step: Next time you get something good, say 'this is good right now' before your mind jumps to losing it.

followUp.prompt: Did money shape your mood today, or did something else matter more?

options.label: A money worry weighed on me
options.reflection: A money worry weighing on your mood can make everything feel heavier, and that is very understandable. Worry often runs ahead of the facts. Tomorrow, you might write down the one money question that matters most, so it isn't spinning around unanswered.

options.label: Something money can't buy made my day
options.reflection: Something money can't buy made your day, which suggests your happiness may rest on deeper things. That is worth remembering on harder days. Tomorrow, you might look for one more moment like it, or make one for someone else.

options.label: A small money win lifted me
options.reflection: A small money win lifting your mood is natural, and it's fine to enjoy it. It may also help to notice how long that lift lasts. Tomorrow, you might compare it with something free that made you smile.

options.label: Money didn't really come into it today
options.reflection: Money didn't touch your mood today, so other things got to shape it instead. Tomorrow, you might notice which moments, people or places tend to lift you most, since those are often the real source.

questions.prompt: If money and fear disappeared tomorrow, what would you do first?

options.label: Travel far, for a long time

insight.reveal: You're hungry for distance as much as adventure. Unfamiliar streets light you up, and you'd order the dish you can't pronounce. Part of the pull is a place where nobody expects you to be the usual you, so you can try on someone new for a while.
insight.step: This weekend, spend one afternoon somewhere nearby where no one knows you.

options.label: Start the thing I keep talking about

insight.reveal: Your dream already has a name, and that puts you way ahead. Somewhere you keep notes, sketches or a half-built plan. The usual snag is the perfect start date, the one that slides a little further away every time you get close.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: This week, write one when-then plan: 'When it's Saturday morning, I'll spend 20 minutes on my idea.'

options.label: Honestly, I don't know what I'd want

insight.reveal: You've been so good at what was needed that your own wants went quiet. You're the dependable one at work and at home, and your wishes speak in a whisper. Not knowing isn't emptiness, though, just a sign those wants have been waiting for some room.
insight.step: Each evening this week, note one moment that made you feel more alive than usual.

options.label: Leave a job or relationship I've outgrown

insight.reveal: You know exactly what you've outgrown, and that clarity matters. What's holding you back is probably fear, not confusion. You've likely rehearsed the conversation in your head more than once, and naming it, even silently, is a real first step.
insight.research: People stuck on a big decision, like quitting a job, let a coin toss decide; those told to make the change were happier six months later than those told to stay.
insight.step: This month, write down one small thing you could change about that situation, without leaving it.

followUp.prompt: Did you take even a small step today toward something you'd do if fear weren't in the way?

options.label: Yes, I took a small real step
options.reflection: Taking even a small real step toward something you would do without fear is braver than it looks. Steps like that tend to add up. Tomorrow, you might pick the next tiny step and give it just a few minutes.

options.label: I looked up places or plans, just to dream
options.reflection: Looking up plans just to dream is often how bigger changes quietly begin. Your curiosity seems to be very much alive. Tomorrow, you might turn one dreamy idea into one small, concrete question you could answer.

options.label: I thought about it, then fear won
options.reflection: Letting fear win once doesn't mean it always will. Fear often shows up most loudly around the things that matter to you. Tomorrow, you might try a step so small that fear barely notices you took it.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Bigger dreams stayed quiet today, and some days are simply for getting through. That is okay. Tomorrow, you might notice whether any small wish comes up when you have a quiet moment to yourself.

questions.prompt: Which kind of regret visits you most often?

options.label: Something I said

insight.reveal: You care a lot about how your words land. You replay conversations in the shower and you're quick to say sorry. Funny how the person you forgive last is you, even for things the other person forgot by lunchtime.
insight.research: People overestimate how much others notice them: in one test, only about half as many people noticed an embarrassing T-shirt as the wearer guessed.
insight.step: Next time a sentence replays in your head, ask the person directly if it bothered them.

options.label: A chance I didn't take

insight.reveal: The roads you didn't take still feel open in your mind. Missed chances bother you more than mistakes do. That's good news, honestly: it can make you braver than you think when the next chance shows up.
insight.step: This week, say yes to one small invitation you'd normally talk yourself out of.

options.label: Someone I lost touch with

insight.reveal: Old friendships stay alive in your heart long after contact fades. There's probably a birthday you still remember for someone you haven't seen in years. You assume they've moved on, when they may be waiting for the very same first message you keep not sending.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how much someone will appreciate a quick message, call or small gift out of the blue, especially when it comes as a surprise.
insight.step: Today, send that person one short message. You don't need to explain the gap.

options.label: Years spent being who others wanted

insight.reveal: You can see the gap between who you were and who you showed. You're deeply tuned in to others, which is how the gap opened in the first place. Chances are you've already started closing it, choosing honesty in small moments that once would have slipped by.
insight.research: Asked about their biggest regret, 76% of people named failing to become the person they hoped to be, and these regrets lasted longer.
insight.step: Tomorrow, make one small choice purely because you want it, not because it pleases anyone.

followUp.prompt: Did an old regret visit you today? What was it about?

options.label: Something I said
options.reflection: Replaying something you said is very common, and it tends to show how much you care about others' feelings. Tomorrow, if it still matters, you might offer a short, kind word to the person, or simply let yourself put it down.

options.label: A chance I let pass
options.reflection: A chance you let pass can tug at you, and that tug often points to what you still want. It may not be too late for some version of it. Tomorrow, you might ask what a smaller chance like that could look like now.

options.label: Someone I've lost touch with
options.reflection: Missing someone you've lost touch with suggests your connections run deep, even across time. That longing often has a simple answer. Tomorrow, you might send them a short message, with no pressure about what comes back.

options.label: No regrets came knocking today
options.reflection: No regrets came knocking today, and that kind of lightness is worth enjoying. Tomorrow, you might notice something from today that you're glad you did, and let that sit with you for a moment.

questions.prompt: Two offers: a safe job, or a risky one doing what you love. You…

options.label: Take the safe job

insight.reveal: Stability is the ground everything else in your life stands on. You'd keep your passion as a side project, where no boss can touch it. That's a smart way to protect what you love, as long as it still gets real hours and not just leftovers.
insight.step: This week, give one hour to the thing you love, with no plan to turn it into money.

options.label: Ask for time and make long lists

insight.reveal: Your gut often decides before your list is even half done. At work your choices are thorough and careful, and people rely on that. But sometimes the pros-and-cons list is really a way to talk yourself out of something you already want.
insight.research: People stuck on a big decision who let a coin toss decide, and were told to make the change, were happier six months later than those told to stay put.
insight.step: Next time you're stuck on a big choice, flip a coin. Notice which side you hope for while it's in the air.

options.label: Take the risk, sort it out later

insight.reveal: You trust yourself to land on your feet, almost wherever you fall. You'll change cities, jobs or haircuts with little warning, and you adapt fast when plans fall apart. Just check now and then whether you're leaping to reach a dream or to escape boredom.
insight.step: Before your next leap, write one line on what you're running to, not just from.

options.label: Take the safe one and wonder forever

insight.reveal: You know your heart well, and you know your fear even better. Fear often wins the vote, yet you cheer louder than anyone when a friend takes the bold road. You'd happily talk someone else into the very risk you won't take, which tells you the courage is in there.
insight.research: Across 51 economies in 2024, nearly half of adults who saw a good business opportunity said fear of failure would stop them starting.
insight.step: This week, take one tiny risk for yourself, the kind you'd happily cheer a friend into.

followUp.prompt: Did you face a choice today between the safe option and the bolder one?

options.label: I chose safe and felt fine
options.reflection: Choosing the safe path and feeling fine about it suggests the choice truly fit you. Steadiness can be its own kind of wisdom. Tomorrow, you might still look for one small, low-risk way to try something new.

options.label: I took the bolder path
options.reflection: Taking the bolder path today shows you're willing to back yourself, even without all the answers. That courage often grows with use. Tomorrow, you might notice how it feels now, once the first rush has passed.

options.label: I chose safe and keep wondering
options.reflection: Choosing safe and then wondering is a very common pattern, and it often means part of you wants more room to grow. Tomorrow, you might ask what a small, safe-enough version of the bolder choice could be.

options.label: No big choices today
options.reflection: No big choices came your way today, and calm days have their own value. Tomorrow, you might notice the small choices instead, and which way you tend to lean when nothing much is at stake.

questions.prompt: Who knows about your biggest dream?

options.label: Everyone. I talk about it a lot

insight.reveal: Telling everyone is how you make a promise you can't back out of. You gather cheerleaders easily, and your excitement gets a whole group going. One sneaky trap: talking about the dream can feel so good that it quietly stands in for doing it.
insight.research: When other people took note of someone's plan to become a certain kind of person, they tended to work less at it, as if being noticed already felt like getting there.
insight.step: This week, take one step toward your dream before telling anyone about it.

options.label: One or two close people

insight.reveal: You guard your dream like something that could break. You choose your audience with care, the few who'll believe in it without asking for proof. In return you're fiercely loyal to other people's dreams, sometimes more openly than to your own.
insight.step: This week, give one of those people an update on your dream, even if there's little to report.

options.label: No one. Saying it would make it real

insight.reveal: It's the look on someone's face you fear, more than failing. You work quietly and show things only when they're finished, which can be really impressive. The trouble is, a dream nobody knows about is also a dream nobody can help with.
insight.step: This week, tell one kind person a small part of your dream. One sentence is plenty.

options.label: I've stopped admitting it even to myself

insight.reveal: Your dream went quiet to protect you from wanting it. It still sneaks up on you, in a song, a book or someone's success that stings more than it should. Oddly enough, that sting is good news: it means the wish is still alive.
insight.step: Next time someone else's success stings, pause and ask what it reminds you of.

followUp.prompt: Did your biggest dream come up in conversation today, even in passing?

options.label: I talked about it openly
options.reflection: Talking openly about your dream suggests you're comfortable letting others see what you want. That openness can bring support you didn't expect. Tomorrow, you might ask one person what they think your next step could be.

options.label: I shared it with one person I trust
options.reflection: Sharing your dream with one trusted person can make it feel more real and less lonely. You seem to choose carefully who you let in. Tomorrow, you might ask them to check in with you about it in a week or two.

options.label: I almost said it, then held back
options.reflection: Almost saying it and then holding back often means the dream matters a lot to you. Keeping it close can feel safer. Tomorrow, you might try writing it down just for yourself, as a gentle first way of saying it out loud.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Your biggest dream didn't come up today, and not every day needs to be about it. Tomorrow, you might give it a quiet minute of your own attention, even if you don't say a word to anyone else.

questions.prompt: Someone your age achieves exactly your dream. You feel…

options.label: Inspired. It's possible!

insight.reveal: Someone else's win is proof to you that there's room for yours. You're a great friend to ambitious people, who often feel judged elsewhere. You'll likely look up how they did it and turn their path into a rough map for your own next move.
insight.step: This week, look up how that person started, and find one step they took that you could take too.

options.label: Fired up to catch up

insight.reveal: A rival fires you up more than any goal on paper. You do your best work when someone is just ahead, and you'll glance at who's winning even at the gym. Out in front on your own, though, your energy can start to drift.
insight.research: A friendly kind of envy pushed people to work harder and do better, but only when they believed they could improve.
insight.step: This week, choose a friendly 'rival' and share one small goal with them.

options.label: Quietly crushed for a day or two

insight.reveal: There's a clock in your head for where you should be by now. You hold high standards and feel things deeply, so the hurt is less about them and more about that inner clock. The good news is that you set the clock, so you can reset it too.
insight.step: Tonight, write down where you thought you'd be by now. Then cross out the date and keep the goal.
