options.reflection: You described yourself today and felt good about it, and that ease is worth noticing. One idea for tomorrow: ask someone else about their work with real curiosity, and give them the same good feeling.

options.label: Yes, and I played it down
options.reflection: You played yourself down today, which many kind people do by reflex. Tomorrow, see if you can practise one sentence about your life that's simply true, without the shrinking words, and keep it ready.

options.label: I steered the talk away from me
options.reflection: You steered away from talking about yourself today. Sometimes that's privacy, sometimes it's shyness. Tomorrow, you might notice which it was, and share one small true thing about your life with someone safe.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No one asked you to explain yourself today, and there's freedom in that. Maybe tomorrow you could notice the moments when you feel most like yourself; they say more about you than any job title.

questions.prompt: You want to wear something bold today, but you're not sure. You…

options.label: Wear it; why not

insight.reveal: You let yourself enjoy how you show up. Friends borrow clothes and courage from you, and on the days you dress boldly you likely stand a little taller and speak up a little more.
insight.step: Today, compliment someone else who's taken a small risk with how they look.

options.label: Wear it, with something safe to balance it

insight.reveal: You like a little sparkle with a safety net. New things come into your life in careful steps, a colour here, a new style there, and over time those steps add up to a look that is entirely yours.
insight.step: This week, take your bold piece one step further than feels comfortable.

options.label: Ask someone if it looks all right

insight.reveal: You value a second pair of eyes, especially on yourself. You often trust other people's taste more than your own, and the people you ask usually say yes, because they've seen it suits you all along.
insight.step: Next time, decide how you feel in it before you ask anyone else.

options.label: Put it back; I'd rather not be noticed

insight.reveal: Being looked at feels like more than you want to carry today. There are probably a few things in your wardrobe you love but rarely wear, and that's okay; they tend to come out on the days you feel most at home in yourself.
insight.research: Students made to wear an embarrassing T-shirt guessed that about 46% of the room noticed; only about 23% actually did. We tend to feel far more watched than we are.
insight.step: This week, wear one small thing you love but rarely wear, even just at home.

followUp.prompt: Did you feel like yourself in what you wore today?

options.label: Yes, I felt like me
options.reflection: You felt like yourself in what you wore today, and that tends to show in how you walk and talk. Tomorrow, notice what made it work, so you can reach for that feeling again.

options.label: I didn't really think about it
options.reflection: Clothes weren't on your mind today, and that's its own kind of ease. One idea for tomorrow: put on one small thing you enjoy wearing, just to see whether it lifts the day a little.

options.label: I felt a bit self-conscious
options.reflection: Feeling watched in what you wore can follow you around all day. Tomorrow, see if you can wear something that feels like a comfortable old friend, and let that be enough.

options.label: I went bold, and it felt good
options.reflection: You took a small risk with how you showed up today, and it felt good. Tomorrow, you might remember that feeling the next time you hesitate in front of the mirror.

questions.prompt: A wedding or big event asks friends and family to chip in. You…

options.label: Give what I can and wish them well

insight.reveal: Calm, steady giving is your style at celebration time. Requests don't throw your money into chaos, and the couple or family will likely remember your warm message as much as whatever you sent.
insight.research: People given a small sum felt happier by evening if told to spend it on someone else rather than themselves, and the amount did not matter.
insight.step: Next time you contribute, add a short personal note; it often means more than the amount.

options.label: Give, and join the planning too

insight.reveal: You don't just fund the big day, you help build it. You end up on the committee or in the group chat sorting chairs, food and transport, and you enjoy the event most when you can see it all running smoothly.
insight.step: At the next event you help plan, take ten minutes to sit, eat and enjoy it as a guest.

options.label: Give more than I can really afford

insight.reveal: Your generosity runs ahead of your wallet. You say yes to every contribution because the people matter, then quietly tighten your own spending for weeks, and they likely have no idea what it cost you.
insight.step: This month, set a giving amount for events before the requests arrive, and keep to it kindly.

options.label: Feel stretched by how often I'm asked

insight.reveal: You love your people, and the requests still add up. Both are true at once. Everyone knows you'll give, which is a compliment, and also why it's fair to sometimes say "this time I can only send my love".
insight.research: In one area of South Africa, families spent about a year's income on average on an adult's funeral, and about a quarter borrowed to pay, driven by pressure to match their standing.
insight.step: This week, decide which one or two events matter most to you this season, and give fully there.

followUp.prompt: Did a contribution, collection or gift for an event come up today?

options.label: I gave, and felt good about it
options.reflection: You gave toward someone's big day and it felt good. That warmth is part of what makes celebrations work. Maybe tomorrow you could send the family a quick message too, so they hear from you, not just your gift.

options.label: I gave, but it stretched me
options.reflection: You gave today even though it stretched you, which says a lot about how much you value your people. Tomorrow, it might help to jot down what you've given this month, so the next decision is easier.

options.label: I said not this time
options.reflection: You said not this time today, and that can feel uncomfortable. Saying it kindly keeps relationships healthy. One idea for tomorrow: send your warm wishes anyway, since your care was never only about money.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No collections or contributions today, so your pocket gets a rest. Tomorrow, think about which coming event matters most to you, so you're ready when the request arrives.

questions.prompt: Your birthday is a week away. Do you let people know?

options.label: No, it's fine if it passes quietly

insight.reveal: A quiet birthday still feels like yours. You tend to mark it in small private ways, a favourite meal or a quiet walk, and you might be surprised how many people would gladly celebrate you if they knew.
insight.research: People asking others for help underestimated how many would say yes by about 48%.
insight.step: This year, tell one person about your birthday and let them do something small for you.

options.label: I drop a hint or two

insight.reveal: You'd like to be remembered without having to ask outright. It slips into conversation, "busy week, it's my birthday Friday", and you're likely the one who never forgets anyone else's either.
insight.research: People tend to underestimate how often others say yes when asked directly: they guessed they'd need to ask about 50% more people than they really did.
insight.step: This week, say it plainly to one friend: "It's my birthday on Friday, let's do something."

options.label: I plan my own celebration and invite people

insight.reveal: You don't wait for joy to be handed to you. The cake, the place and the guest list are often in your hands, and people love being invited, because you make it so easy for them to show up.
insight.step: This year, let one friend take charge of one part of your birthday, and leave it to them.

options.label: No, and I quietly watch who remembers

insight.reveal: Your birthday tells you something about where you stand. Every message, and every missing one, gets noticed, which shows how much your people matter to you, even if a busy friend's silence was never meant to hurt.
insight.step: This year, tell two people the date yourself; being remembered still counts when you helped.

followUp.prompt: Was there a birthday today, yours or someone else's? How did it go?

options.label: Yes, and we celebrated well
options.reflection: There was a birthday today and it was celebrated well, and moments like that build friendships. Tomorrow, you might send a photo or a kind line to someone who was there, to keep the good feeling going.

options.label: I remembered someone else's
options.reflection: You remembered someone's birthday today, and that small act often means more than a gift. Maybe tomorrow you could add a few more dates to your calendar, so your care keeps reaching people on time.

options.label: Someone forgot, and it stung
options.reflection: A forgotten birthday stung today, and that's a fair feeling. It usually says more about busy lives than about love. Tomorrow, it might help to reach out first, gently, and let them make it up to you.

options.label: No birthdays today
options.reflection: No birthdays to mark today. One idea for tomorrow: check whose birthday is coming up this month, so you can plan one small surprise that tells them you remembered.

questions.prompt: Someone you knew a little has died, and the burial is far away. You…

options.label: Send my condolences to the family

insight.reveal: You reach out in words when you can't be there in person. A short, sincere message from you means more to a grieving family than you'd guess, and some families reread those messages long after the funeral is over.
insight.step: This week, add one memory of the person to your message, even a small one.

options.label: Send a contribution with someone going

insight.reveal: You show care in ways that lighten the load. Funerals bring real costs and long days, and you understand that practical help is a kind of comfort, so you send what you can and make sure it reaches the right hands.
insight.research: In one area of South Africa, families spent on average about a year's income on an adult's funeral, and about a quarter of households borrowed to pay.
insight.step: Next week, call the family once the crowds have gone; that's often when they need it most.

options.label: Make the trip; being there matters

insight.reveal: For you, showing up is the message. You'll travel through the night, help with chairs or food and stay for the burial, and families often remember who came long after they forget who sent what.
insight.research: Grieving people in the Netherlands mostly found funerals and rituals helpful.
insight.step: Next time you travel for a funeral, plan one quiet hour for yourself on the way home.

options.label: Feel it stir up my own losses

insight.reveal: Each goodbye reminds you of the ones you've already said. Grief often arrives in company like this, with old memories surfacing in the days around a funeral, and that's love still looking for somewhere to go.
insight.research: People who did a small ritual after a loss felt less grief, mainly because it gave them a sense of control, even if they did not believe in rituals.
insight.step: This week, do one small thing in memory of someone you've lost: a call, a visit, a favourite song.

followUp.prompt: Did a loss, a funeral or someone's grief touch your day today?

options.label: I sent a message or called
options.reflection: You reached out to someone grieving today, and your words will likely stay with them. Tomorrow, see if you can set a reminder to check in again in a few weeks, when most people have stopped asking.

options.label: I helped out or showed up
options.reflection: You showed up for a grieving family today, and that kind of presence is never forgotten. Tomorrow, you might make room for your own tiredness too, because being there takes more out of you than it seems.

options.label: I found myself missing someone
options.reflection: You were missing someone today, and that ache shows how much they meant. Maybe tomorrow you could say their name out loud to someone who knew them, or simply sit with a happy memory for a while.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Loss didn't touch your day today, and quiet days like this are a gift worth noticing. Tomorrow, you could call someone you love just to talk, for no reason at all.

questions.prompt: You give a gift you chose with care, and they barely look at it. You…

options.label: Shrug; it's theirs now

insight.reveal: Once a gift leaves your hands, you let it go. You rarely chase a reaction, which makes you a relaxed giver, and people enjoy receiving from you because no pressure comes attached.
insight.step: Next time you give a gift, ask nothing about it, and see whether they bring it up themselves.

options.label: Ask later if they liked it

insight.reveal: You want to know your care landed. Gifts sit in your thoughts for days before you give them, so a flat reaction leaves a question hanging, and a simple "I love it" later on can make your whole week.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you notes underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would feel.
insight.step: This week, tell someone how much a gift they gave you meant, even an old one.

options.label: Feel a small sting all evening

insight.reveal: Your gifts carry a piece of you, so a shrug can hurt. You remember what everyone likes, their colours, their songs, their favourite foods, and it helps to know that people tend to value a gift for how they use it later, not the moment they open it.
insight.research: Gift givers tend to aim for the 'wow' moment of unwrapping, while people receiving gifts care more about how useful or enjoyable the gift will be over time.
insight.step: Next time, give the gift with a short note saying why you chose it, so the care is clear.

options.label: Wonder if I really know them at all

insight.reveal: A flat reaction can feel like a missed connection. Giving is your way of saying "I see you", so a quiet response shakes that feeling, though it usually says more about their day than about how well you know them.
insight.research: People liked gifts they had asked for more than surprise gifts, though givers expected surprise gifts to be valued more.
insight.step: This week, ask that person what they've been enjoying lately, and simply listen.

followUp.prompt: Did you give or receive a gift today? How was the moment?

options.label: It landed well
options.reflection: Your gift moment went well today, and that warm exchange is worth savouring. One idea for tomorrow: remember what made it work, the timing, the thought or the person, and keep it in mind for the next one.

options.label: It fell a bit flat
options.reflection: A gift moment fell a little flat for you today, and that can sting. Tomorrow, keep in mind that people show thanks in different ways, and some only find the words a day or two later.

options.label: I got something unexpected
options.reflection: Someone surprised you with a gift today. Tomorrow, you might tell them exactly what you liked about it; that often means more to the giver than the thank-you itself.

options.label: No gifts today
options.reflection: No gifts given or received today. Maybe tomorrow you could notice the small things people give you without wrapping, a lift, a favour, a listening ear, and thank one of them for it.

questions.prompt: It's the morning after a big celebration. How do you feel?

options.label: Tired, but happy

insight.reveal: You spend yourself fully on the good days. You danced, talked and stayed late, and the next morning's tiredness feels like proof it was worth it. People quietly count on you to bring the energy.
insight.step: Today, send one message to someone you enjoyed seeing last night.

options.label: Busy sorting photos, leftovers and thank-yous

insight.reveal: A celebration isn't over for you until it's tidied up. You're the one returning borrowed chairs and sharing the photos in the group, and without people like you, nobody would ever get their dishes back.
insight.step: Today, leave one task for someone else, and spend that time resting.

options.label: A bit flat now that it's over

insight.reveal: The quiet after a big day hits you harder than most. You feel the build-up deeply, and when the music stops the house can seem very still; that dip usually means the day truly mattered to you.
insight.research: Holidaymakers were happier than others before their trip, mostly from looking forward to it, but once home most were no happier than people who stayed.
insight.step: This week, plan one small thing to look forward to: a coffee, a call, a walk with a friend.

options.label: Relieved; it was a lot to hold together

insight.reveal: You were holding more of that day than anyone saw. Big days often rest on someone's quiet planning, worrying and smoothing over, and that was probably you, checking on everyone's needs while barely eating yourself.
insight.research: Interviews with 35 couples found that the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often goes unseen.
insight.step: Today, do one thing that is only for you, before anything else on your list.

followUp.prompt: Was there a celebration in your life today, or one just behind you? How are you feeling?

options.label: Still glowing from it
options.reflection: You're still carrying the glow of a good celebration, so let it last. Tomorrow, it might help to write down one moment you want to remember, before the details fade into the busy weeks ahead.

options.label: Still clearing up after it
options.reflection: You're still tidying after a big day, which often means you gave a lot to make it happen. One idea for tomorrow: ask for a hand with the last bits, and let someone else share the work.

options.label: Feeling a bit of a come-down
options.reflection: You're feeling a dip after a big day, which is very normal; the contrast is just loud. Tomorrow, see if you can get outside for a while, or call someone who was there, to ease back into ordinary life.

options.label: No celebrations lately
options.reflection: No big celebrations lately, and ordinary days have their own quiet rhythm. Tomorrow, you might mark one small thing anyway, a finished task or a good meal, because little celebrations count too.

questions.prompt: A new year begins. What do you actually do with it?

options.label: Celebrate and not think too hard

insight.reveal: You meet new beginnings with a party, not a plan. The countdown is more your thing than resolutions, and your goals tend to form along the way, sparked by a person or a moment rather than a date.
insight.research: Among 1,066 people in Sweden, 55% felt they had kept their New Year's resolution a year later, and 'start doing' goals worked better than 'stop doing' goals.
insight.step: This week, pick one thing you'd like more of this year and tell a friend.

options.label: Make a few resolutions

insight.reveal: You like a fresh page with a few promises on it. You start strong in the first weeks, and your resolutions stick best when they're specific, small and tied to something you already do every day.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Today, turn one resolution into "When X happens, I will do Y", and write it where you'll see it.

options.label: Look back over the whole year first

insight.reveal: You read the old page before turning to a new one. You go over the year's highs and lows before planning anything new, and that habit makes your plans wiser, because they're built on what really happened.
insight.step: Tonight, name three things the past year taught you, and keep the list somewhere safe.

options.label: Feel the clock ticking on what I meant to do

insight.reveal: New years remind you of the plans still waiting. You carry big hopes from year to year, and that ticking feeling is a sign of how deeply you care about your life, not proof that you've failed at it.
insight.research: New beginnings tend to spark fresh effort: US searches for 'diet' jumped 82% at New Year.
insight.step: This week, choose one waiting plan and take the very first, smallest step.

followUp.prompt: Did this year, and where it's heading, cross your mind today?

options.label: Yes, and I feel on track
options.reflection: You looked at your year today and felt on track, which is worth enjoying. Maybe tomorrow you could write down what's working, so you can lean on it when the months get busy.

options.label: Yes, and I feel behind
options.reflection: The year felt like it was slipping away today, and that can weigh on you. Tomorrow, it might help to choose one small thing to finish by the weekend, because one done thing quietly changes how the whole year feels.

options.label: I made a small plan
options.reflection: You made a plan today, and plans have a way of pulling you forward. One idea for tomorrow: decide exactly when you'll take the first step, and set a reminder so it doesn't slip.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: The year ahead didn't cross your mind today, and living one day at a time has its own wisdom. Tomorrow, name one thing you're glad happened this year, however small.

questions.prompt: A family introduction or engagement party is coming up. What's on your mind?

options.label: The food, the outfits, the fun

insight.reveal: You're here for the joy, and you bring it with you. Your outfit is planned early, you know every dance, and the hosts are glad of a guest who simply enjoys the day.
insight.step: At the next celebration, introduce yourself to one elder from the other family.

options.label: Getting every custom and detail right

insight.reveal: You honour the traditions by getting them right. You know the order of the speeches, who sits where and which gifts are expected, and families come to rely on you as the keeper of how things are done.
insight.research: A review of 32 studies found regular family routines and rituals, like shared meals and holiday traditions, go with happier marriages and better-adjusted children.
insight.step: This week, teach one younger relative a tradition you know well, and why it matters.

options.label: What it'll cost, and who's paying

insight.reveal: You see the bills behind the beautiful day. Celebrations like this can carry heavy expectations, and while others enjoy the speeches you're quietly working out the numbers, which can save families from regrets later.
insight.research: In a survey of over 3,000 married or once-married Americans, couples who spent more on the engagement ring and wedding tended to have shorter marriages.
insight.step: This week, have one honest talk with family about what's affordable, before plans grow.

options.label: My own future family, or the one I hoped for

insight.reveal: Other people's big days make you think about your own. During the speeches you find yourself imagining who would stand up for you, and that wish is worth listening to: it tells you what kind of love and family you want.
insight.step: Tonight, write one sentence about the family life you'd like, and keep it somewhere private.

followUp.prompt: Did talk of engagements, introductions or family events come up today?

options.label: Yes, and I'm looking forward to it
options.reflection: You're looking forward to a family celebration, and that anticipation is part of the joy. Tomorrow, you might do one small thing to get ready, an outfit, a gift or a call, so the excitement has somewhere to go.

options.label: Yes, and the planning is a lot
options.reflection: Family event planning is weighing on you today, and that's a lot to carry. Maybe tomorrow you could hand one task to someone else, even a small one, and notice how it feels to share the load.

options.label: It made me think about my own life
options.reflection: A family event got you thinking about your own life today, and those thoughts are worth keeping. Tomorrow, it might help to share one hope about your future with someone you trust, and let it be heard.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No family events on the agenda today, and calm stretches like this are welcome. One idea for tomorrow: call a relative you haven't spoken to in a while, before the next big gathering brings you together.

questions.prompt: Christmas, Eid or your biggest holiday is a week away. How do you feel?

options.label: Excited, I love the build-up

insight.reveal: The build-up is half the holiday for you. The music, the cooking plans and the countdown start with you before anyone else, and your excitement tends to pull even the tired people in your house along.
insight.research: Waiting for an experience, like a trip, a concert or a party, tends to feel more pleasant and exciting than waiting for a new thing to arrive.
insight.step: This week, invite one person who might be alone over the holiday to join part of it.

options.label: Busy with lists and plans

insight.reveal: You make the holiday happen, list by list. You know who's bringing what, who's travelling when and what's still missing, and the calm day everyone enjoys is often built on lists you wrote at midnight.
insight.step: Today, hand one list to someone at home and let them own it.

options.label: Worried about the cost and the pressure

insight.reveal: You feel the weight behind the celebrations. Holidays bring expectations about food, gifts and travel, and you're often the one quietly juggling them, while the people you love mostly want your company, not your spending.
insight.research: In a 2023 US poll, 89% said something about the holiday season stressed them, most often money, yet 84% said it brings togetherness.
insight.step: This week, choose one shared moment, a meal or a walk, and put your effort there instead of gifts.

options.label: Missing someone who won't be there

insight.reveal: Your holiday has an empty chair in it. The days that bring everyone together make an absence feel louder, and you may find yourself telling their story or playing their song, keeping them close in small ways.
insight.research: People who did a small ritual after a loss tended to feel less grief, mainly because it gave them a sense of control.
insight.step: This holiday, do one small thing in their honour, and tell someone why you're doing it.

followUp.prompt: Did the coming holidays or a big festival cross your mind today?

options.label: Yes, and I'm excited
options.reflection: The holidays are on your mind and you're excited, so hold on to that. Tomorrow, see if you can do one small thing that gets you in the mood, a song, a recipe or a call to someone you'll see.

options.label: Yes, I was planning or shopping
options.reflection: You spent some of today getting ready for the holidays, and that work is a gift too. Tomorrow, you might do one part of it with someone else, so the preparing becomes part of the celebration.

options.label: Yes, and it felt heavy
options.reflection: The holidays felt heavy today, whether from cost, pressure or someone missing, and that's real. Maybe tomorrow you could tell one person what's hard about it; it often lightens just by being said.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Holidays and festivals weren't on your mind today, and there's no rush. Tomorrow, it might help to notice what you'd love this year's celebration to feel like, before plans and lists take over.

questions.prompt: Someone close graduates or reaches a big milestone. What do you do?

options.label: Send a big message of congratulations

insight.reveal: You're quick to cheer and generous with your words. Your message is often first in the group, with the most exclamation marks, and people feel celebrated by you even from far away.
insight.research: When people shared good news, an eager, interested reply added to their joy, while a flat or dismissive reply took it away.
insight.step: This week, follow your congratulations with a call, and ask what the milestone means to them.

options.label: Show up with a gift or flowers

insight.reveal: You celebrate people in person, with something in your hands. Look through their photos from the day and you're right there beside them, and that kind of presence is what people remember most.
insight.step: Next time, add a handwritten line to your gift about why you're proud of them.

options.label: Make a speech or a fuss in front of everyone

insight.reveal: You want the whole room to know how proud you are. You lead the cheers, the toast or the song, and the people you celebrate this way often remember your words for years.
insight.research: People about to give a compliment underestimated how good it would make the other person feel.
insight.step: This month, also tell someone in private exactly what you admire about them.

options.label: Feel proud, and think about my own path

insight.reveal: Their big day makes you look at your own road. Happiness for them and unease about yourself can arrive in the same moment, and you often come home from these events with a fresh plan, or at least a question.
insight.step: This week, write down one milestone you'd love to reach, and one tiny step toward it.

followUp.prompt: Did you celebrate someone else's milestone today, a graduation, a new job, a new home?

options.label: Yes, I cheered them on
options.reflection: You celebrated someone else's milestone today, and your cheer likely meant a lot. One idea for tomorrow: ask them what comes next, since people often feel a little lost after a big achievement.

options.label: Yes, with mixed feelings
options.reflection: Someone's good news brought up mixed feelings for you today, which is honest and human. Tomorrow, see if you can write down what you'd like for yourself, so the feeling turns into direction instead of weight.

options.label: I missed the chance to say something
options.reflection: You missed a moment to celebrate someone today, and that's easily mended. Tomorrow, you might send a late message; most people love a second wave of congratulations after the first one fades.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No big milestones around you today. Maybe tomorrow you could notice a small achievement by someone near you, a test passed or a goal kept, and tell them you saw it.

questions.prompt: At a wedding, where are you most likely to be found?

options.label: Near the food, enjoying every bite

insight.reveal: Good food is how you take in a celebration. Weddings stay in your memory by their food as much as their vows, and you're likely the guest who thanks the cooks and gets sent home with extra.
insight.research: People writing thank-you notes tended to underestimate how happy the receiver would be and overestimate how awkward it would feel.
insight.step: At the next celebration, thank one of the people who cooked or served, by name.

options.label: On the dance floor

insight.reveal: When the music starts, you're in. At least one shy cousin gets pulled onto the floor by you at every wedding, and the photos usually catch you mid-laugh, which tells everyone the party was a good one.
insight.research: Across 60 experiments, moving in time with others, like singing or dancing together, made people feel closer and act more helpfully toward each other.
insight.step: Next time you're dancing, invite someone who's been sitting alone to join you.

options.label: Helping out behind the scenes

insight.reveal: Your joy at a wedding is in making it work. Carrying crates, counting chairs, calming the cook: couples often find out only later how much of their day ran on your quiet help.
insight.step: At the next event, take a full half hour off duty to sit and enjoy it.

options.label: Teary during the vows and speeches

insight.reveal: Love being promised out loud moves you every single time. The exact words of a good speech stay with you, and other people's weddings tend to remind you what you value most in your own relationships.
insight.research: Sharing an experience at the same moment as someone else tends to make it feel stronger: good chocolate tasted better when tasted together.
insight.step: This week, tell someone you love one thing you'd say about them if you ever gave a speech.

followUp.prompt: Did love, weddings or someone's big day come up in your world today?

options.label: Yes, I'm helping plan something
options.reflection: You're helping someone's big day come together, and that's a real gift of time. Tomorrow, it might help to pause long enough to enjoy the part you're helping with, not just the to-do list.

options.label: Yes, someone shared happy news
options.reflection: Happy news reached you today, and it's lovely to be included. One idea for tomorrow: send a warm reply or ask how you can help, since big days are built by many hands.

options.label: It made me a little wistful
options.reflection: Someone else's love story made you a little wistful today. That feeling usually points to something you hope for. Tomorrow, see if you can name that hope to yourself, gently, without rushing to fix it.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No weddings or big days in your world today. Tomorrow, you might ask a couple you know how they met; people love telling that story, and it may brighten both your days.

questions.prompt: A friend calls to say they'll be at your door in ten minutes. You…

options.label: Put the kettle on and open the door

insight.reveal: Your door is open, mess and all. You judge a visit by the conversation, not the floor, and guests tend to stay longer at your place than they meant to. Chances are you've fed more surprise visitors than you could count.
insight.research: Strangers who spent 45 minutes taking turns answering slowly deeper personal questions felt closer than pairs who made small talk.
insight.step: Next time someone drops by, ask them one question you've never asked them before.

options.label: Hide the mess in one room and shut the door

insight.reveal: You're a master of the ten-minute rescue. Somewhere in your life there's a room, cupboard or bag that quietly holds the overflow, and honestly, it works. The same knack shows up elsewhere: you can make almost anything presentable at short notice.
insight.step: This week, give that hiding-place room just ten minutes, so it's ready for the next surprise.

options.label: Clean in a rush, then apologise for the mess anyway

insight.reveal: You want people to feel welcome, maybe a little too much. Odds are you'll apologise for a mess your guest never even saw. It's the mark of a generous host: you hold yourself to a standard no visitor would ever ask of you.
insight.research: We feel far more watched than we are: students in an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about half the room noticed it, but only about a quarter did.
insight.step: Next time a guest arrives, skip the apology and open with 'I'm so glad you came.'

options.label: Quietly wish I could pretend I'm not home

insight.reveal: Home is where you recharge, not where you perform. An unplanned knock can feel like someone walking into your head, not just your house. With people you've invited, you're likely warm and generous, especially once you've had time to want them there.
insight.step: This week, tell one friend the best time to drop by, so visits come when you have room for them.

followUp.prompt: Did anyone turn up at your door today, invited or not?

options.label: Someone came by and it was lovely
options.reflection: Unplanned company can be the best part of an ordinary day. It sounds like your home did what homes do best: it made someone feel welcome. Before the week is out, think of who you haven't seen in a while and send them a quick hello.

options.label: Someone came, and I felt caught off guard
options.reflection: Being caught off guard doesn't mean you did it badly. Most guests remember the welcome, not the floor. If it happens again, try greeting them before you glance at the room, and see how much lighter it feels.

options.label: I was the one who dropped in on someone
options.reflection: You were someone's surprise today. Turning up in person says 'I thought of you' in a way a message can't. Tomorrow, think about whether someone might be waiting for an open invitation from you, too.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A quiet day at home has its own kind of comfort. Your space was all yours, and that counts for something. If you'd like more company soon, you could invite one person over this week, on your own terms.

questions.prompt: The clean laundry is dry. What happens to it next?

options.label: Folded and put away the same day

insight.reveal: You like your home finished, not almost finished. You're likely the one who refills the water jug and replaces the soap before anyone asks. Small loose ends nag at you, which is exactly why so few of them stay loose for long.
insight.research: Unfinished tasks are not remembered better than finished ones, but people do tend to go back and finish tasks that were interrupted.
insight.step: Tonight, leave one small thing undone on purpose and notice that the evening carries on just fine.

options.label: It waits on a chair for a few days

insight.reveal: For you, washing is the job and folding is optional. Big pushes are your strength; finishing touches can wait. That chair may well have cousins elsewhere in your life: a bag never quite unpacked, a few almost-sent replies.
insight.research: Putting things off is very common, and people tend to delay most when a task feels boring or unpleasant.
insight.step: Next time the laundry comes in, fold just five things straight away and let the rest wait.

options.label: I wear things straight from the pile

insight.reveal: To you, the clean pile is a perfectly good wardrobe. You save your energy for what feels like it matters, and that works more often than tidier people expect. Mornings may need some digging, but you rarely lose an evening to a shirt.
insight.step: This week, set out tomorrow's clothes before bed, just one outfit, and see how the morning feels.

options.label: The pile grows when my week is hard

insight.reveal: Your laundry keeps an honest diary of your week. When life is calm, your home tends to be calm too, and when things get heavy, the pile is the first to know. That's useful: it can tell you how you're doing before you've said it out loud.
insight.research: In a small study of working couples, wives who described their homes as cluttered or unfinished had lower mood through the day and less healthy stress-hormone patterns.
insight.step: Next time the pile grows, ask yourself what else has felt heavy this week, before you fold a thing.

followUp.prompt: How did the laundry look by tonight?

options.label: Washed, folded, put away
options.reflection: There's a quiet satisfaction in a job that's fully finished. You gave your future self an easier morning. In the morning, see if you can bring a little of that same finish to one other small task.

options.label: Clean, but still waiting to be folded
options.reflection: Clean is the hard part, and you did it. Folding can wait a day without anything bad happening. If it's still there tomorrow evening, give it five minutes with something good playing and call that enough.

options.label: Piling up, like a few other things
options.reflection: When the pile grows alongside everything else, it's usually a sign of a full week, not a failing. Go easy on yourself tonight. Tomorrow, pick just one small corner to sort, and let that be your win.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Not every day has room for chores, and that's fine; your home will wait for you. If laundry day is coming, you might pick the time now, so it doesn't sit on your mind in the meantime.

questions.prompt: Think of the people you live with. How are the chores shared?

options.label: I live alone, so it's all me

insight.reveal: Your home runs exactly as well as you decide it will. Living alone makes you quietly expert in your own rhythms: you know what can slide and what can't. If you ever share a space, it may feel strange at first, simply because you built this one so well.
insight.step: Tonight, pick the chore you always put off and give it exactly ten minutes, with music on.

options.label: Shared out fairly, more or less

insight.reveal: A home works, in your book, when everyone pulls a little. Somewhere along the way, someone had a plain talk about the bins or the dishes, and there's a good chance it was you. Fairness at home rarely happens by luck.
insight.research: Even in US marriages where both partners earn about the same, wives spend about 4.6 hours a week on housework and husbands about 2.
insight.step: This week, thank someone at home for one job they do that nobody ever mentions.

options.label: Honestly, others do more than me

insight.reveal: It takes honesty to admit you're the lucky one at home. You probably notice more than you do, and a small guilt follows you past the sink. Saying it out loud already puts you one step from fixing it: one job, claimed for good, changes the picture.
insight.research: When couples each rated their share of household jobs, the two shares usually added up to more than the whole: we notice our own effort more than other people's.
insight.step: Choose one chore today and make it yours for good, without waiting to be asked.

options.label: I do more, and it's quietly building up

insight.reveal: You keep the house going, and too few people see it. You spot jobs before anyone else does, which is exactly what makes your work invisible. Resentment at home rarely grows from one big thing; it's the small, unthanked jobs, and naming just one can lighten the load fast.
insight.research: In interviews with 35 couples, the mental work of running a home, like noticing what is needed and keeping track, often went unseen and caused friction.
insight.step: This week, hand over one specific job by name, like 'Could you take the rubbish out on Thursdays?'

followUp.prompt: Who kept the home running today, and how did that sit with you?

options.label: We all did our bit
options.reflection: A day where everyone pitches in is easy to overlook, but it's the backbone of a calm home. You're part of something that works. A simple 'thanks for doing that' over breakfast could help keep it working.

options.label: Mostly me, again
options.reflection: Carrying most of it, again, can wear you down even when you don't say a word. Your effort is real, even if nobody named it today. Tomorrow, try asking for one small, specific thing, and let someone else do it their way.

options.label: Someone else carried more today
options.reflection: Noticing that someone else carried more is a kind thing to do, and often it's all it takes for them to feel seen. Tomorrow, you could take one job off their hands before they get to it.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Some days the house just ticks along and nobody needs to think about it. That's a good sign in itself. If something is due soon, you might mention it tomorrow, before anyone has to wonder whose turn it is.

questions.prompt: Something at home breaks, and fixing it is your landlord's or someone else's job. You…

options.label: Report it the same day

insight.reveal: Small problems don't get to settle in around you. You're likely the one who reports the broken light, the late delivery and the dripping tap, and people quietly rely on you for it. Fixing things early saves you whole weeks of low-level irritation.
insight.step: Next time you report something, add a friendly line of thanks for whoever comes to fix it.

options.label: Fix it myself; asking takes longer

insight.reveal: Waiting on others costs you more than doing it yourself. Your toolbox, real or improvised, gets more use than most, and you rarely sit stuck for long. Just notice the day 'quicker' turns into 'I always end up doing it.'
insight.step: This week, let someone else handle one small fix, even if you could do it faster.

options.label: Live with it for longer than I should

insight.reveal: You can make your peace with almost anything. Chances are you've stepped around the same loose tile for weeks and told yourself it's fine, because it nearly is. That easygoing streak keeps you calm, and it can also leave you putting up with too much.
insight.research: Putting things off is very common: an estimated 15-20% of adults do it chronically, and people delay most when a task feels unpleasant.
insight.step: Today, write down one thing at home you've been living around, and send one message about it.

options.label: Delay asking so I don't seem like trouble

insight.reveal: You'd rather go without than be a bother. Requests get rehearsed in your head and softened until they barely ask for anything. Here's the thing: asking for what you're owed doesn't make you difficult, and most people respect a clear, polite request.
insight.research: People asking strangers for help guessed they would need to ask about 50% more people than they really did: others say yes more than we expect.
insight.step: Next time something needs fixing, send the request in one plain sentence, with no apology in it.

followUp.prompt: Was there anything at home today that needed fixing, and did you speak up?

options.label: Yes, and I asked for it to be fixed
options.reflection: Speaking up about something at home is a small act of self-respect. You looked after your space and yourself in one go. If there's no reply by tomorrow, a short, friendly nudge is completely fair.

options.label: I sorted it out myself
options.reflection: Sorting it yourself shows you trust your own hands, and that's a real strength. Just make sure it was a choice and not a habit you can't put down. Sometime this week, you might let someone help you with one small thing.

options.label: I noticed it, but said nothing
options.reflection: Saying nothing is sometimes about keeping the peace, and you care about that. Your comfort at home matters too, though. Tomorrow, you could write the message you'd send, then decide once it's in front of you.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Nothing broken, nothing to chase: that's a calm day at home, and you can enjoy it for what it is. If there's an old fix you've been ignoring, a quiet day like this is a good time to finally note it down.

questions.prompt: A door handle at home comes loose. When does it actually get fixed?

options.label: That day, with whatever tool is nearby

insight.reveal: Broken things don't stay broken long around you. A butter knife has doubled as your screwdriver more than once, hasn't it? Friends and family bring you whatever's wobbling, because you make problems look smaller than they are.
insight.step: This week, show someone at home how to do one small repair you know well.

options.label: I look up how, and enjoy learning it

insight.reveal: Every broken thing is a small lesson to you. You'll watch a ten-minute video and end up knowing more about hinges than you ever planned to. That curiosity shows up elsewhere as well: you'd rather understand something than just get it done.
insight.step: Next time something breaks, try fixing it for five minutes before you look anything up.

options.label: When someone else gets round to it

insight.reveal: You know your strengths, and fixing handles isn't one of them. That's fair. Your energy goes to the things only you can do, while home repairs wait in a gentle queue. Just watch that the queue doesn't quietly turn into a list.
insight.research: Delaying jobs that feel dull or unpleasant is very common; an estimated 15-20% of adults put things off chronically.
insight.step: Today, pick one small repair and either do it or ask someone, by name, to do it this week.

options.label: Never. I've learned the trick to open it

insight.reveal: You're brilliant at living around problems. Your home is probably full of small workarounds only you understand: the drawer you lift, the tap you turn just so. It's a real kind of resourcefulness, though the same habit can keep bigger things 'nearly fine' for years.
insight.step: This week, fix one thing you've learned to work around, and notice how it feels to stop.

followUp.prompt: Did you fix anything around the house today, big or small?

options.label: Yes, and it felt good
options.reflection: There's a particular pleasure in a thing that works again. You took something broken and made it whole, and that feeling is worth noticing. Tomorrow, see if there's one more tiny fix you could knock off in five minutes.

options.label: I asked someone else to do it
options.reflection: Asking someone else is a perfectly good way to solve a problem. You got it moving, which is what counts. Once it's done, a quick thank-you will make the next favour easier for both of you.

options.label: Something's still broken and I'm used to it
options.reflection: Getting used to broken things is very human. Your patience is real, but you deserve a home that works for you. Tomorrow, choose the one fix that annoys you most and give it a date, even if it's next week.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day with nothing to fix is a gentle one: your home held together without asking anything of you. You could use the calm to notice one small thing that's been wobbling, before it turns into a bigger job.

questions.prompt: There's a drawer or corner at home full of things you never use. Why is it still full?

options.label: I just haven't got round to it

insight.reveal: Clutter is simply low on your list, and fair enough. Bigger things compete for your time, and a drawer doesn't shout. When you do get to it, you're the type to clear the lot in one satisfying afternoon.
insight.step: This week, empty that one drawer onto a table and only put back what you've used this year.

options.label: Those things might be useful one day

insight.reveal: You're the person people come to for a spare cable. Planning ahead is part of how you feel safe, and sometimes it pays off spectacularly. The catch is that 'one day' things can quietly crowd out the things you use every day.
insight.research: People tend to value things more once they own them: in classic experiments, people given a mug wanted far more to sell it than others would pay for it.
insight.step: Today, pick three 'one day' things and give them to someone who needs them now.

options.label: Throwing things away feels wasteful

insight.reveal: Waste bothers you more than clutter does. There's a good chance you learned early to mend, reuse and pass things on, and it stuck. That instinct is generous to the planet; it just means your things need somewhere to go other than the bin.
insight.step: This week, find one person or place that would actually use something from that drawer, and take it there.

options.label: Some of it holds memories I'm not ready for

insight.reveal: You keep memories in objects, not just in your head. A ticket, a note or an old phone can hold a whole chapter of your life. Keeping them isn't a problem. When you're ready, you may find it feels good to keep just the one that matters most.
insight.research: Thinking back to fond memories tended to lift people's mood and help them feel closer to others, though nostalgia can also feel bittersweet.
insight.step: Next time you open that drawer, hold one object for a minute, let yourself remember, then decide.

followUp.prompt: Did you keep, clear or simply notice any clutter at home today?

options.label: I cleared a little
options.reflection: Clearing even a little can make a room feel like it breathes again. You made space today, and space has a way of calming a mind. Tomorrow, notice whether that spot stays clear, and enjoy it if it does.

options.label: I looked, but kept everything
options.reflection: Looking and keeping everything is still a step: you know what's there now. Some things simply aren't ready to leave, and that's okay. Tomorrow, you might pick the one thing that's easiest to let go of and start there.

options.label: I found something that brought back a memory
options.reflection: Stumbling on a memory can stop you in your tracks. It sounds like an object did its job and kept something precious safe for you. If you feel like it, share that memory with someone who was there.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Clutter can wait; it isn't going anywhere, and your day clearly had other things in it. If that corner starts to bother you, give it ten minutes at the weekend, with no pressure to finish.

questions.prompt: It's dinnertime at home. Who usually ends up cooking?

options.label: Me, and I enjoy it

insight.reveal: The kitchen is one of your happy places. You taste as you go, change recipes without asking, and feel quietly proud when the plates come back empty. Cooking, for you, is often how love gets said without words.
insight.step: This week, teach someone one dish you make well, from start to finish.

options.label: Whoever gets hungry first

insight.reveal: Appetite, not a schedule, runs your kitchen. Good days bring proper meals and busy ones bring creative ones, and nobody minds much. Easygoing kitchens like yours work well, as long as the same person isn't always the hungriest.
insight.step: Tonight, cook a little extra so tomorrow's first hungry person has something ready.

options.label: Someone else, and I'm thankful

insight.reveal: Being looked after is something you never take for granted. Odds are you're the one who washes up, fetches the bread or says 'that was lovely' every time. Small thanks like those are exactly what keep someone happy at the stove.
insight.research: People who wrote thank-you letters underestimated how happy and surprised the receivers would feel, and expected far more awkwardness than there was.
insight.step: This week, cook one simple meal for the person who usually cooks for you.

options.label: Me, every time, even when I'm worn out

insight.reveal: You feed everyone, even on the days you're running on empty. 'I can't tonight' rarely leaves your mouth, so nobody thinks to offer. You're allowed a night off, and asking for one will likely go better than you expect.
insight.research: People asking for help underestimated how many others would say yes, by about 48%, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: Pick one evening this week to say 'I'm not cooking tonight,' then let someone else sort it.

followUp.prompt: Who cooked today, and how did the meal turn out?

options.label: I cooked and enjoyed it
options.reflection: Cooking you enjoy is a gift to yourself as much as anyone else. You turned an ordinary job into something good today. Next time, you might try one small twist on a dish you know well, just for fun.

options.label: I cooked, though I was worn out
options.reflection: Cooking when you're worn out is love in its most practical form. You kept everyone going, and you deserve the same care back. Tomorrow, think of one meal someone else could take on, and ask them early.

options.label: Someone else cooked for me
options.reflection: Being cooked for is a small luxury that's easy to rush past, and you were looked after today. A word of thanks, or doing the washing up next time, could make that person's evening too.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Some days meals just happen without much thought, and that's fine; you ate, and that matters. If you'd like a better one tomorrow, you could decide now what it'll be, so it's one less choice later.

questions.prompt: Someone you live with leaves their dirty dishes out again. You…

options.label: Wash them; it's quicker than talking

insight.reveal: You'd rather have peace than prove a point. Mess gets cleared around you, often before anyone notices there was a problem. It keeps things smooth, though the house may be learning that dishes wash themselves.
insight.step: Next time, wash yours and leave theirs for one evening, and see what happens.

options.label: Give a light, friendly reminder

insight.reveal: You say things before they turn into things. A quick joke or a 'hey, the dishes' is your style, and it usually works better than silence. Homes with someone like you in them tend to have fewer big arguments.
insight.step: This week, suggest one simple house rule out loud, like 'we wash up before bed.'

options.label: Leave them there until they get the message

insight.reveal: Grown-ups, you feel, should notice their own mess. Fair enough, though a silent message often lands as a puzzle rather than a point. Your own sense of fairness is strong, which makes it harder to understand when others don't share it.
insight.research: People tend to expect honest talks to hurt their relationships more than they do; in tests, being honest felt better and more connecting than predicted.
insight.step: Next time, swap the silent message for a short, plain one: 'Could you wash these tonight?'

options.label: Say nothing, but it stays on my mind all day

insight.reveal: Small things at home take up more room in your head than you'd like. You replay the moment, plan what you'll say, and then say nothing at all. That isn't pettiness; you care about fairness and peace at once, and they can pull in different directions.
insight.research: Going over and over a problem in your head without acting on it tends to deepen low mood and make the problem harder to solve.
insight.step: Today, say the one sentence you've been rehearsing, kindly, and let the rest of the story go.

followUp.prompt: Did sharing a home with others test your patience today?

options.label: No, it was easy today
options.reflection: Easy days at home are easy to forget, so it's nice that you noticed. Living well alongside others takes more give and take than it looks. Tomorrow, you could say something warm to someone you live with, just because.

options.label: A bit, and I said something
options.reflection: Saying something takes nerve, especially at home where you can't walk away. You stood up for the space you share. Over the next few days, notice whether it changed anything, and say thanks if it did.

options.label: Yes, and I kept it to myself
options.reflection: Keeping it to yourself can feel like keeping the peace, but then you carry it alone. Your irritation makes sense. Tomorrow, try saying it in one kind sentence, and see how much lighter you feel afterwards.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Whether you live alone or the day just ran smoothly, home was calm, and you can enjoy that. If you share a space, tomorrow could be a good day to thank someone for something small they do.

questions.prompt: Rent or another big home payment is due this week. How does it feel?

options.label: Like any other week; it's sorted

insight.reveal: You've built a home that doesn't keep you up at night. Paying for it early is probably one of a dozen quiet systems you rely on. Others may never notice the planning, only that you always seem unhurried.
insight.research: Across 102 studies, self-control showed up more in steady, automatic routines than in one-off choices: self-controlled people tend to lean on good habits.
insight.step: This week, share one of your little systems with someone who'd find it useful.

options.label: A small sigh, then it's done

insight.reveal: You feel the weight, then you put it down. That's a healthy rhythm: you notice the cost without letting it run your week. Most grown-up jobs seem to go this way for you: a moment of grumbling and then straight on with it.
insight.step: On the day you pay it, do one small thing that makes your home feel more like yours.

options.label: I check my account more than once

insight.reveal: Keeping a roof over your head matters to you a great deal. Checking twice is how you reassure yourself, and it shows how seriously you take it. Often the money is already there; it's the not-knowing that wears on you.
insight.research: In a lab game, people felt most stressed when a bad outcome was uncertain, more than when it was very likely: not knowing can feel worse than knowing.
insight.step: This week, check once, write the number down, and let that note do the worrying for you.

options.label: It hangs over my whole week

insight.reveal: Your home feels safe, but never quite settled. When a payment is coming, it follows you into other conversations and dims the good bits of the week. That weight is real, and you carry it more quietly than anyone knows.
insight.research: In a 2022 US survey, 66% of adults named money as a major stress, and among them more than half said it caused tension in the family.
insight.step: Tonight, write down the date, the amount, and one thing you'd do if it went wrong. Worries often look smaller on paper.

followUp.prompt: How did the cost of keeping a roof over your head feel today?

options.label: It didn't weigh on me
options.reflection: A day without that weight is worth noticing. You may have built more security than you give yourself credit for. Before bed, enjoy one small thing at home simply because it's yours.

options.label: It crossed my mind a few times
options.reflection: Thoughts about rent or bills drifting in and out is completely normal, and you noticed them without letting them take over. Tomorrow, if one comes back, try giving it a time slot, like 'I'll think about it at six.'

options.label: It weighed on me all day
options.reflection: That's a heavy thing to carry around all day, and it makes sense that you're tired. You're doing your best to keep your home steady. Tomorrow, talk it through with one person you trust; worries tend to shrink once said aloud.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: Not every day needs to be about bills, and today wasn't. Your mind had room for other things. If a payment is coming soon, you might jot its date somewhere you'll see it, so it can't surprise you.

questions.prompt: When does a proper deep clean happen at your place?

options.label: On a set day, most weeks

insight.reveal: You clean by the calendar, and it suits you. Knowing what each day is for gives you a steadiness that spills into the rest of your life. On the rare week the clean gets skipped, you'll feel it by midweek.
insight.research: Self-control tends to show up in fixed routines more than in one-off choices; people who seem steady and disciplined often lean on good habits.
insight.step: This week, let one part of your cleaning day go and put something fun in its place.

options.label: When guests are coming

insight.reveal: Visitors are your best cleaning motivation. You want people to feel comfortable in your home, and a deadline makes the work feel worth it. Your home probably looks its best on exactly the evenings you most want to share it.
insight.step: Next time you clean, invite someone over that same evening, so you get to enjoy it together.

options.label: When I'm avoiding something else

insight.reveal: Your home is never cleaner than when you're avoiding something. Scrubbing the stove suddenly feels urgent the moment a hard message or task is waiting. It isn't laziness: you're picking a job you can finish over one that feels bigger than it is.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan ("When X happens, I will do Y") had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Next time, try a when-then: 'When I finish this shelf, I'll do five minutes of the real task.'

options.label: When I'm upset; scrubbing helps me think

insight.reveal: When your mind is a mess, you put the house in order. Scrubbing, sorting and sweeping give your hands a job while your head catches up. It can be a wise habit: by the time the floor is clean, you often know what you want to say.
insight.research: In a small experiment, people made nervous about giving a speech spent longer cleaning an object, with more repeated hand movements, than calmer people did.
insight.step: Next time you clean to calm down, finish by writing one line about what was really on your mind.

followUp.prompt: Did any proper cleaning happen today, and what got you started?

options.label: Yes, it was the usual day for it
options.reflection: Keeping to your rhythm brings its own calm, and you did it. Your home and your week feel a little more in order. In the morning, enjoy the clean space for a minute before the day takes over.

options.label: Yes, to avoid something else
options.reflection: Cleaning to escape a harder job is one of the most common dodges there is, and at least your home benefited. Tomorrow, give the task you were avoiding five minutes first thing, before the cloth comes out.

options.label: Yes, it helped me calm down
options.reflection: Using your hands to settle your mind is a good instinct. It sounds like today needed some calming, and you found a way. Tomorrow, see if you can name what stirred you up, even just to yourself.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day without cleaning is still a perfectly good day; your home doesn't need to be spotless for you to rest in it. If a clean is due, pick the day for it now and stop carrying it around in your head.

questions.prompt: What does your breakfast usually look like?

options.label: The same thing most days

insight.reveal: You've solved breakfast, and you're not going back. One less decision in the morning leaves more room for the ones that matter. A few other quiet routines like this probably carry you through busy weeks, too.
insight.research: About a third to almost half of everyday actions are habits, done nearly every day in the same place, often while our thoughts are elsewhere.
insight.step: This week, swap one ingredient in your usual breakfast and see if the morning feels new.

options.label: Tea or coffee, and that's it

insight.reveal: Your morning starts with a warm cup, not a plate. Breakfast is more ritual than meal for you, a few calm minutes before the day begins. Hunger may well arrive all at once by mid-morning, when you'll eat whatever's closest.
insight.step: Tomorrow, add one small thing to your cup, like fruit or bread, and notice how the morning goes.

options.label: Whatever I can grab on the way out

insight.reveal: Your mornings move fast, and food has to keep up. You eat with one hand while sorting the day with the other. That's a real talent for getting going, though breakfast may get eaten without ever really being tasted.
insight.step: Tonight, set out something for tomorrow's breakfast, so the grab is a good one.

options.label: Everyone else eats first; I get what's left

insight.reveal: You feed others before yourself, even first thing in the morning. Making sure everyone has eaten and left on time is probably your job, official or not. It's a big kind of love, and you're allowed a proper plate too.
insight.research: Worldwide, unpaid care work like cooking, cleaning and looking after others is shared very unevenly: women do about three quarters of it.
insight.step: Tomorrow, sit down for five minutes with your own breakfast before you serve anyone else.

followUp.prompt: What did breakfast actually look like this morning?

options.label: A proper breakfast, sitting down
options.reflection: Sitting down to eat in the morning is a small act of care that's easy to skip, and you gave yourself a good start. Think back: did that calm beginning show up anywhere later in your day?

options.label: Something quick, on the run
options.reflection: A breakfast on the run still counts, and you got going. Your mornings are busy, and you're keeping up. Tomorrow, you might slow down for just the first bite or sip, and let that be your moment.

options.label: I fed everyone else and forgot myself
options.reflection: Looking after everyone else first is generous, but you need fuel too; you matter as much as the people you feed. Tomorrow, try setting your own plate down first, even if it's just a piece of bread.

options.label: I skipped it, or barely noticed it
options.reflection: Some mornings breakfast doesn't happen, or happens without anyone noticing. Your day found its own shape. If you'd like tomorrow to start differently, you could choose tonight one simple thing you'll eat.

questions.prompt: You're hungry and there's no plan for dinner. What happens?

options.label: Cook something simple at home

insight.reveal: You can make a meal out of almost nothing. A few eggs, some rice, whatever's left in the cupboard, and you're fine. That calm, practical streak shows up when other plans fall through too: you just start with what's there.
insight.step: This week, cook one dish you've never made, using only what's already in your kitchen.

options.label: Buy something ready on the way

insight.reveal: You value your evening more than the washing up. After a long day, you'd rather spend your energy on rest than on chopping, and that's a fair trade. No doubt you know exactly which nearby place does the best quick meal.
insight.research: People who spend some money to save time, such as paying for help with chores, tend to be more satisfied with life, and this held at every income level.
insight.step: One evening this week, cook something easy instead, and see whether you enjoy the slower evening.

options.label: Go out; I need a change of scene

insight.reveal: Eating out, for you, is as much about the change of air as the food. A new room, other voices and someone else's cooking can reset your whole mood. You're likely the friend who says 'let's just go somewhere,' and it's usually the right call.
insight.step: This week, ask someone you don't see often to join you next time you eat out.

options.label: Look around the kitchen, then just eat bread

insight.reveal: At the end of a long day, bread is the easy answer. By evening, choosing dinner can feel like one question too many, so you take the simplest option. That isn't laziness; it's a full head asking for a break.
insight.research: Self-control was linked more to automatic, routine behaviour than to one-off decisions: people who seem disciplined tend to lean on good habits.
insight.step: Tonight, write down three easy dinners you like and keep the list where you'll see it tomorrow evening.

followUp.prompt: How did dinner come together tonight?

options.label: I cooked something
options.reflection: Cooking for yourself at the end of a day is quietly impressive. You looked after yourself with your own hands. Tomorrow, you could make a little extra, so future you gets a night off.

options.label: I bought it ready-made
options.reflection: Buying dinner is a perfectly good way to look after yourself, and you saved your energy for something else. Tomorrow, notice which you'd rather have more of, time or home cooking, and choose with that in mind.

options.label: I ate out with someone
options.reflection: A meal out with someone feeds more than hunger, and it sounds like your evening had good company in it. A quick message to them tomorrow, about something you talked about, would keep the evening going a little longer.

options.label: It was a blur; I barely noticed
options.reflection: Some evenings dinner just slips past, especially when your head is full. Be gentle with yourself; it's been a long day. Tomorrow, try deciding on dinner by lunchtime, so the evening has one less question in it.

questions.prompt: Someone at the table asks to try some of your food. You…

options.label: Push the plate over: help yourself

insight.reveal: Food tastes better to you when it's shared. You order with the table in mind and enjoy watching someone love a bite of what you chose. Meals with you feel generous and loose, never measured.
insight.research: Tasting the same chocolate at the same moment as another person made good chocolate taste better: sharing an experience tends to make it feel stronger.
insight.step: Next time you eat with someone, order one thing just for sharing.

options.label: Cut them a proper piece myself

insight.reveal: You share, but on your terms, and neatly. You'll hand over the best bite, served properly, rather than watch a fork wander across your plate. That same care likely shows in how you give gifts and lend things.
insight.step: This week, offer someone a taste before they ask, and see how it changes the meal.

options.label: Share, while quietly guarding the best bit

insight.reveal: You're generous, with one small exception. Everyone has a corner of the plate they've been saving, and you're honest enough to admit yours. In the rest of your life, you're probably more open-handed than you think.
insight.step: Next time, give away the best bite on purpose and notice how you feel a minute later.

options.label: Say no: my plate is my plate

insight.reveal: You know what you want, and you ordered it. A friendly no to a small request takes more confidence than most people have. Your other boundaries are likely clear too, and the people close to you always know where they stand.
insight.research: People asking for help underestimated how often others would agree, mostly because they forgot how awkward saying no feels.
insight.step: Next time you say no, add an offer, like 'Shall we get you one?' You keep the no and the warmth.

followUp.prompt: Did you share food with anyone today, or keep it to yourself?

options.label: I shared, and enjoyed it
options.reflection: Sharing food is one of the oldest ways of saying 'you're welcome here,' and you did that today. This week, think of someone who'd love a taste of something you enjoy, and bring them some.

options.label: I shared, but part of me didn't want to
options.reflection: Sharing when part of you didn't want to is still kind, and noticing the mixed feeling is honest. Both are allowed. Tomorrow, give yourself a treat that's just for you, no sharing required.

options.label: I kept it all for myself
options.reflection: Keeping your food for yourself is completely fair; you looked after your own appetite today. Tomorrow, if someone eyes your plate, remember you get to choose freely. Either answer is fine.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: No sharing moments today, and that's alright; meals come and go without much ceremony. If you'd like a warmer one, you could invite someone to eat with you this week, even something simple.

questions.prompt: You open a packet of something tasty. When does it get put away?

options.label: After a handful or two

insight.reveal: A handful, enjoyed, and you're happy to stop. That easy rhythm is rarer than it looks, and it shows elsewhere: one episode, one coffee, then on with the evening. Pleasure doesn't have to be all or nothing for you.
insight.research: Across six studies, short breaks made pleasant experiences more enjoyable afterwards, yet people tended to avoid interrupting the things they enjoy.
insight.step: Next time you open a treat, put some in a bowl and really taste the first bite.

options.label: When it's been passed around

insight.reveal: A packet, to you, is something to pass around. You open snacks with others in mind, and a shared bag gets a room talking. You barely notice how much you had yourself, because the fun was in the sharing.
insight.research: Across 42 studies, people tended to eat more when dining with friends or family than when eating alone, but not when eating with strangers.
insight.step: This week, bring something small to share with people you see every day.

options.label: When it's suddenly empty, somehow

insight.reveal: Your hands are faster than your attention. When you're absorbed in a show, a chat or a task, the packet just melts into the moment. That's often habit and setting at work, not greed, and a sign of how fully you sink into things.
insight.research: Cinema-goers with a strong popcorn habit ate stale popcorn about as much as fresh, but not in a meeting room: habits are set off by places, not just taste.
insight.step: Next time, pour some into a bowl before you sit down, and enjoy every bit of it.

options.label: It's hidden where nobody else will find it

insight.reveal: You keep a little private treat, and that's allowed. In a home where everything gets shared, one hidden packet might be the only thing that's just yours. That says more about how much you give than about how much you take.
insight.step: This week, notice what else you'd like that's just for you, and give yourself one small piece of it.

followUp.prompt: Did any snacks find their way into your day today?

options.label: A few, and I enjoyed them
options.reflection: A snack you actually enjoyed is a small, good moment, and you gave yourself a little pleasure today. Tomorrow, notice which one you liked most and save it for a moment you want to savour.

options.label: I shared some around
options.reflection: Passing food around turns an ordinary moment into a small gathering, and you made someone's day a little brighter. Next time, see who else might enjoy a share of whatever you're having.

options.label: Some, while I was busy with other things
options.reflection: Eating while busy happens to everyone, especially on full days; your attention was simply elsewhere. Tomorrow, try pausing for one bite and really tasting it, just to bring yourself back to the moment.

options.label: It didn't come up today
options.reflection: A day without snacks simply means your day had a different shape, and your meals carried you through. If tomorrow looks long, you might pack something you love, just in case.

questions.prompt: After a really hard day, what do you most want to eat?

options.label: Whatever's there; food is food

insight.reveal: Your mood doesn't rewrite your menu. You eat what's there and save comfort for other things, like a call, a walk or an early night. That steadiness may help hard days pass through you faster than they do for others.
insight.step: Tonight, notice what does comfort you after a hard day, even if it isn't food.

options.label: Something warm and simple

insight.reveal: Warmth is your shortcut back to feeling okay. Soup, tea, porridge, rice: something soft that asks nothing of you. It wouldn't be surprising if you looked after others the same way, with a hot drink before any advice.
insight.step: This week, make a big pot of your favourite warm dish and save some for the next hard day.

options.label: A dish that tastes like home or childhood

insight.reveal: On hard days, you reach for where you came from. A familiar dish can feel like a hand on your shoulder from people who aren't in the room. You carry those people with you more than they know.
insight.research: Nostalgia often comes on when people feel low or lonely, and thinking back to fond memories tended to lift mood and make people feel closer to others.
insight.step: This week, call or message someone who used to make that dish and tell them you still crave it.

options.label: Nothing. My appetite disappears
